Deletion of a managed principal is a guardian or platform-administrator action only. An educator cannot delete one, even one that never received a guardian; orphan cleanup is an administrative task. This starts strict on purpose and is revisited only on evidence.

docs.title: Identifier
docs.text: Principal.identifier is the email when one exists; otherwise a generated handle (human:<principal-id>). It is a lookup key, not an address, and is documented as such. Attaching an email updates it.

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text: The base SpiceDB schema gains guardian and educator relations on principal, with platform permissions (manage_account, manage_credentials, view_profile). Applications add domain permissions (progress, certificates, play limits) through their own facets, as the cross-Forge conventions already prescribe.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• No current consumer changes behavior: with both flags off, a human without an email cannot be created, and the only visible change is that HumanPrincipal.Email is now optional in Go types and claims.
  • Every code path that assumed an email exists is audited and made conditional: social-login linking by verified email, invitations (which target an email and therefore never produce managed principals; managers add them directly), signup, SCIM (userName becomes the identifier; emails is omitted when absent), OIDC userinfo and ID-token email claims, relying-party principal views, and marketplace purchasing (managed principals cannot purchase; billing is a guardian action).
  • Consent records, age handling, and regulatory obligations (COPPA, FERPA, and their non-US equivalents) remain application concerns. SystemForge gives the application a manager with the authority to consent and delete; it does not record the consent itself.
  • A reusable login_token is password-equivalent for the managed principal. The mitigations are structural: managed sessions carry reduced capabilities, the exchange endpoint is rate-limited and reveals nothing on failure, tokens expire, and managers see and can revoke every token and session. Applications that need stronger assurance can request single-use tokens or add device binding.
  • Account was deliberately not used anywhere in this vocabulary: in a multi-tenant platform with marketplace billing it reads as the tenant or the paying relationship, not the person.
  • Released in v0.14.0 together with INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-008, rather than as a separate v0.15.0: nothing was released between them, and the local auth-go replace directive left no earlier commit that could be tagged. The Go-level change to Email is noted in the release notes.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-007 ROADMAP (execution RMIs).
  • ADR-004 (single identity root), ADR-003 (verified email), and docs/authz-conventions.md (facet model the authorization change follows).
  • Affected surfaces: identity/ent/schema/{human,application,credential}.go, a new identity/managedprincipal package, identity/credential, identity/systemauth (login-token exchange, claims, userinfo), identity/{invite,signup,scim,relyingparty}, authz/spicedb_base.go, marketplace (purchaser checks), docs/identity/*.

docs.title: ADR-006: Organization Lifecycle — Signup, Personal and Team Organizations, Slugs
docs.text: Status: Accepted Deciders: @grokify Relates to: ADR-002 (social login creates principals), ADR-004 (the Principal root), ADR-005 (managed principals), ADR-007 (memberships as claims), ADR-008 (resource-scoped collaborators). Updates: docs/design/architecture/organizations.md (lifecycle, slugs, conversion, plans and entitlements).

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
SystemForge already models organizations with a type (personal, team, enterprise), a plan, an owner, memberships with roles, invites, and ownership transfer (identity/organization, identity/invite). The identity/signup package creates a principal together with a personal organization. What is missing is the lifecycle around them:

  • Social login does not sign up. SystemAuth's GitHub and Google login (ADR-002) creates a bare principal and never calls signup, so a person's first sign-in leaves them in no organization. Every application then needs an operator step before the person can do anything.
  • Slugs have no rules. Update can change a slug freely; nothing remembers a freed slug, so a rename can be followed at once by someone else taking the old name, and links to the old slug break.
  • A personal organization cannot become a team. When a solo user wants members, their only path is a new organization and moving everything.
  • Personal organizations do not refuse members. The type exists but nothing enforces what makes it personal.

The model to follow is GitHub's: a person always has a personal account (here, a personal organization) and belongs to zero or more organizations. The person's handle is theirs; organizations have their own names in the same namespace.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. A first login is a signup. SystemAuth's social login calls signup.SignupOrGetExisting for a principal it has not seen: the principal and its personal organization are created in one transaction, with the principal as owner. A later login resolves to the existing principal by provider identity first, then by verified email (ADR-002).
  2. The personal slug comes from how the person arrived:
  3. GitHub login: the GitHub username;
  4. Google login: the local part of the email address (before @);
  5. a managed principal (ADR-005): a name its manager enters, or a generated slug that reveals nothing about the person (for example two words and a number);
  6. on collision, a numeric suffix.
  7. A personal organization has exactly one member: its owner. AddMember and invites to a personal organization are refused, except for collaborators (ADR-008). TransferOwnership of a personal organization is refused; it is the person's own.
  8. Personal and team organizations share one slug namespace, and the person always keeps their handle:
  9. a personal organization's slug is the person's handle and stays with the person;
  10. to give a handle to an organization, the person first renames their personal organization, then the organization takes the freed slug.
  11. Every slug change frees the old slug into a 7-day cooling-off period, whether a personal or team organization is renamed. During those 7 days only the principal that gave the slug up, or an organization that principal owns, may take it. After 7 days it is free for anyone. The same rule applies in every direction: person to organization, organization to person, organization to organization, and a person who changes their mind reclaims their handle.
  12. A freed slug resolves to its previous organization as an alias for the cooling-off period, so existing links keep working, until it is reassigned or the period ends. Slug lookups consult aliases after exact matches.
  13. A personal organization can be converted to a team organization in one transaction:
  14. the organization keeps its ID, data, plan and memberships, and its type becomes team; its owner becomes the team's first owner;
  15. it takes a new slug chosen at conversion, which must be free (the person can hand over their handle by renaming first, under 5);
  16. a new personal organization is created for the person, with their handle.
  17. Plans are independent of type, and pricing and packaging are the application's. A personal organization can hold any plan, subscription or license a team organization can. SystemForge provides pricing and packaging through marketplace (listings with tiers, subscriptions, licenses with seats, Stripe billing) and does not fix the policy:
  18. plans move in either direction: free to paid, paid to free, and between tiers, with downgrades and cancellations taking effect at the period end where the application wants that;
  19. packaging is per product or bundle, so an organization may be on a free tier of product A and a paid tier of A+B, as with Zoom's products;
  20. freemium or not, and trials with a configurable length (30 days by default) that convert or lapse, are the application's choices, expressed as listings and tiers;
  21. an organization's entitlements (ADR-007 apps) derive from its active subscriptions and licenses per listing, not from one organization-wide plan. The plan column on sf_organizations is removed: it was a placeholder from before the marketplace, set at creation and never consulted, and a single value cannot describe an organization holding several subscriptions. A plan's human-friendly name lives on its marketplace listing, resolved through the subscription, never copied onto the organization.

docs.title: Schema
docs.text:
• sf_slug_reservations (slug, released_by_principal_id, released_from_organization_id, released_at, expires_at): one row per freed slug, deleted when reassigned or expired. SlugAvailable and GetBySlug read it.
  • No change to sf_organizations; org_type and slug already exist.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
• organization.Service gains Rename(ctx, orgID, slug), ConvertToTeam(ctx, orgID, teamSlug) and ResolveSlug(ctx, slug) (exact or alias).
  • signup gains SlugForLogin(provider, providerLogin, email) so SystemAuth and other callers derive the personal slug the same way.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A new person has a working organization after one login, with no operator involved. Applications that read memberships from SystemAuth (ADR-007) can provision themselves for it on first use.
  • Renames are safe and reversible for a week, and old links keep working for that week.
  • Going from solo to team keeps the organization's ID, so applications keyed by organization ID see no change; only the type and slug change.
  • AddMember and TransferOwnership gain a type check; existing tests that add members to personal organizations must use team organizations.
  • Entitlement is per listing, not per organization. Applications read what an organization may use from its subscriptions and licenses. The Plan field leaves the organization API's create, update, list filter and responses (and SCIM's default), replaced by an entitlements summary derived from the marketplace; the organization.Plan* constants go with it.
  • Slug derivation lives in one place, so every login provider and the managed-principal flow produce the same shape of handle.

docs.title: ADR-007: Organization Memberships and Entitlements as Claims
docs.text: Status: Accepted. Amended by ADR-010: decision 9 (freshness and revocation) is superseded by real-time invalidation. Deciders: @grokify Relates to: ADR-002 (relying parties federate to SystemAuth), ADR-006 (organization lifecycle), ADR-008 (resource-scoped collaborators), INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-005 (relying-party contract). Updates: docs/design/architecture/organizations.md (memberships, application roles, claims).

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
SystemForge intends SystemAuth to be the source of truth for organization memberships, roles and entitlements. The relying-party package says so (identity/relyingparty/memberships.go): a MembershipSource may read them from claims, "until SystemAuth emits them, the default source reads an app-local table".

SystemAuth does not emit them yet, so every application keeps its own membership table, fed by operators or by its own invite flow. In a deployment of several applications behind one SystemAuth, the same organization has to be created in each application, and a person has to be added to each, separately. Removing someone from an organization in one application does not remove them from another.

The marketplace already records what an organization is entitled to (subscriptions, licenses, seats), and authz.FeatureAuthorizer can answer feature questions, but applications cannot learn an organization's entitlements from a login either.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Access has three layers, and the claims carry the first two.
  2. Organization role (owner, admin, member, collaborator from ADR-008): governs the organization itself, its members, billing and settings.
  3. Application role, per application the organization is entitled to: one of the roles the application declares in its authz.AppVocabulary (the standard ladder is viewer, contributor, maintainer, admin; an application may declare more). It governs what the principal may do inside that application. Where the application is seat-licensed, holding an application role consumes a seat.
  4. Resource grants (ADR-008) are the application's to look up; they are not claims.

SystemAuth emits the principal's organizations in the ID token and at the userinfo endpoint as an orgs claim: a list of objects with id, slug, name, type (personal, team, enterprise), role (the organization role) and apps, a map from application identifier to the principal's application role there. An application absent from apps is one the principal may not open. 2. Owners hold admin in every entitled application, implicitly, so no application can become unadministrable. Admins do not: an admin manages the organization (members, invites, application roles, settings) and holds only the application roles assigned to them, like a member. An admin may assign application roles to themselves; the assignment is explicit and audited, which is the point. Members hold only the application roles assigned to them. Collaborators hold none; their access is by resource grant. 3. Members and admins get no application access by default. Adding or inviting one requires choosing an application role for at least one entitled application; applications left unselected stay closed to that person. Roles are changed per application without touching the membership, and removal from the organization removes every application role and grant. 4. Custom roles are not supported. The roles available in an application are the ones its vocabulary declares. Organization-defined roles (permission bundles) and teams (groups that carry application roles) are deferred; if assigning roles one person at a time becomes the problem, teams are the first addition. 5. JWT access tokens carry a compact form: orgs as a list of {id, role, apps} with apps as a map of application identifier to role, and no slug or name, to keep the token small. Applications that need slug, name or entitlements read them from the ID token, userinfo, or the memberships endpoint. 6. Large membership lists are truncated, not dropped. A token carries at most 50 organizations, ordered personal first, then by most recent membership, and sets orgs_truncated: true when it omitted any. GET /userinfo/memberships returns the full, paginated list for the presenting token's principal. 7. The relying-party package reads memberships from claims by default. relyingparty gains ClaimsMemberships (from the ID token or userinfo) and RemoteMemberships (from the memberships endpoint, used when orgs_truncated is set or the compact access-token form is all the application has). LocalMemberships remains for development and tests and is documented as not for production. 8. Entitlements come from the marketplace. The applications an organization may assign roles in are derived from its active subscriptions and licenses, mapped to application identifiers registered through authz.AppVocabulary. A deployment may declare applications every organization is entitled to by default. Application roles are stored per (principal, organization, application) in a new sf_app_roles table, which replaces seat assignments as the record of who may use what; a seat-licensed application counts its rows against the license. 9. Freshness is bounded by token lifetime, and removals revoke. Removing a principal from an organization, or changing their role, revokes the principal's refresh tokens, so the next refresh carries the new memberships; access-token lifetime bounds how long the old ones are honored. Applications must handle a membership that disappears between requests. 10. Applications stop keeping membership and role tables. An application keys its data by the SystemAuth organization ID, reads the principal's application role from the claims, and provisions itself for an organization on first use by a principal holding a role in it; it does not store who the members are or what their roles are.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One invite carries the person's application roles, chosen by the inviter per application, and one removal takes every role away. Nobody gets into an application by being a member alone.
  • Applications need no organization, membership or role tables, only an organization ID on their own records and a mapping from their vocabulary roles to permissions.
  • Invitation and member-management screens become role pickers: the entitled applications, each with its ladder, none selected by default.
  • Token size is bounded by the 50-organization cap; applications with users in more organizations than that must use the memberships endpoint.
  • SystemAuth is on the path of every organization decision. Relying parties cache memberships for the token lifetime and must tolerate the endpoint being unavailable (serve from the last token).
  • The marketplace becomes the entitlement source, so an application that is free for everyone must still be registered as a default entitlement, or every organization is refused.

docs.title: ADR-008: Resource-Scoped Collaborators on the Authorization Substrate
docs.text: Status: Accepted Deciders: @grokify Relates to: ADR-006 (personal organizations have collaborators, not members), ADR-007 (memberships as claims), INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-001 (base authorization schema), docs/authz-conventions.md (the cross-application authorization contract). Updates: docs/design/architecture/authorization.md (modes, collaborators, resource roles).

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
SystemForge authorization is a two-gate model (docs/authz-conventions.md): the principal's organization role must grant an operation's permission, and the presenting credential's scopes must include it. Applications register an authz.AppVocabulary with their roles, permissions, scopes and a SpiceDB schema fragment whose {app}_-prefixed definitions attach to the shared organization through an {app}_org facet. Two providers exist: simple (role hierarchy) and spicedb (ReBAC), with Ent hooks syncing organizations, members and licenses into relationships.

Every grant is organization-wide: a member sees the whole organization. There is no way to give someone access to one resource — a project, a document, a site — without making them a member of the organization. That is what solo users need for contractors (ADR-006 gives personal organizations no members), and what teams need for outside reviewers. GitHub's outside collaborators are the model: access to a repository, not to the organization.

Applications could each build this themselves, as they built their own membership tables. The substrate already has the pieces (relationships, vocabularies, lookups), so the pattern should be defined once.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. The base schema gains a collaborator relation on organization. A collaborator is a principal with a membership of role collaborator. They have no permission on the organization itself: view, edit and manage exclude them. They gain only list, a new permission (list = manage + member + viewer + collaborator) that lets an application show the organization in the person's organization switcher. Personal organizations accept collaborator memberships (the one exception in ADR-006).
  2. Applications declare which resource types accept collaborators in their SpiceDB fragment, using a standard ladder of resource roles:
  3. viewer: read the resource;
  4. contributor: also change it and create items within it;
  5. maintainer: also manage its settings and its collaborators.

A fragment looks like:

definition myapp_project {
    relation org: organization
    relation viewer: principal
    relation contributor: principal
    relation maintainer: principal

    permission view   = viewer + contributor + maintainer + org->view
    permission edit   = contributor + maintainer + org->edit
    permission manage = maintainer + org->manage
}

Organization members keep their organization-wide access through the org facet; collaborators have only their direct relations. The ladder's names are reserved in authz-conventions.md so every application means the same thing by them. 3. Grants are a substrate operation, supported by both providers. authz gains GrantResourceRole(ctx, principal, resource, role), RevokeResourceRole and ListResourceGrants. The rebac engine writes relationships; the rbac provider stores grants in a new sf_resource_grants table (principal, organization, resource type, resource ID, role) and consults it in its checks. Granting to a principal who is not a member of the resource's organization adds a collaborator membership; revoking the last grant removes it. 4. Applications filter by lookup, not by trust. Authorizer gains ListResources(ctx, principal, resourceType, permission) (SpiceDB LookupResources; an indexed query in rbac). An application uses the result to constrain queries and row-level security to the resources a collaborator may see, in addition to checking each request. The scope gate still applies: a collaborator's credential must carry the operation's scope. 5. Invites can target a resource. sf_invites gains optional resource type, resource ID and resource role. Accepting such an invite creates the collaborator membership and the grant in one transaction. 6. Collaborators appear in claims. The orgs claim (ADR-007) lists a collaborator's organizations with role collaborator; the resources they may access are the application's to look up, not a claim. 7. Agents and managed principals are granted the same way. A grant to an agent principal confines it to those resources; an application's agent-facing scopes (for example per-resource AAuth scopes) are checked against the same relationships.

docs.title: Naming the providers by what they do
docs.text:
The modes are named for the model they evaluate, not the technology:

  • role-based (rbac): roles, plus direct grants on resources. The package is authz/rbac (formerly authz/simple).
  • relationship-based (rebac): permissions derived through relationships, evaluated by an engine. SpiceDB is the engine today, as authz/rebac/spicedb (formerly authz/spicedb); another engine, for example OpenFGA, would sit beside it under the same mode without changing an application's configuration vocabulary.

An application configures authz.mode: rbac | rebac, and for rebac an engine. The same names are used in configuration, documentation, the architecture pages and the vocabulary registry. The packages were renamed before this ADR is implemented, so the grants, lookups and tests it adds land under the mode names once; the old paths forward to the new ones as deprecated packages for one release. "Coarse-grained" and "fine-grained" are not used: after this ADR both modes grant per resource, and the relationship engines market themselves as fine-grained, so the pair would mislead in both directions.

docs.title: Choosing a mode
docs.text:
Both modes implement the same platform contract — organization roles, application roles (ADR-007), resource grants, ListResources — with the same semantics, verified by the shared providertest suite. An application written to the contract switches from rbac to rebac by configuration; its relationships are rebuilt from the membership, role and grant tables. The cost of rebac is operational (a service with its own datastore, schema management, relationship sync), not a function of whether the application is paid.

Use rbac while Switch to rebac when Access is organization roles, application roles and direct grants on resources Permissions flow through relationships: nested groups or teams, folder-style hierarchies, "shared with me" graphs One level of inheritance (organization → resource) is enough Resources inherit from parents more than one level deep ListResources over an organization's resources is a SQL query Lookups span very large organizations or need SpiceDB's consistency tokens One deployment, one process Several services or regions share one authorization graph

In terms of what each provider can answer:

Question rbac today rbac with this ADR rebac Does the principal's organization or application role grant this action? yes yes yes Does the principal own this resource? yes yes yes Does the principal hold a direct grant on this specific resource? no yes, from the grants table yes Does a permission reach the principal through relationships (team membership, a parent resource, a share with a group)? no no yes, through the schema fragment

The grants this ADR adds to rbac are one hop: principal, role, resource. That is enough for collaborators. What rebac adds beyond the contract is the application's schema fragment: relations and inheritance rbac cannot express. An application that needs them declares its fragment and switches; until then it declares none and the contract is all it uses.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One collaborator model for every application, administrable in the IAM console from the registered vocabularies, instead of a per-application sharing feature.
  • Applications must filter aggregates and cross-resource references for collaborators (counts, dependency views), since a collaborator may hold grants on some resources of an organization and not others. The substrate supplies the permitted set; the filtering is the application's.
  • The schema parity test and authz-conventions.md change: the base schema gains collaborator and list, and the resource-role ladder is added to the conventions.
  • The rbac provider grows a table and indexed queries over it; providertest keeps it in step with rebac on the contract, so choosing it is not a dead end.
  • Moving a resource between organizations, if an application supports it, must move its grants and the collaborator memberships they imply.

docs.title: ADR-009: Management Is a Relationship, Not the Absence of an Email
docs.text: Status: Accepted Deciders: @grokify Relates to: ADR-005 (managed principals; this ADR amends its definition and its invariant 4), ADR-003 (verified email), ADR-006 (organization lifecycle: slugs for managed principals). Updates: docs/design/architecture/managed-principals.md.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR-005 introduced managed principals for humans who cannot hold an email or their own credentials, with the motivating case of young children in a learning application. It defined the state by the email:

  • a managed principal is "a Principal(type=human) whose Human.email is null";
  • a managed principal that later attaches a verified email "is an ordinary human", after which its managers may be removed;
  • managedprincipal.IsManaged tests Human.email IS NULL.

Two consumer cases do not fit that definition:

  • Children who have an email. Many elementary-school students have a school-issued address. They still need a guardian or educator in control of their account: creating it, issuing sign-in, seeing activity, revoking and deleting. Under ADR-005 such a child cannot be created as managed at all, because the email makes them "ordinary".
  • Adults whose account is managed by arrangement. A matchmaking application in which a family member manages a profile on an adult's behalf, with that adult's agreement. The adult has an email and may sign in themselves, and the manager's authority comes from the relationship they both accept, not from an email gap.

In both, the email and the relationship are independent facts. The email answers "can this person be contacted and verified"; the relationship answers "who may act for this person". ADR-005 conflated them because its first consumer had neither.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. A managed principal is a human with at least one active manager relationship. Management is derived from the relationships, not from the email. While managed, CanManageProfile and CanDelegate are false, as ADR-005 specifies.
  2. Email is independent of management. A managed principal may have an email (attached at creation or later, verified per ADR-003) and keep its managers. Attaching an email changes nothing about management.
  3. Email still decides whether management may end. ADR-005's invariant 1 stands: a human without an email must have a manager at all times. The last manager of a principal can be removed only when the principal has a verified email; that removal releases the principal, which becomes self-managed. This is the only rule in which email matters.
  4. A managed principal may hold its own credentials when a manager allows it: a password, a social login linked to its email, or login tokens. The manager role's authority (consent, deletion, credential revocation, session revocation) is unchanged by the principal signing in itself.
  5. A self-managed human may enter management by consent. A manager relationship with an existing self-managed principal is created only by that principal accepting a manager invitation, since it gives up control of its own profile. Creation by a manager (ADR-005) remains the path for principals the manager creates.
  6. Managers are unchanged: an active human with a verified email that is not itself managed.
  7. What a managed principal may do for itself is the application's decision, expressed in its authorization vocabulary: a learning application may let a child do nothing to the account; a matchmaking application may let the adult read and the manager edit, or the reverse. The platform supplies the relationship, the roles, and the managed claim; it does not fix the split.

docs.title: Changes to the implementation
docs.text:
• IsManaged answers from active manager relationships; ErrNotManaged means "has no active manager", not "has an email".
  • ErrLastManager keeps its meaning (the last manager of a principal without a verified email cannot be removed) and its wording changes to say so.
  • Creating a managed principal accepts an optional email, verified like any other (ADR-003) before it counts for release.
  • A release operation removes the last manager of a principal with a verified email and clears the managed state in the same transaction.
  • Manager invitations to existing principals: a new invite kind carrying the manager role, accepted by the signed-in principal.
  • The managed session claim is derived from relationships.
  • Slugs for managed principals (ADR-006) keep the manager-entered or generated form whether or not an email exists; an email's local part is not used for a managed principal, so a manager never exposes a child's address through a handle.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Students with school email addresses are supported, and a child's account need not lose its guardian when the school issues an address.
  • Adults can be managed by arrangement, with their consent recorded as the accepted invitation.
  • Release is an explicit event, auditable, instead of a side effect of attaching an email.
  • Code that used the email as a proxy for management must change: IsManaged, the managed claim, and any application that inferred management from a missing email.
  • No change for ADR-005's original consumer: a child created without an email behaves exactly as before.

docs.title: ADR-010: Real-Time Invalidation of Access on Membership Change
docs.text: Status: Accepted Deciders: @grokify Relates to: ADR-007 (memberships and entitlements as claims; this ADR amends its decision 9), ADR-002 (relying parties), ADR-008 (collaborators, whose grants change the same way). Updates: docs/design/architecture/organizations.md (freshness of claims), docs/design/architecture/authorization.md (revocation cache).

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR-007 puts a principal's organizations and application roles into the access token as claims. A relying party verifies the token's signature and reads the claims; it does not ask SystemAuth anything per request. That is what makes claims cheap, and it has a cost: a change to the principal's access is not seen until the token expires and the client refreshes.

Removing someone from an organization at 10:00 leaves a token issued at 09:58 with a fifteen-minute lifetime valid until 10:13. ADR-007 bounds the window with short lifetimes and revokes the refresh token at removal, so the next refresh is refused, but it cannot close the window. For routine offboarding that is tolerable. For a contractor cut off during a dispute, a compromised account, or an agent whose mission was revoked, it is not.

The alternatives:

  • Opaque tokens checked by introspection on every request. Immediate, but every request to every product becomes a round-trip to SystemAuth. It does not scale with the suite, and it reintroduces the network hop the claims model removed.
  • Even shorter lifetimes. Shrinks the window; never closes it.
  • A revocation signal with a small cache. SystemAuth announces access changes; relying parties remember them only for as long as an affected token could still exist. Per-request cost is a map lookup, and the memory is bounded by the number of changes within one token lifetime.

The modular monolith (pbhq-cloud ADR-001) makes the signal almost free for the suite: SystemAuth and the products share a process, so the announcement is a function call.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Access tokens stay self-contained JWTs with short lifetimes. The default lifetime is 10 minutes, configurable per deployment up to 15. Lifetime is the fallback bound; it is not the mechanism.
  2. SystemAuth records and announces every access change. An access change is any event after which a principal's existing tokens may claim more than the principal now has:
  3. removal from an organization, or a change of organization role;
  4. change or removal of an application role (ADR-007), or of a resource grant that reduces access (ADR-008);
  5. deactivation of the principal, or revocation of its sessions;
  6. a managed principal's manager revoking its sessions (ADR-005).

Each change is stored as (principal_id, organization_id or null, changed_at, reason) in sf_access_changes, and announced. 3. Relying parties keep a revocation cache keyed by principal. On an announcement they store principal_id → changed_at (per organization when the change is organization-scoped). On every request they accept a token only if its iat is at or after changed_at plus a clock-skew margin for its principal (and organization); a token stamped within the margin is treated as issued before the change. Otherwise they answer 401 with the standard "token expired" error, which makes the client refresh. Entries are dropped once changed_at plus the maximum access-token lifetime plus the margin has passed: after that, no token issued before the change can be accepted by any verifier, however its clock drifts. The margin defaults to 30 seconds and is configurable; 15 seconds is the floor, enough where clocks are NTP-disciplined, and the margin is moot in-process, where both timestamps come from one clock. The cache is therefore bounded by the number of changes within one lifetime. 4. The cache is shared memory in the monolith; delivery exists only at process boundaries. - Same process: in a modular monolith (pbhq-cloud) SystemAuth and the relying parties share one cache instance. SystemAuth writes to it in the transaction that records the change, and every product reads it on each request. There is no delivery and no delay; the check is a lookup in the same memory. - Replicas of the same monolith: instances behind a load balancer share the database, not memory. Each instance polls sf_access_changes for rows newer than its last read, every second or two: one indexed query per instance per interval, independent of request volume. The change is visible on every replica within the polling interval. - Separate deployments: a relying party in another process receives a signed event, an OIDC Back-Channel Logout token carrying an access_change event with the same fields, at a registered endpoint. Delivery is retried, and failures are logged against the client.

The relyingparty package implements the cache, the poller and the back-channel receiver, so an application adds one line of configuration for whichever boundary it sits on. 5. A refresh after a change issues new claims rather than ending the session. ADR-007's decision 9 ("removals revoke refresh tokens") is amended: a change of role or membership does not log the person out of every organization; their next refresh carries the reduced claims. Only deactivation and explicit session revocation revoke refresh tokens. 6. Relying parties recover a lost cache by replay. After a restart, a relying party calls GET /access-changes?since=<now − max lifetime> and rebuilds the cache before serving. Until the call succeeds it treats every token as suspect and refreshes claims from the memberships endpoint on first use, so a restart never widens the window. 7. Agent tokens are out of scope. AAuth tokens carry their own revocation (cascading, keyed by jti); a mission revocation reaches resources through that path. This ADR covers SystemAuth-issued tokens.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Access changes take effect within one request in the same process; within the polling interval on other replicas; within the back-channel delivery time for separate deployments; and within one token lifetime if a signal is lost, which is the bound ADR-007 already had.
  • Per-request cost is a map lookup, and the cache holds only the changes of the last lifetime: tens of entries for a large deployment, not one per user.
  • SystemAuth gains a table, an announcement in the membership and role transactions, a replay endpoint, and back-channel delivery with retry.
  • Relying parties gain the cache, the receivers and the replay call, all in the relyingparty package. Applications that bypass it must implement the same check.
  • A role change no longer logs the person out. Products must handle claims that shrink between requests without a new login.
  • The token lifetime is a visible setting, not an assumption. The architecture pages state the default and the maximum.

docs.title: ADR-011: Lifecycle States, Data Classification and Privacy Rights
docs.text: Status: Proposed Deciders: @grokify Relates to: ADR-005 and ADR-009 (managed principals; this ADR amends the release decision of ADR-009), ADR-006 (organization lifecycle), ADR-010 (access changes), ADR-012 (enforcement and the semantics of a hold). Updates: docs/design/architecture/managed-principals.md, docs/design/architecture/organizations.md, a new docs/design/architecture/data-governance.md.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
SystemForge holds personal data for every product built on it, and several decisions so far assumed an account either exists or is "deactivated". Four needs do not fit that:

  • Hiding without destroying. An account that should disappear from customer-facing applications, such as a departed member or a closed profile, while staff can still see it and restore it.
  • Deleting without breaking references. Principals are referenced by memberships, audit records, work items and grants. Deleting the row would either cascade through those or fail on foreign keys.
  • Privacy rights. GDPR and similar regimes give a data subject access, portability, rectification, restriction and erasure. These are cross-cutting: every product stores data about the same person. They belong in the platform layer so each product does not reimplement them, and so there is one place that knows which columns hold personal data.
  • Dead and unwanted accounts at scale. A free tier accumulates accounts that were abandoned and accounts created by spammers. Soft deleting every one and keeping a tombstone is the wrong answer for spam, which should leave no personal data and no row behind, and abandoned accounts should not be kept indefinitely, which the storage-limitation principle also requires. Versioned entities, whose history grows with every edit, add unbounded growth of their own.

Managed principals add a related question. ADR-009 says releasing a principal removes its managers at once. In practice the end of a management arrangement is a process: the manager may need to finish handover, and the record of the arrangement should be editable and, like a release object on a code host, correctable or removable before it is final.

docs.title: Lifecycle states
docs.text:
1. A principal and an organization have a lifecycle state: provisional, active, archived or deleted. Transitions: provisional → active (graduation, decision 19), active ⇄ archived, and active or archived → deleted. Deleted is terminal. A subject may also be purged (decision 20), which removes it and is not a state it stays in.
  2. Archived is reversible and means "not for customers to see":
  3. it is excluded from listings, search, mentions and pickers in customer-facing applications;
  4. platform administrators and the owners' admin tooling can still list, read and restore it;
  5. it cannot sign in at all, so that "archived" has one clear meaning, and its sessions are revoked when it is archived (an access change, ADR-010); an archived organization's members lose access to it through their claims; data export for an archived subject is performed by an administrator;
  6. memberships, grants and history are preserved.
  7. Deleted is a soft delete. The row stays so references hold, and every column classified as personal data (below) is erased according to its erasure strategy. The identifier is replaced by a non-reversible tombstone, credentials, external identities, sessions, consents and claims are removed, and memberships and relationships are deactivated. Deletion of personal data is irreversible; the tombstone is not.
  8. The delete transition never removes the row. deleted keeps a tombstone so references hold. Removing rows is a separate operation, purge (decision 20), allowed only where nothing depends on them and nothing forbids it. An application that must remove tombstoned rows after a retention period does so through the platform's purge, not its own job.
  9. Transitions require authority and are recorded: an actor with the account-management permission (or a platform administrator), an access-change reason for each transition (ADR-010), and an audit record that holds no personal data.

docs.title: Data classification
docs.text:
1. Every persisted field is classified, on two independent axes.
  2. Visibility is public or internal. public may be shown to application users, subject to the application's own authorization. internal is system data not shown to application users: flags, counters, security stamps, internal references and operational state.
  3. Tags, each on or off: pii (personal data about an identifiable person) and secret (credentials, tokens, keys, anything whose disclosure grants access). The axes are independent: a display name is public and pii; a login record's IP address is internal and pii; a password hash is internal and secret. One rule ties them: secret implies internal, and validation rejects a secret field marked public. Visibility is never defaulted: an unclassified field is an error, not a public one. A field also carries optional attributes: an erasure strategy (clear, tombstone, hash, delete_row, shred or retain with a stated reason) and an export flag. An entity carries the subject key (how a row maps to a data subject), whether it is in privacy scope, whether it can be placed under hold, whether it is versioned, and a retention note.
  4. The model is a separate, generic module, and the classification is metadata in Go next to the schema. The catalog model, its validation and its audience filtering live in github.com/grokify/datacatalog, a public, dependency-free module that other tools (a query guard such as guardsql, documentation generators, a future management application) consume without depending on SystemForge or on an ORM. SystemForge adds the pieces that are specific to it: Ent annotations on each field of its own schemas, collected into a catalog by a small dataclass package, and the orchestration of export, erasure and holds. Applications annotate their own entities the same way and register them. A test fails when a field has no classification, so a new column cannot ship unclassified.
  5. The catalog is the single source for governance tooling. It drives export and erasure (below), log redaction, response filtering (a serialization helper omits every internal field unless the caller asks for a staff or system view), and query gating: a query guard such as guardsql blocks internal and secret columns for customer queries always, and pii columns unless the profile allows them. The guard adopts the catalog's own predicate, so there is one definition of what a customer query may touch.

docs.title: Privacy rights
docs.text:
1. SystemForge provides the operations; applications decide policy.
  2. Access and portability: Export(subject) returns the subject's records from every registered entity where export is set, in a structured, machine-readable form.
  3. Erasure: Erase(subject) is the delete transition above, applied to the subject's rows in every registered entity per their strategies, reporting which entities were erased and which retained rows (with the retention reason).
  4. Restriction: archiving a subject, plus a flag that processing is restricted for the applications that need to honor it.
  5. Rectification: ordinary edits.
  6. Erasure is orchestrated, not assumed. Products store their own data; each registers an eraser for its entities (or relies on annotations for simple cases). Erase runs them, records per-entity results without personal data, and can be resumed after a partial failure.
  7. Retention is a policy input, not a platform constant. SystemForge records retention per field and per entity (decision 24) and runs the purge, dormancy and offload operations below, but does not fix periods: they follow the product's tier and packaging, which the application configures.
  8. Erasure can be held. A subject may be covered by one or more legal holds (ADR-012). While any hold covers it, Erase, the delete transition, purge and edits to pii fields refuse with ErrHeld, and archive remains available. Holds are placed and released by a legal manager, not by a platform administrator acting alone. ADR-012 defines holds, what they preserve, and how they are enforced. SystemForge models the hold and its custodians; legal case management stays outside it.
  9. The audit log is exportable. Lifecycle transitions, erasure results and hold changes are recorded without personal data, and an administrator can export them (by organization and time range), so a customer can evidence what was erased, when and under whose authority. This is independent of the hold: the export serves accountability, the hold serves refusal.
  10. Managed principals are covered. A managed subject's request is made by an authorized manager, and the audit record names that manager's authority; once released, the principal acts for itself.
  11. A request is verified before it is honored. Verification of the requester's identity is the application's responsibility; SystemForge exposes the operations behind the authorization checks of decision 5.

docs.title: Release of a managed principal (amends ADR-009, decision 3)
docs.text:
1. Release is a record with a state, not an instant. Releasing a principal creates a release record in state open. While it is open:
    • the principal is self-managed: it may act for itself, and the managers' authority over it is suspended (managed is false);
    • the manager relationships are retained, dormant, so a mistaken release can be reversed;
    • the record may be edited (for example its note and effective details) and may be deleted, which restores the management arrangement.
  2. Closing a release is the formal end of management. Closing removes the manager relationships and cannot be undone by a manager. After a release is closed only a platform administrator may change or reopen it.
  3. ADR-009's other rules stand: a principal without a verified email must have a manager, so release still requires a verified email, and email remains independent of management.

docs.title: Dead accounts, purge and storage tiering
docs.text:
1. An account that has not proven itself is provisional. A principal created by a signup that has not yet verified an email or taken a first meaningful action is provisional. A deployment sets the graduation criterion and a short time to live. A provisional account that does not graduate within it is purged (decision 20), with no tombstone. Spam that never graduates therefore never becomes an identity record that other records reference. A deployment may further restrict what a provisional account can do (for example, it holds no roles and is not referenced as an author), so that graduation is the point at which other records begin to depend on it.
  2. purge removes a subject's rows when everything that depends on them can also be removed. It differs from deleted in that no row, and no personal data, remains. A subject is purgeable when every record that references it, directly or transitively, is itself purgeable: it belongs to the same subject, is declared cascade (below), and is not covered by a hold. Otherwise the purge is refused with a dependency report and the caller may fall back to the ordinary delete, which keeps a tombstone. The report names the entity, the count and the reason for each blocker and never the contents of another subject's rows.

  3. Relationships carry a purge disposition in the catalog. Each edge between registered entities is declared:

    Disposition Meaning Example cascade The dependent is owned by the subject and is purged with it Sessions, API keys, preferences, memberships of the subject's personal organization detach The dependent stays and its reference is cleared or replaced by a placeholder A comment authored in another organization's workspace restrict The dependent blocks the purge Billing records, a membership in an organization that still exists, another subject's data

    An edge without a disposition is an error at registration, as an unclassified field is. Where a deployment's product has content shared with other subjects, which of restrict and detach applies is the product's decision. 22. Purge is orchestrated by the platform, not by database cascades. Executing a purge marks the subject purging, which the enforcement hook (ADR-012) uses to refuse new dependent writes, then removes dependents leaf first in batches that can be resumed, and finally the subject. Foreign keys on registered entities stay RESTRICT, as a safety net that makes an undeclared dependency fail loudly. Every step runs through the same hook, so hold checks, before-images and audit apply; the audit record carries counts and no personal data. A versioned entity's before-images are part of the closure and are purged with it unless a hold covers the subject. 23. Purge leaves an abuse fingerprint, not personal data. So a purged account is not simply recreated, the platform may retain a keyed hash of the verified email (and, if the deployment chooses, network indicators) under a key managed as ADR-013 decides. The fingerprint cannot be reversed, is classified in the catalog, has its own retention period, and is used only to block re-registration and to measure abuse. The lawful basis and the period are the deployment's decision and need review for its jurisdictions. 24. Dormant accounts follow a ladder, and retention is structured. - An account records when it was last active, updated at most once a day so activity does not become a write on every request. - A deployment sets, per tier, a dormancy period after which the owner is notified, then the account is archived (decision 2), then deleted after a further period, and purged where decision 20 allows. - Accounts with active billing, a covering hold, or the sole ownership of an organization that has other members are excluded until that is resolved. - The notice tells the owner how to keep the account: signing in before archive resets the period, and an archived account is restored on request. - Retention in the catalog is structured as keep (a duration) and then (purge or offload), per entity, with the periods supplied by configuration (decision 11). 25. Archive in storage terms is "offload", and it is a separate tier. archived (decision 2) is a visibility state and stays in the database. Moving rows out of the primary database is offload, defined as: - Data eligible for offload is historical and cold: tombstones past their period, before-images of versioned entities, snapshots whose holds were released, and old audit records. - Offloaded rows are written to the snapshot store (ADR-012, decision 13), a database table set or an S3-compatible object store with Parquet files, with a manifest recording the catalog version, row counts and digest, and a stub left where a reference requires one. - Before-image and audit storage is partitioned by time from the first version, so that cold partitions can be detached, exported and purged without rewriting live tables. Hot queries use partial indexes and default scopes that exclude archived and deleted rows. - Offload is not destruction, so it is allowed under a hold, but it is a custody change and is audited. Offloaded data stays reachable by subject for export, erasure and hold: encryption under per-subject keys (ADR-013) lets erasure destroy a subject's key and cover the offloaded copy without rewriting files. - Purge is the only deletion. It is explicit, retention-driven and hold-aware.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Accounts can be hidden without losing history, and an administrator can restore them.
  • Deletion never breaks references, and the personal data in a deleted row is gone by construction rather than by convention.
  • One registry answers "where do we keep personal data?" for the platform and for every product built on it, and CI keeps it complete.
  • Products take on work: annotate their entities and register erasers. The cost is small for simple tables and explicit for the rest.
  • Release becomes reversible until it is closed. The cost is a second state and a dormant-relationship rule that every authority check must honor, including the managed claim.
  • ADR-009's "release removes managers" becomes "closing removes managers". Code and docs that equate release with removal change.
  • Spam and abandoned accounts do not accumulate. Provisional accounts expire without a trace, the dormancy ladder reclaims the rest, and purge is safe because it refuses whatever still has dependents.
  • Every relationship needs a disposition. Adding an edge between registered entities now carries a decision, which is the same discipline as classifying a field and is enforced the same way.
  • Large histories have somewhere to go. Time-partitioned history and the offload tier bound the growth of the primary database, at the cost of a second place to look when data is subject to a request or a hold.
  • ADR-011's earlier "no hard delete" is withdrawn. Row removal exists, as purge, but only where the dependency rule allows it.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Retention periods, which follow product tier and packaging decisions.
  • Whether organizations get the same Erase semantics for their member data, or only archive and delete of the organization record.
  • The shape of the export format (one archive per subject, with a manifest).
  • What counts as graduating from provisional: a verified email, a first meaningful action, or either.
  • The retention period and lawful basis for the abuse fingerprint, which need legal review per jurisdiction.
  • Whether an account under investigation needs a suspended state between active and purge, or whether archive covers it.
  • The default disposition for content shared with other subjects, restrict or detach, per product.
  • The dormancy periods per tier, which follow packaging.

docs.title: References
docs.text:
• guardsql: the pii and secret data classes.
  • GDPR Articles 15–18 and 20 (access, rectification, erasure, restriction, portability).

docs.title: ADR-012: Data Governance Catalog, Legal Holds and Enforcement
docs.text: Status: Proposed Deciders: @grokify Relates to: ADR-011 (lifecycle states, data classification and privacy rights; this ADR defines the catalog, holds and enforcement behind them; it replaces ADR-011's single erasure flag with holds), ADR-007 (roles), ADR-010 (access changes), ADR-013 (key management, which owns snapshot encryption). Updates: a new docs/design/architecture/data-governance.md.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR-011 defines a classification registry, lifecycle states, access and erasure operations, and an erasure hold. It leaves two questions open:

  • What does a hold preserve? A mailbox hold works because email is immutable once sent: "preserve" means "do not delete". A row in a CRUD database is overwritten by an update, and the earlier state is often the evidence. Preserving only against deletion would let the data be altered instead.
  • How is any of it enforced in applications? Each product keeps its own data in its own schema and database. Governance that only covers SystemForge's tables protects little, and routing every product's queries through a SystemForge data service would make the platform the data layer for all of them, contradicting the modular monolith (a product must be able to split out) and adding latency for rare operations. It would not even enforce anything: a holder of a database credential bypasses any interface.

Governance that spans products is what makes the platform valuable to a product team: classification, privacy rights and holds that work for their data without each team building them. The design below delivers that without taking over their data access.

docs.title: The data catalog
docs.text:
1. The classification registry is a central data catalog. Each registered entity and field is described once, in the model of github.com/grokify/datacatalog (ADR-011, decisions 6 and 7), and the catalog is the answer to "what data do we hold and what rules apply to it". Per entity it records: the owner (product or platform), the data subject key, whether it is subject to access and erasure requests (GDPR scope), whether it can be placed under hold, whether it is versioned, its structured retention (keep, then purge or offload; ADR-011, decision 24) and its eraser. Per field it records the visibility (public or internal), the pii and secret tags, the erasure strategy and the export flag. Per relationship to another registered entity it records the purge disposition (cascade, detach or restrict; ADR-011, decision 21).
  2. The catalog is queryable and published. It is available through an API and a command, and rendered as a documentation page from the same source, so a data protection review, a customer questionnaire and the enforcement code read one definition. Products' entries appear in it when they register (decision 16).

docs.title: Legal holds
docs.text:
1. A hold means preserve, and preservation covers alteration as well as deletion. A subject covered by a hold has its data preserved as of the hold and protected from change.
  2. A hold is an object, and a subject may be on several at once. A hold has an identifier, a name, an optional external reference (a matter number that the platform stores and does not interpret), a reason, a state (active or released), its placing and releasing actors, and a set of custodians: the subjects it covers. A subject is held while at least one active hold covers it. Releasing one hold never clears another; the subject becomes erasable only when no active hold remains.
  3. Custodians are subjects, grouped by the hold. A hold lists its custodians explicitly. As a convenience a hold may be placed on an organization, which adds the organization's members at that time and records the hold against the organization. Whether members who join later are also added is chosen when the hold is placed (include_future_members), and defaults to no. The setting is recorded with the hold and changing it is an audited change by the legal manager. The platform understands the grouping (which subjects a hold covers, and which holds cover a subject) and nothing about the matter itself.
  4. Placing a hold snapshots each custodian. For every custodian the platform runs the same Export operation (ADR-011, decision 9) and stores the result as a sealed, immutable artifact with a digest, time, actor and hold. The snapshot answers "what did it say when the hold began". A subject added to a hold later is snapshotted at that moment.
  5. While any hold covers a subject:
  6. erasure, deletion and purge of its records are refused with ErrHeld, and a dependent row covered by a hold blocks the purge of the subject it references (decision 22);
  7. edits to pii fields are refused with ErrHeld, so the snapshot remains the true state, except for versioned entities (decision 9);
  8. archive remains allowed (it destroys nothing) and is how a subject is hidden from customers during a dispute;
  9. operational writes continue: sign-in bookkeeping, session and token records, credential rotation and membership or role changes, each of which is already an auditable access change (ADR-010). The refusal names the holds, to administrators and to the legal manager only.
  10. Refusals are recorded. A refused erasure, deletion or correction is an audit event, so the deferral of a data subject's request is evidenced.
  11. Versioned entities keep every before-image. An entity registered as versioned allows edits under a hold and stores each previous state (all fields, not only pii) in an append-only history. Such entities are marked in the catalog, and their history is subject to the hold: it is not purged while any hold covers the subject. The platform's own identity tables use the freeze (decision 7), not versioning.

docs.title: Roles and notification
docs.text:
1. Two platform roles for privacy and legal, with privacy under legal. (A third, trust_safety_manager, for purging abusive accounts, is defined in decision 24.) Organizations place privacy inside legal, so the roles are separate in permission and nested in default assignment:
    • privacy_manager handles data subject requests: the catalog (read), access and portability exports, restriction (archive), and erasure and deletion requests, which are refused while a hold applies.
    • legal_manager places, changes and releases holds, decides whether a hold is disclosed, and holds every privacy_manager permission. A hold overrides erasure, so the role that can place one must be able to see the requests it defers. Both are platform-level roles in the SystemForge vocabulary (ADR-007), separate from platform administration, so that placing a hold or erasing a person is not available to everyone who can administer accounts. Permissions are named (privacy.request.manage, privacy.catalog.read, legal.hold.manage, legal.hold.disclose, audit.read) so a deployment whose privacy office sits outside legal can assign them differently. Holds and snapshots are readable only to legal_manager and to administrators with audit.read. The roles and permissions are part of the platform so every product gets the same generic capability; an application may extend them with its own roles or narrower permissions in its vocabulary, but may not weaken the platform's refusals (a hold still blocks erasure).

  2. Destructive and disclosing actions are requests. Erasure, deletion, hold release and disclosure run as a request with states requested, approved, executed or cancelled, so there is one audited path whatever the policy. A deployment sets a policy per action:

    • none: the requester's authority is enough and the request executes at once. This is the default, since many businesses start with one person who holds every role.
    • delay: the request executes after a configurable period, during which it can be cancelled and the stated notification is sent. This protects a single operator from a mistake without needing a second person.
    • approval: a second principal holding the permission, different from the requester, must approve. The approver cannot be the requester or the subject, and an unapproved request expires. The policy can be tightened without a code change as the business grows.

  3. A hold is marked internally, and notification is the legal manager's decision. The marker is visible to staff in admin tooling. Whether and how the person is told is set per hold: not at all, in the application (a notice the product renders from a claim or an API field), or out of band (a message the legal team sends). The default is not to notify, so a hold is not disclosed to a subject by accident. A subject whose erasure request is deferred is told only that the request is pending review, unless the legal manager has chosen to disclose.

docs.title: Snapshot storage
docs.text:
1. The snapshot location is configurable. Two stores are supported behind one interface: the database (a sealed, encrypted record, the default and the one used at first, since the volume is expected to be small) and an S3-compatible object store, with the snapshot written as a file (Parquet for tabular exports) and referenced from the database by location and digest. Moving to the object store is a configuration change; existing snapshots remain readable through their recorded location. The same store, with the same manifest, holds data offloaded from the primary database under ADR-011, decision 25.
  2. Snapshots are personal data. They carry the classification of their contents, are encrypted at rest under keys managed as ADR-013 decides, are excluded from ordinary exports, and are removed only when every hold covering the subject has been released and the subject's own erasure has proceeded. The key hierarchy (per hold, per subject or platform-wide) is ADR-013's decision, not this one's.

docs.title: Enforcement in applications
docs.text:
1. Applications reach their own data directly. SystemForge does not sit between a product and its database. Identity and organization data stays behind SystemForge's services, because it owns them; product data goes through the product's own access layer.
  2. Registration is mandatory and verified. A product annotates its Ent entities with classification (ADR-011, decision 7) and registers them in the catalog. dataclass.Verify runs at startup and fails in production, and warns in development, when a registered field has no classification or an entity with personal data has no subject key and eraser.
  3. SystemForge ships the enforcement as an Ent hook. A mutation hook consults the catalog and the holds covering the subject and refuses the writes that decision 7 forbids; for versioned entities it writes the before-image; for a subject marked purging it refuses new dependent writes (decision 22). A product installs it once on its client, so enforcement sits in the write path without a data service.
  4. A conformance test is provided. It fails in CI when a registered entity can be mutated without the hook installed, which catches a second client or a bulk path that skips it.
  5. Where tables share a database with SystemForge, a trigger or row-level-security policy may back the hook as defense in depth. This is optional and engine-specific, and it lives in the engine-specific packages, not in the portable core.
  6. What this does not stop is stated. Raw SQL, a bulk import script or a direct console session bypasses an ORM hook. The mitigations are operational and documented: lint rules against raw SQL in product code, guardsql for query paths, and control over who holds a database credential. The platform promises what a library can promise.

docs.title: Purge
docs.text:
1. Purge planning is a walk of the catalog's relationships. Given a subject, the platform follows its registered entities and their edges, counts the rows each would remove, and classifies each dependent: it cascades (owned by the subject), it detaches (reference cleared), or it blocks. Anything that blocks produces the dependency report of ADR-011, decision 20: a row of another subject, a restrict edge with rows present, a row covered by a hold, an edge in the Ent schema that the catalog does not declare. The same walk is the dry run. The report holds entity names, counts and reasons and never row contents, and is shown only to a holder of the permission in decision 24.
  2. Execution runs through the hook, in the platform, not in the database. The plan is executed as ADR-011, decision 22 says: the subject is marked purging, new dependent writes are refused by the hook, dependents are removed leaf first in resumable batches, each batch is re-checked against the holds at the moment it runs (a hold placed mid-purge stops it with ErrHeld, and the rows removed so far are recorded), and the subject is removed last. Database cascades are not used on registered entities: they run inside the engine and skip the hook, so they would bypass hold checks, before-images and audit. Foreign keys stay RESTRICT.
  3. The catalog's relationships are verified against the schema. A registration check and the conformance test compare every edge of a registered Ent entity with the catalog and fail on an undeclared edge or a foreign key that is not RESTRICT. An entity added without a disposition cannot ship, as a field without a classification cannot.
  4. Purge is a separate permission and role. account.purge.plan runs the dry run and reads the dependency report; account.purge executes. They belong to a platform role, trust_safety_manager, separate from privacy_manager and legal_manager, because removing spam at volume is an abuse-handling duty and carries none of their authority over holds and data subject requests. Purge is a destructive request under decision 11, and its policy can differ by origin: expiry of provisional accounts is system-initiated and uses none, a single purge by an operator uses the deployment's policy, and a bulk purge by criteria (signup window, email domain, network range) always starts with a dry run and, above a configurable row threshold, requires approval where a second principal exists.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• A hold is meaningful for mutable data. The sealed snapshot plus the freeze answers "what did it say then" without a history store on every table, and versioned entities cover records that must stay editable.
  • Several matters can cover one person. Release of one matter leaves the others in force, and the platform can answer "which holds cover this person" and "who is on this hold".
  • Placing and disclosing a hold are separate decisions held by a legal role, not by whoever administers accounts.
  • Products get governance by registering, not by building it. The catalog makes the platform's coverage inspectable and auditable.
  • The platform stays out of product data paths. No added hop, and a product can still split out. The cost is that enforcement is by convention, hook and test, and not by a mandatory interface.
  • Annotating entities is real work for each product; the startup check makes omissions loud.
  • The platform now models holds and custodians. It still does not model matters, deadlines, counsel or discovery; those stay in the legal team's systems, referenced by the external reference.
  • Purge is safe because it is planned and refused. A subject with dependents the catalog does not mark as owned cannot be removed, and the reason is reported, like a cloud provider's dependency violation.
  • Dependency edges are one more thing a product declares, and the verification step keeps that list from rotting.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• A single hold flag per subject. Rejected: it cannot express several matters, and releasing one would clear the rest.
  • All application data access through SystemForge. Rejected: makes the platform the data layer for every product, couples their schemas and deployment, adds latency, and still does not stop a credential holder.
  • Preserve against deletion only. Rejected: alteration defeats the purpose of a hold on mutable data.
  • Freeze every write under hold. Rejected: breaks sign-in, rotation and membership operations; the account must stay usable and secure.
  • Rely on ON DELETE CASCADE for purge. Rejected: cascades run inside the database and bypass the hook, so held rows could be removed, before- images skipped and no audit written.
  • Hard delete as the ordinary delete. Rejected: references to a deleted principal would break or cascade; the tombstone stays the default and purge is the narrow exception.
  • Tombstone everything, including spam. Rejected: it keeps a row, and an identifier, for each junk account at free-tier volumes, and retains data the platform has no reason to keep.
  • Versioning everywhere by default. Deferred: a history store on every classified table is heavy for a first version; kept as a per-entity option and recorded in the catalog.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• How a data subject access request interacts with a hold the subject must not be told about (decision 12 defaults to "pending review").
  • The default delay period for the delay policy.
  • Whether a deployment with one principal can satisfy approval through an external approver (for example a named advisor with a scoped, temporary role), or must stay on none or delay.
  • The row threshold above which a bulk purge requires approval, and whether it differs for provisional accounts.
  • Whether a hold placed during a long purge should roll back the rows already removed (it cannot) or only stop and report, which is what decision 22 specifies.

docs.title: ADR-013: Key Management
docs.text: Status: Proposed Deciders: @grokify Relates to: ADR-012 (snapshots and held data are encrypted under keys this ADR manages), ADR-011 (erasure and its strategies). Builds on: keyforge, the generic key-lifecycle library and control plane whose specifications define the mechanism. Updates: a new docs/design/architecture/key-management.md.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
SystemForge already encrypts data in more than one place, each with its own small mechanism: sealed session secrets in the relying-party store, the BFF session cookie encryption, and signing keys for tokens. ADR-012 adds sealed snapshots under legal hold, which may live in the database or an object store and must survive for as long as a hold lasts.

Those uses share needs that ad hoc code does not meet: rotation without re-encrypting everything, a record of which key protected which data, a choice of where root keys live, and, for privacy, the ability to make data unrecoverable on purpose. A platform that promises erasure has to answer what happens to backups and replicas of erased data. Encrypting personal data under a key that can itself be destroyed answers that, and so key management is part of the privacy design, not a separate concern.

Many SystemForge businesses start as a single person on one host, and some will run in a cloud with a managed key service. The design has to work with a local file key on day one and with a managed service later, without changing the data. Because none of this is specific to identity, the mechanism is its own module, keyforge, usable by every PlexusOne product.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Key management is a generic capability, so its mechanism lives in a separate module, keyforge, and not in SystemForge. This ADR records what SystemForge decides on top of it: that the platform uses keyforge for every encryption need, the policy it applies, and the points where platform policy (holds, approvals, roles, the catalog) plugs into it. Decisions 2 to 6 and 10 to 13 state the platform's requirements; keyforge's technical requirements specify how they are met, and where the wording differs the keyforge specification governs the mechanism while this ADR governs the policy.

  1. SystemForge adopts keyforge as its one key library and control plane. Every encryption use in the platform goes through it, replacing the per-package mechanisms over time; applications use it for their own data through the same interface. SystemForge provides a thin keys package that wires keyforge to the platform:
  2. Store: the keyforge registry runs on SystemForge's database through Ent (SQLite or PostgreSQL), in the same deployment as everything else. The first version of keys uses keyforge's single-host setup instead: the keyring and a SQLite registry live together in one directory, so they are backed up together. Moving the registry to the platform database needs keyforge to accept an external registry, and follows.
  3. Guard: keyforge's DestroyGuard is implemented from ADR-012: holds protect keys (decision 7), and destruction follows the platform's delay or approval policy. keyforge does not know about holds.
  4. Audit: keyforge's audit events flow into the platform audit trail (decision 8).
  5. Authorizer: control-plane actions are authorized by SystemForge's authorization, with the privacy_manager and legal_manager roles of ADR-012 where the action concerns erasure or held data.
  6. Catalog: an entity registered in the data catalog (ADR-012) states its data-key granularity (decision 10), and the catalog is the inventory of which data a purpose protects.
  7. Root key: the local provider's root key is read through omnivault, so a deployment supplies it from its secret manager.
  8. Mounting: the keyforge control plane is mounted in the same process, like SystemAuth, and split out only when another process needs it. Encrypt and decrypt stay in process and make no network call.
  9. Envelope encryption. Data is encrypted with a data key (DEK); DEKs are encrypted (wrapped) by a key-encryption key (KEK) held by a KeyProvider. Ciphertext carries the identifier and version of the key that wrapped it, so any record can be decrypted, rotated or destroyed knowing only what is stored beside it.
  10. Providers are pluggable. A provider wraps and unwraps and never exposes a KEK. The KEK may be a symmetric key or an asymmetric keypair; Wrap and Unwrap are the same either way (decision 11). Initial providers: a local provider (a key file or environment-supplied key, for development and single-host deployments) and a cloud KMS provider interface with a first implementation for the hosting target. A deployment selects the provider by configuration. The local provider is marked as such in the catalog and in startup logs, so it is not mistaken for a managed one.
  11. Keys are scoped by purpose. Separate keys for session secrets, token signing, snapshots, and per-product data, so exposure or destruction of one does not touch the others. Purpose is part of the key identity and of the encryption context bound to each ciphertext.
  12. Rotation re-wraps, it does not re-encrypt. Rotating a KEK re-wraps its DEKs; rotating a DEK applies to new data and to data re-encrypted on write or by a background job. Old versions stay available for decryption until nothing references them. Rotation is online and needs no downtime: ciphertext carries the key version that wrapped it, so old and new versions are read side by side. Schedule and procedure are decision 12.
