  13. Crypto-shredding is a supported erasure strategy. An entity may be registered with a per-subject DEK (ADR-011's erasure strategies gain shred): erasure destroys that subject's DEK, which makes the subject's ciphertext unrecoverable everywhere it was copied, including backups. This is an option for data too widespread to rewrite, not the default.
  14. Holds protect keys as well as data. A key that protects data under a hold cannot be destroyed while any hold covers the subject (ADR-012), and destruction is a request with the delay or approval policy of ADR-012's decision 11.
  15. Key use and lifecycle are audited. Creation, rotation, wrapping failures, access by an administrator and destruction are recorded without key material. Ordinary encrypt and decrypt are not logged one by one; rates and failures are metered.
  16. Snapshot keys. Snapshots are encrypted under a purpose key for snapshots with a DEK per hold (so releasing a hold and erasing its snapshots can destroy that DEK). A per-subject DEK is added when a subject's data participates in more than one hold or when crypto-shredding is selected for the subject.

  17. Data keys have a configurable granularity, chosen when an entity or store is registered:

    Granularity Fits Cost Per object Files, exports, snapshots; erasing one object is trivial One wrap and unwrap per read; with a remote KMS, a call per read unless the unwrapped key is cached Per subject or per hold Rows tied to a person or a hold (decision 9) Erasure or release destroys one key Per purpose High-volume, low-sensitivity data such as sessions A cap on encryptions per key (decision 12)

    There is no single default: the registration states one, and the catalog (ADR-012) records it. 11. Bulk data is never encrypted directly with an asymmetric key. An asymmetric KEK is used as a hybrid: a random symmetric data key (AES-256-GCM) encrypts the data and is wrapped to the public key (RSA-OAEP or HPKE), with the wrapped key stored beside the ciphertext; reading unwraps with the private key, then decrypts. Asymmetric KEKs are for components that must encrypt without being able to decrypt, such as hold snapshots and exports sealed to a key held in a managed service or offline. Symmetric KEKs from a managed service or the local provider are the default for ordinary platform data. Rotating an asymmetric KEK creates a new keypair and keeps old private versions for decryption, subject to decision 7. 12. Rotation is automatic, with defaults by key type. Each is configurable per purpose.

    Key Default Notes KEK 365 days; floor 90 Re-wraps data keys; no data is re-encrypted Data key New key every 90 days or after N encryptions per purpose, whichever is first Applies to new writes; old data is re-encrypted lazily on write, or by a throttled, resumable background job after a compromise or policy change Token signing key (if in scope, see open questions) 90 days, with a published overlap longer than relying parties' JWKS cache time Snapshot, per-hold and per-subject keys Never by schedule Destroyed by release or erasure (decisions 6 and 9)
    • A managed provider rotates automatically. The local provider rotates automatically only after its keyring is verified as backed up; otherwise it warns and requires an operator keys rotate, because a restored backup that predates a rotation would lose everything wrapped under the newer version. keys status flags a keyring not backed up since its last rotation.
    • Rotation never deletes old versions. Retirement is a separate step with its own delay, and never while a hold covers the data (decision 7).
    • The last two versions, the active one and its predecessor, are always kept, so a bad rotation can be rolled back. Older versions retire only when nothing references them, the delay has passed, no hold applies and the guard allows it; the count is a floor, not a trigger to delete.
    • A failed or overdue rotation raises an alert; a key past its period is reported, not silently kept.
    • Real keys are not rotated weekly. A weekly rotation drill runs the full lifecycle on a built-in canary purpose that holds no data, so the mechanism is exercised and its failures surface within a week, without the version churn and keyring-backup burden of rotating real keys that often.
    • Emergency rotation is a separate procedure from scheduled rotation. If a KEK is compromised, re-wrapping is not enough: the old KEK version is destroyed (subject to holds, with the approval path of ADR-012's decision 11 available but not blocking an emergency) and the data keys are rotated. If a data key is exposed, its data is re-encrypted under a new key. Both are audited, and the procedure is documented with the provider.
    • Post-quantum algorithms are adopted from the Go standard library as they appear, hybrid first. The standard library now provides ML-KEM (crypto/mlkem, FIPS 203), HPKE with ML-KEM and hybrid KEMs (crypto/hpke, which adds MLKEM768X25519 and MLKEM768P256), and ML-DSA (crypto/mldsa, FIPS 204). The platform's position is:
    • Symmetric keys need no change. AES-256-GCM encryption and key wrapping are already adequate against a quantum adversary, so KEKs and DEKs under decision 2 stay as they are.
    • Asymmetric KEKs are hybrid. When asymmetric KEKs are introduced (decision 11) the default KEM is a hybrid of a classical and a post-quantum scheme through crypto/hpke, not a classical-only one. Long-lived confidentiality, such as hold snapshots, exports and backups, is exposed to harvest-now-decrypt-later, and these are the uses that justify it first.
    • Signatures follow ecosystem support. Signing keys (decision 12) move to ML-DSA, or a hybrid, when the formats that carry them (token and key set specifications) and the relying parties support it. Until then they stay on Ed25519 or ECDSA.
    • Standard library only. No third-party post-quantum implementation is used. The envelope's algorithm identifier makes each of these a format addition, not a change to stored data.
    • FIPS 140-3 operation is a supported configuration of the selector, and the platform starts without requiring it. The Go standard library includes a FIPS 140-3 cryptographic module, selected at build time (GOFIPS140) and enabled at run time (GODEBUG=fips140=on, or only to make non-approved algorithms fail).
    • Start in the standard profile. The first release does not require FIPS mode and implements no non-approved algorithm. Its one algorithm, AES-256-GCM through cipher.NewGCMWithRandomNonce, is approved in both profiles, so the code stays valid under fips140=only by construction.
    • The selector is the deliverable (decision 16). Requiring FIPS-only operation, or adding the first non-approved algorithm, is then a registry entry and a configuration change. A FIPS-only CI job and the recording of which module version a build uses are added when FIPS operation is first required.
    • Reasons to run outside FIPS mode are stated, not assumed away: a dependency that needs a non-approved algorithm, a module version that lacks an algorithm the deployment wants (the validated v1.0.0 module has no ML-DSA), or a development environment.
    • FIPS is a constraint, not a security guarantee. It validates a module on tested platforms; it does not cover the rest of an application. This ADR does not claim a deployment is "FIPS compliant".
    • Algorithms are a platform policy that keyforge owns.
    • Everything goes through keyforge. Every protection of stored data and of keys uses an algorithm from keyforge's registry. Platform and application packages do not choose or call primitives for that purpose. Transport security (TLS) and password hashing are outside this rule and are decided where they live.
    • Algorithms are named exactly. A mode and a size are always stated: "AES-256-GCM", never "AES-256", because the bare name does not say whether the mode authenticates. Specifications, configuration, logs and the ciphertext's algorithm identifier all carry the full name.
    • The floor is an authenticated mode. AES-256-GCM is the floor for encrypting data and wrapping keys. ECB, CBC, CTR and any unauthenticated mode are never offered. "Better" means an authenticated algorithm added to the registry from the standard library (or golang.org/x/crypto where the standard library has none), after review.
    • Two profiles, fips and standard. Each is a fixed, reviewed set of algorithms compiled into keyforge. fips contains only algorithms the Go cryptographic module approves; standard adds non-approved ones (for example ChaCha20-Poly1305). A process selects its profile from its FIPS mode by default; configuration may narrow a profile (deny an algorithm, or run the fips profile outside FIPS mode) and may never widen it.
    • The sets are code, not configuration. Acceptable algorithms change rarely, and the standard library's set changes with Go releases. Hard- coding the profiles keeps them reviewable and keeps the platform's claims truthful. Adding an algorithm is a keyforge release, with the envelope identifier and vectors that implies.
    • Reads follow the profile. A process in the fips profile refuses to decrypt an envelope that used a non-approved algorithm, with a typed error that says so, and the data is migrated by re-encrypting it in a standard process. A purpose may pin its profile, so data meant for a FIPS deployment is never written with a non-approved algorithm.
    • keyforge is the single system of record for the platform's cryptographic choices, and it feeds the crypto specification.
    • Authoritative for what it selects and enforces. The algorithms, profiles, purposes, keys, versions, providers and rotation state that keyforge governs are facts keyforge owns. They are not restated by hand anywhere else.
    • Reference for what it does not control. Cryptography configured elsewhere, such as edge TLS at a CDN or TLS between internal services, may be registered in keyforge as external boundaries, so that there is one place to answer "what cryptography do we rely on". A registered boundary carries the expectation (for example minimum protocol version, permitted suites, key exchange groups, certificate key strength), an owner, where the real configuration lives, and a review date. keyforge records the expectation and does not claim to enforce it.
    • The system's crypto specification is generated, not written. keyforge exports the facts it owns and the external boundaries it holds as a systemspec-crypto document. Enforced facts carry evidence from keyforge's own configuration and runtime state; declared external facts are marked as attested or awaiting review, with the owner and review date; a declaration past its review date drops out of "verified".
    • Verification is a separate step. Test applications and scanners exercise the deployed system and compare what they observe with the generated specification and the registered expectations. A scan result is evidence attached to a claim, not an edit to the inventory. A mismatch is a finding. keyforge is not a scanner.
    • Metadata only. The export never contains key material or secret values, and a use of a primitive outside keyforge is found by source and dependency analysis rather than assumed absent.
    • Recovery is proven by an automated drill, and judgment is by agents.
    • A recovery drill restores the registry and keyring from backup into an isolated environment, decrypts a sentinel for every retained key version, measures recovery time and recovery point against configured limits, runs negative checks that must fail, and destroys the environment. It runs quarterly and after any change to the provider or backups, with no person involved.
    • Objective results are the engine's and are final. Judgments such as severity, trends against earlier drills, likely cause and recommendations are written into a DR report by an analyst agent that receives metadata only, never key material, plaintext or access to the restored environment.
    • The report is evidence for the system's crypto specification: objective results are verified; the analyst's conclusions are inferred until someone attests them, and the analyst cannot change policy or key state.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One place to rotate, audit and replace keys, instead of several private mechanisms.
  • Erasure that covers backups is available for the data that needs it, at the cost of managing per-subject keys.
  • A single-person business can start with a file key and move to a managed key service by configuration, without rewriting stored data.
  • The platform takes on the operational duty of protecting root keys. The local provider is only as safe as the host; the documentation says so and recommends a managed provider for any deployment holding data under hold.
  • A dependency on keyforge, and a control plane to run. The registry adds tables, an admin API and a CLI that need the same care as SystemAuth, but only the library is on the data path.
  • Rotation needs no downtime and no cutover, at the cost of keeping old key versions until nothing references them.
  • Migration work: existing sealed secrets and signing keys move onto the package incrementally, each behind its own change.
  • A compliance-driven deployment is a configuration change, not a fork. The selector already distinguishes the profiles, so the work when a customer requires FIPS-only operation is to enable and test it.
  • Some existing choices are outside FIPS-approved algorithms. The identity credential service hashes passwords with Argon2id, which is not an approved algorithm and is not part of the standard library's module. A deployment that must use only approved algorithms needs a PBKDF2 option there; that is a separate change to the credential service and is not decided here.
  • Hybrid post-quantum KEMs carry a classical component. Where that component is X25519, FIPS-only mode refuses it, so such a deployment selects a hybrid built on a NIST curve (MLKEM768P256).

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Leave each package to manage its own keys. Rejected: rotation and audit cannot be done consistently, and erasure cannot reach backups.
  • Build the mechanism inside SystemForge. Rejected: it is not specific to identity, other products need it, and key custody deserves its own small, separately reviewed module.
  • Require a cloud KMS everywhere. Rejected: excludes single-host and local development, and ties the platform to one vendor.
  • A remote key service on the data path. Rejected: it adds latency and an availability dependency to every read and write. Keys are unwrapped once and cached in process.
  • Encrypt bulk data directly with an asymmetric key. Rejected: payload limits and cost; hybrid encryption (decision 11) gives the same separation of encrypt and decrypt.
  • Encrypt the database as a whole only. Insufficient: it does not give per-purpose or per-subject destruction, and it does not protect exports, snapshots or object-store files.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Which KMS provider to implement first, and whether it supports ML-KEM or hybrid wrapping natively.
  • Which hybrid KEM is the default outside FIPS mode and which inside it, and when asymmetric KEKs ship.
  • How per-subject keys are stored and cached so that reads stay fast.
  • Whether the key package also provides signing-key management for tokens in its first version, or only data encryption. Decision 12 gives the rotation policy that would apply if it does.
  • The default N for the encryptions-per-key cap, and the default delay before a retired key version is destroyed.
  • Key escrow and recovery for the local provider.
  • Interaction with the database's own encryption at rest and with customers who bring their own keys.

docs.title: ADR-014: Application Roles and Marketplace Seat Assignments Are Separate Records
docs.text: Status: Proposed Deciders: @grokify Relates to: ADR-007 (memberships and entitlements as claims; this ADR amends its decision 8), ADR-008 (resource-scoped collaborators). Updates: docs/design/architecture/organizations.md (seat accounting) and docs/design/architecture/authorization.md (application roles). Both already describe the behavior below; they are not changed by this ADR.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
ADR-007 decision 8 says that application roles are stored in sf_app_roles, "which replaces seat assignments as the record of who may use what", and that a seat-licensed application counts its rows against the license. The initiative's TRD went further and planned for SeatAssignment to become a view derived from sf_app_roles, kept for one release and then removed.

The implementation does the second half of the sentence and not the first:

  • Seat limits are enforced on application roles. The seat limit of an application is the sum of the seats of its valid seat_based licenses; approle counts sf_app_roles rows for (organization, application) against it and refuses with ErrNoSeats. There is no limit when any entitlement for the application is not seat-limited.
  • Seat assignments were not replaced. sf_seat_assignments, the marketplace seat endpoints, License.used_seats, CheckPrincipal and the SpiceDB seat_holder relation (license#use) all remain, and none of them is derived from application roles. Assigning a role creates no seat assignment, and assigning a seat grants no role.

Replacing one record with the other would not be a rename, because they describe different things:

Application role Seat assignment Keyed by (principal, organization, application) (license, principal) Answers What may this person do inside the application? Does this person hold a seat of this license? Needs an application Yes, a registered AppVocabulary No: a listing need not name an application Carries a level Yes, a role from the vocabulary No Counted by approle, per application used_seats, per license

A listing that names no application (a template, a dataset, a service sold without an in-product role) has seats and no application roles. An application entitled through several licenses, a subscription and a default has one set of roles and several license records.

Leaving the ADR as written means a reader looking for "who may use application X" finds two answers, and the architecture pages already say that the marketplace's seat assignments remain a separate record while ADR-007 says they were replaced.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Application roles are the record of who may act inside an application. Applications decide access from the orgs claim's apps map and never from seat assignments. This confirms ADR-007's decision 1 and the first clause of decision 8.
  2. Seat assignments remain the marketplace's record of who holds a seat of a particular license. They are not replaced, not derived from application roles and not required for application access. ADR-007 decision 8 is amended: sf_app_roles does not replace seat assignments.
  3. Seat limits for an application are enforced on application roles, as implemented: a principal holding a role in a seat-licensed application consumes one seat for that application, whether or not a seat assignment exists. Owners' implicit roles hold no seat.
  4. The two counters are different numbers. License.used_seats counts seat assignments of one license. The number of seats an application is using is the count of its application roles (approle.Service.ListForOrganization(org, application)). Interfaces that show seat usage for an application must use the second, and the marketplace response is not a substitute for it.
  5. A listing that names an application is entitled through the marketplace, and its access is granted by application role. For such a listing the seat endpoints are legacy. They keep working, so existing integrations are not broken, and they do not grant application access. For a listing with no application, seat assignments are the only per-person record and keep their present behavior.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• ADR-007's text is wrong on one point and this ADR corrects it, so the record matches the architecture pages and the code. ADR-007's status line gains "decision 8 amended by ADR-014" when this ADR is accepted.
  • No code changes. The behavior this ADR records is the behavior of the code; the TRD's derived-view plan is withdrawn.
  • A deployment can show a principal with a role and no seat assignment, or the reverse, and both are valid states. Support and billing tooling should not treat a mismatch as an error.
  • Two ways to give someone a seat remain for listings that name an application. This is the cost of keeping the marketplace's licensing record intact, and it is accepted until decision 5's open question is settled.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Derive seat assignments from application roles, as the TRD planned. Rejected: it cannot cover a listing with no application, loses the per-license attribution that a customer with several licenses of one product needs, and breaks the marketplace seat API for no gain in access control.
  • Make application roles require a seat assignment. Rejected: it makes the licensing record an access gate, so changing a license changes access invisibly, and it forces a seat per person even for applications the deployment grants to everyone.
  • Remove seat assignments and keep only application roles. Rejected for the same reason as deriving them; it also drops the seat_holder relation that the relationship-based provider reads for license use.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Whether the seat endpoints should refuse, or be marked deprecated in the API schema, for a listing that names an application, so there is one way to give a person a seat of such an application.
  • Whether a seat-based license that names an application should report used_seats from application roles instead of seat assignments, which would make decision 4's two numbers one for that case.

docs.title: ADR-015: Identifier Policy, Slug Namespaces and Portability Across Deployments
docs.text: Status: Proposed Deciders: @grokify Relates to: ADR-006 (organization lifecycle, slugs, cooling-off), ADR-007 (memberships and entitlements as claims; decision 4 stands), ADR-014 (application roles). Updates: docs/design/architecture/organizations.md (identifiers and slugs).

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Several applications run on one SystemForge deployment and share a single sign-in and organization model, so one person sees one set of organizations across them. Three questions have come up that ADR-006 and ADR-007 do not answer on their own:

  • Which identifier is safe to show customers? Identifiers appear in tokens, URLs, exports and logs. Platforms sold to security teams are reviewed for metadata disclosure, and a time-ordered identifier carries the creation time of the thing it names.
  • What may an application key its data by? Today an application can key tenant rows by organization slug. A slug can be released, reserved for seven days and then taken by someone else (ADR-006), so data keyed by it can follow the name to a different owner.
  • Can an application leave a deployment, or another deployment join one? Splitting an application off, or merging a deployment in after an acquisition, must not depend on names that two deployments may both have claimed.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. Identifier classes. Every identifier SystemForge issues belongs to one class, and the class fixes how it is generated.
Class Examples Generator Identity and tenancy entities principal, organization, membership, client, credential, application and customer-facing resource IDs UUIDv4 (random) Append-only records whose own time is already visible access changes, audit and activity events, request evidence UUIDv7 (time-ordered) Credentials and secrets API keys, session cookies, invite tokens, OAuth state and nonces CSPRNG bytes, stored hashed where possible; never a UUID
  • The test is whether the creation time is itself sensitive. An account's or organization's creation time is metadata a customer did not choose to publish, so those IDs are random. An event already carries its time, so a time-ordered ID discloses nothing new and keeps insertion local in the database.
  • A UUID never authorizes. RFC 9562 section 8 says UUIDs must not be used as security capabilities and should not be assumed hard to guess. Authorization is checked on every request whatever the ID looks like.
  • The choice of v4 for identity entities is conservative, not mandated. The RFC describes the timestamp in a v7 UUID as a very small attack surface; the platform avoids it because it costs nothing and shortens security review.
  • One identifier per entity. There is no separate public and internal ID. A table that truly needs both time-ordered inserts and a random external ID may add a second column only by amending this ADR with the measured problem, because an internal ID that leaks through logs, joins and exports defeats the purpose.

  • In code: UUIDMixin and BaseMixin generate v4; TimeOrderedUUIDMixin generates v7 and is opt-in.

  • Applications key tenant data by organization ID, never by slug. The slug is a label resolved from the memberships the person already holds (the orgs claim, ADR-007). A rename, a conversion to a team organization or a released slug changes the label and nothing else.

  • SystemForge owns slugs. One slug registry per deployment serves every application, so one organization slug opens all of them in a single experience. Applications do not store, validate or reserve organization slugs themselves; they ask SystemForge.

  • Slugs live in namespaces. A slug is unique within a namespace, stored as (namespace, slug).

  • org: organization slugs, shared by personal and team organizations as ADR-006 decision 4 requires.

  • app:<application-id>: slugs of resources an application owns (for example a published site or a shared dashboard). Two applications may use the same slug without conflict, and a slug an application owns moves with that application.
  • Cooling-off applies per namespace with the same seven days and the same claim rule as ADR-006 decision 5.

  • Schema (not part of this ADR's first implementation): the unique indexes on sf_organizations.slug and sf_slug_reservations.slug become unique on the namespace and slug together, with the namespace defaulting to org.

  • Portability: split and merge. Organization and principal IDs are random UUIDs, so they do not collide across deployments and are kept as they are.

  • Splitting an application off takes its data, which is keyed by organization ID, together with the organizations and principals that data references and the application's namespace of slugs.

  • Merging a deployment in imports organizations and principals with their IDs. A slug that is already taken is not overwritten: the importing deployment applies a declared policy, either renaming the incoming slug or reserving it, and the old name resolves as an alias for a cooling-off period.

  • Principal subject continuity across an issuer change is an open question below.

  • Probing is bounded. Slug availability and alias resolution are rate limited, and a resource the caller may not see returns the same response as one that does not exist.

  • Customer-defined roles remain out of scope. ADR-007 decision 4 stands: roles are the ones an application declares. Customer-defined roles, permission bundles and teams matter for larger organizations and are deferred to a later tier; the first audience is individual builders and small teams. This ADR does not change the role model.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Account and organization metadata does not leak through IDs, which keeps penetration-test and questionnaire answers short.
  • Data stays with the organization through renames and conversions, and a freed slug cannot inherit another tenant's data.
  • Applications written against slugs must change to key by organization ID. Existing rows keyed by a slug are attached to the organization's ID by an operator step before the key is switched.
  • Event tables keep cheap, ordered inserts without a mapping layer.
  • Splitting or merging is a data-and-registry operation, not a re-identification of every row.
  • The slug registry becomes a shared dependency of every application, so its availability and rate limits matter.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• UUIDv7 for every table. Rejected: it discloses account and organization creation time for a gain that is negligible at identity-table volumes.
  • UUIDv4 for every table. Rejected: append-only tables take most of the writes and benefit from ordered inserts, and their IDs disclose nothing their rows do not.
  • A private v7 key plus a public v4 key on every table. Rejected as the default: extra column, index and mapping for a benefit identity tables do not need (decision 1).
  • Encrypting or obfuscating identifiers. Rejected: it adds key management and loses ordering, and protects nothing that slugs and error responses do not already show. Identifiers are not secrets.
  • Keep keying tenants by slug. Rejected: a released slug can pass to a new owner after the cooling-off period.
  • A separate slug namespace for every application's organizations. Rejected: it breaks the single, shared experience across applications.
  • Pairwise subject identifiers per application. Not adopted now: it prevents cross-application correlation, which a single shared experience does not want. Reconsider if a deployment must isolate applications from each other.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Subject continuity on a split: an application that leaves keeps principal IDs, but the token issuer and sub it trusts change. Whether a deployment issues tokens under both issuers for a transition, or the application maps old subjects to new, is undecided.
  • Namespace of a deployment: whether the org namespace also needs a deployment qualifier so two deployments' registries can be merged without a policy, or whether the import policy is enough.
  • Which application-owned resources get slugs in the registry, and whether an application may keep its own slug table with only the namespace reservation held by SystemForge.
  • Rate limits for probing, their values, and whether availability checks require a signed-in caller.

docs.title: ADR-016: No Static API Keys — OAuth Grants for Non-Interactive Access
docs.text: Status: Proposed Deciders: @grokify Relates to: ADR-007 (memberships and entitlements as claims), ADR-010 (real-time access invalidation), ADR-015 (identifier policy; credentials are CSPRNG secrets, never identifiers). Updates: docs/design/architecture/authentication.md (non-interactive access).

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Applications on SystemForge have offered long-lived API keys for the cases a browser session does not cover: a command-line tool, an MCP server, a script, a CI job. An API key is a static bearer secret, and its authorization has to come from somewhere:

  • From the key itself (a role recorded at creation, or claims inside a JWT key): the role is frozen when the key is minted. Removing a person from an organization does not reach a key that outlives the access-change window, because ADR-010's revocation cache keeps entries only for the access-token lifetime.
  • From a lookup on every request: every application then needs its own membership source for keys, which ADR-007 decision 10 removes, and every key check becomes a database or network call.

Both make the key a second, weaker authorization path beside the token path every application already verifies. Security reviews also treat long-lived static secrets as a finding to be justified.

SystemAuth already issues short-lived JWT access tokens carrying the orgs claim, rotates refresh tokens on every use, revokes the token family when a used refresh token is presented again, and bounds a family's absolute lifetime.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. SystemForge offers no static API keys. Every non-interactive caller holds a credential that it exchanges at SystemAuth's token endpoint for a short-lived access token. Applications verify access tokens only; there is one authentication path, and the orgs claim in it is always current to within one token lifetime.

  2. The grant depends on who is calling.

Caller Grant What the caller holds A person at a terminal (CLI, MCP) Authorization code with PKCE and a loopback redirect (RFC 8252), then refresh tokens A refresh token: rotated on use, revoked as a family on reuse, bound to the client, with an absolute lifetime A person on a host without a browser Device authorization grant (RFC 8628) The same refresh token Automation holding a key pair (servers, scripts) Client credentials, authenticated with private_key_jwt (RFC 7523 section 2.2) A private key; SystemAuth stores only the public key CI and cloud workloads with their own identity JWT bearer grant (RFC 7523 section 2.1) trusting the platform's token, such as GitHub Actions OIDC Nothing stored: the platform issues the assertion per run AI agents AAuth (agent, resource and mission tokens) The agent's key; unchanged by this ADR

  1. Client credentials never use a shared secret in production. A client_secret for the client credentials grant is a static API key by another name. Confidential clients that call it authenticate with private_key_jwt or through federation; client_secret_basic and client_secret_post remain only for web relying parties completing an authorization code flow, and for development.

  2. Automation acts as a service principal in an organization. A client used for client credentials or the JWT bearer grant is owned by an organization and represented by a service principal that holds application roles there (ADR-007), assigned like a person's. Its access tokens carry an orgs claim with that one organization, so applications authorize it exactly as they authorize people. A client's access ends when its roles are removed or the client is disabled, through the same access-change records (ADR-010).

  3. Refresh tokens for people keep the existing policy: rotation on use, family revocation on reuse, an absolute lifetime (default 30 days), and revocation at sign-out. Native clients store them in the operating system's credential store where one exists.

  4. Migration. Applications remove their API-key routes, tables and checks. Tools that sent a static bearer token gain a login command using decision 2's grant for their caller.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One way in. Applications verify JWT access tokens and AAuth requests, nothing else; there is no per-application key table to secure, rotate or audit.
  • Current authorization everywhere. A role change reaches every caller within one access-token lifetime, or at once through the revocation cache.
  • No server-side secrets for automation. SystemAuth keeps public keys and federation trust, not shared secrets.
  • Every token issuance is an auditable event, at one place.
  • Command-line tools must implement a login (loopback browser flow, later device flow) instead of reading a key from the environment, and until they do, those tools cannot reach a hosted deployment.
  • Service principals in organizations are new work (decision 4): today a client-credentials token has no orgs claim.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Opaque API keys checked by each application. Rejected: a second authorization path, per-application tables, and stale roles unless every check calls SystemAuth.
  • API keys as long-lived JWTs carrying claims. Rejected: claims frozen at minting, outliving the revocation cache, readable by anyone holding the key, and all invalidated by a signing-key rotation.
  • Opaque API keys exchanged for access tokens (RFC 8693 token exchange). Workable, but it keeps a static secret where a refresh token (people) or a key pair or federation (automation) does the same job with standard grants and no stored secret.
  • Client credentials with a client secret. Rejected for production by decision 3: it is a static key.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Whether the device authorization grant is built on the current OAuth library or waits for a version that includes it.
  • How a federation trust maps an external subject (a repository and workflow, a cloud service account) to a service principal, and who in an organization may create one.
  • Whether a person may create a service principal in an organization, or only owners and admins.

docs.title: ADR-017: External Connections
docs.text: Status: Proposed Deciders: @grokify Relates to: ADR-013 (credentials are encrypted under keys it manages), ADR-008 (resource-scoped grants), ADR-015 (connections are keyed by organization ID, never by slug), ADR-002 (social sign-in identities, which this ADR keeps separate), ADR-016 (no static API keys for callers of the platform; it does not govern the credentials a third-party service issues). Builds on: connectforge, the generic connection-management library whose specifications define the mechanism. Updates: a new docs/design/architecture/connections.md.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Applications on SystemForge integrate with services their customers already use: a code host, a CDN, product analytics, monitoring, payments. Each integration needs an organization to authorize access to an account at that service and the application to use that authorization later, often from a background job. Without a shared mechanism every application stores its own tokens, in its own tables, with its own refresh logic and no common way to test, revoke or audit them.

The needs are the same across applications and providers:

  • One inventory per organization of what it has connected, shown in one place, reusable by every application the organization uses.
  • Credentials encrypted under managed keys, with tenant isolation as strong as the rest of the platform's data.
  • Connections that are tested, so a revoked token is found by a check, not by a failed feature.
  • Refresh and rotation that are safe when several processes use one connection.
  • Authorization and audit consistent with the platform's: who may use, share or disconnect a connection, and a record of each.

None of this is specific to identity, so the mechanism is its own module, connectforge, usable outside SystemForge. Its primary consumer is SystemForge, and this ADR records how the platform adopts it, in the same way ADR-013 records the adoption of keyforge.

There are already credentials in SystemForge, and they are a different thing. identity/credential holds what a principal uses to sign in; external_identity links a principal to a social sign-in account. A connection is what the platform uses to reach out to a third-party service on an organization's behalf. ADR-016 removes static API keys from the first direction. It cannot remove them from the second: many services issue only API tokens, and a connection stores what the service issues, preferring short-lived or app-based credentials (OAuth, GitHub App installations) where the service offers them.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
1. SystemForge adopts connectforge as its one mechanism for outbound connections to external services. Applications do not store third-party tokens themselves. SystemForge provides a thin connections package that composes connectforge with the platform, as keys does for keyforge (ADR-013 decision 1).
  2. connectforge owns the connection domain, including its schema. SystemForge imports its Ent-backed sqlstore, runs its migration on the platform database and does not copy, regenerate or merge the schema into SystemForge's Ent client. The two share the database, not code generation. connectforge's tables are prefixed connectforge_.
  3. The import direction is one way. SystemForge imports connectforge, keyforge and omnivault. connectforge imports none of them, nor any application. The connections package holds the adapters between them:
connectforge port SystemForge implementation Cryptographer keyforge client, purpose connectforge.credential (ADR-013) Stores and Leaser connectforge sqlstore on the platform database Authorizer authz.Authorizer, with connections as resources (decision 6) Auditor the platform audit trail (contract/audit) SecretSource omnivault, for platform-held secrets (decision 8) Tenant transaction hook rls, setting the organization for each transaction
  1. Connections belong to an organization. The connectforge owner is the organization ID, stored as text in owner_id (ADR-015: never a slug). A personal organization (ADR-006) can hold connections like any other.
  2. Tenant isolation holds twice. sqlstore filters every query by owner in code. On PostgreSQL, SystemForge also enables row-level security on every table sqlstore reports, with an rls migrator configured for the owner_id column, and primes each connectforge transaction through its hook so SET LOCAL applies. A bug in either layer alone does not expose another organization's connections.
  3. Connections are authorization resources. A connection is a resource of type connection in the platform's authorization, with the actions view, use, manage, share and disconnect.
  4. Organization owners and admins may manage, share and disconnect every connection in the organization.
  5. The principal who created a connection manages it.
  6. Members may view connections; collaborators (ADR-008) see none unless a connection is granted to them. Using a connection requires a grant, given to a principal, a service principal or an agent, through the resource-scoped grants of ADR-008.
  7. Every broker call checks use against current authorization; a saved job or an agent is re-checked when it runs, not only when it was set up.
  8. The actions map onto ADR-008's resource ladder, on resources of type systemforge_connection: view is view, use is edit, and manage, share and disconnect are manage. So a viewer grant lets a principal see a connection, contributor lets it use one, and maintainer lets it manage one. Organization owners and admins hold edit and manage through the organization; members hold only view.
  9. Applications reach a connection through SystemForge, not through connectforge directly. SystemForge exposes the connection operations in its API and SDK:
GET    /api/v1/providers
GET    /api/v1/organizations/{org}/connections
POST   /api/v1/organizations/{org}/connections
GET    /api/v1/organizations/{org}/connections/{id}
PATCH  /api/v1/organizations/{org}/connections/{id}
POST   /api/v1/organizations/{org}/connections/{id}/test
POST   /api/v1/organizations/{org}/connections/{id}/reconnect
GET    /api/v1/organizations/{org}/connections/{id}/bindings
PUT    /api/v1/organizations/{org}/connections/{id}/bindings
DELETE /api/v1/organizations/{org}/connections/{id}/bindings
GET    /api/v1/organizations/{org}/connections/{id}/grants
PUT    /api/v1/organizations/{org}/connections/{id}/grants/{principal}
DELETE /api/v1/organizations/{org}/connections/{id}/grants/{principal}
DELETE /api/v1/organizations/{org}/connections/{id}

Grants on a connection are the platform's resource grants (ADR-008), not a second authority held by connectforge: SystemForge registers the resource type systemforge_connection with its own vocabulary, so a grant is a role on a resource of that type and the role-based provider reads it.

The organization is in the path: it is the row-level security tenant of the request. Reads need the scope systemforge:connections:read and changes systemforge:connections:write. OAuth authorization, its callback and credential replacement join these routes when connectforge supports them.

In process, an application asks the connections package for an authenticated *http.Client and hands it to the provider's SDK. No API response, log or audit event contains a secret, and no browser code ever receives one. 8. Provider registration is the application's; platform secrets are the deployment's. An application registers the providers it needs, with their manifests and adapters, at startup. Secrets that belong to the deployment rather than to an organization, such as an OAuth client secret or a GitHub App private key, are read through omnivault and never stored in connectforge's tables. A GitHub App connection stores only the installation ID. 9. Sign-in and connections stay separate even when one provider serves both. The same GitHub App may be used for social sign-in (ADR-002) and for repository access. Signing in creates an external_identity for a principal; installing the app for an organization creates a connection. Neither implies the other, and disconnecting one does not affect the other. 10. Bindings make dependencies visible. An application records a binding when a feature starts depending on a connection. Disconnecting shows the bindings that would stop working, and requires confirmation when any exist. 11. Connection management is mounted in process. Like SystemAuth and the keyforge control plane (ADR-013 decision 1), it runs in the platform process; validation and refresh run as platform jobs. It is split out only when another process needs it. 12. The user interface is shared. Connection pages and widgets are built once, over the SystemForge API, so every application can embed a connection picker or a full settings section instead of building its own. Their component library is decided separately.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One inventory and one audit trail for every organization's external connections, across applications.
  • Applications stop holding third-party tokens. They receive an authenticated client, which removes most of the ways a token leaks.
  • A dependency on keyforge in production. Credentials cannot be read without it; a connection whose credential cannot be decrypted is not used. This makes ADR-013's wiring a prerequisite, and keyforge's release v0.1.0 is the minimum version.
  • More tables in the platform database, owned and migrated by another module. A connectforge upgrade can change the schema; it is applied by SystemForge's migrate command with the rest.
  • Row-level security covers tables SystemForge did not define, using a tenant column name other than its default. The rls migrator runs a second configuration for them.
  • Background jobs need an organization context to use a connection, so jobs run with the organization set, as requests do.
  • Provider coverage is the applications' work. SystemForge ships no provider-specific code beyond what connectforge provides.

docs.title: Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Each application stores its own tokens. Rejected: duplicated refresh and audit logic, no shared inventory, and every application becomes a place secrets can leak.
  • Build the mechanism inside SystemForge. Rejected for the same reasons as keyforge (ADR-013): it is not specific to identity, it deserves its own review, and other products can use it.
  • Extend identity/credential. Rejected: those credentials authenticate principals to the platform; outbound connections have a different owner (an organization), lifecycle (refresh, provider revocation, health) and threat model.
  • Generate connectforge's schema into SystemForge's Ent client. Rejected: it couples the two modules' code generation and Ent versions, and makes connectforge's schema changes SystemForge edits.
  • Store connection secrets in omnivault. Rejected for per-organization credentials: omnivault holds deployment secrets and returns plaintext; per-organization credentials need tenant isolation, versioning and envelope encryption bound to the connection.
  • A separate connection service on the data path. Deferred: in process is simpler and faster; the port boundaries let it move out later.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Whether usage is recorded as counters per connection and period, or as sampled events.
  • Whether an organization can share a connection with another organization (for example an agency and its client), and how that interacts with row-level security.
  • How agent-delegated authorization is expressed in grants when it is added.
  • Which roles, beyond owner and admin, may connect a new provider, and whether connecting a provider is gated by the organization's entitlements.

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text:
This page describes the authorization substrate as implemented in authz and its providers: the two-gate model, the application vocabulary, the base schema shared by every application, the role-based and relationship-based providers and what each can answer, the conformance suite that keeps them in step, and how identity changes reach them. The last section states the rules for application roles and for revocation in request authorization. The normative cross-application contract is Cross-Forge Authorization Conventions.

Decisions: ADR-007 (application roles), ADR-008 (resource-scoped collaborators, provider naming), ADR-010 (revocation cache as part of request authorization), ADR-005 (the manager relations in the base schema, see Managed Principals).

docs.title: The two-gate model
docs.text:
Every API operation is guarded by two independent checks, and both must pass:

Gate Question Evaluated against Role gate May this person ever do this? The principal's role in the organization, through authz.Authorizer.Can Scope gate May this credential do it right now? The OAuth scopes of the presenting credential (requestprincipal.RequestPrincipal.Scopes, from the access token, API key or session)

Effective access is the intersection: an organization admin presenting a token scoped to one read operation is read-only on that token. Scopes are namespaced per application ({app}:{resource}:{verb}, blanket {app}:admin) and never cross applications.

docs.title: Application vocabulary (authz.AppVocabulary)
docs.text:
An application registers its vocabulary at startup; registration validates it, and the IAM console and the composed SpiceDB schema are rendered from the registry.

type AppVocabulary interface {
    App() string                 // short lowercase identifier, ^[a-z][a-z0-9]{1,31}$
    Roles() RolePermissions      // role -> dotted permissions
    Hierarchy() RoleHierarchy    // every role in Roles() must appear
    Scopes() []string            // {app}:{resource}:{verb} or {app}:admin
    SpiceDBSchema() string       // "" when only the role-based provider is supported
}
Function Rule ValidateScope(app, scope) Scope matches the convention and its prefix is app ValidateAppSchema(app, schema) Every definition in the fragment is prefixed {app}_, so a fragment can never redefine a base or another application's definition; a definition that declares any of the reserved resource-role relations viewer, contributor, maintainer declares all three, binds each to principal, and has relation org: organization CollaboratorDefinitions(schema) The definitions of a fragment that declare the whole ladder, that is, the resource types that accept collaborators VocabularyRegistry.ValidateResourceType(type) {app}_{type} whose application is registered and, when the vocabulary carries a fragment, whose definition is collaborator-able; a vocabulary with no fragment accepts any type of its application VocabularyRegistry.CollaboratorResourceTypes(app) The sorted collaborator-able types of an application's fragment ValidateVocabulary(v) App name, non-empty roles, hierarchy covering every role, scopes valid and unique, schema prefixed VocabularyRegistry.Register(v) Validates; refuses a duplicate app VocabularyRegistry.AllScopes() Every registered scope, sorted, for consent screens and AllowedScopes VocabularyRegistry.ComposeSpiceDBSchema() Base schema followed by each registered fragment in registration order; fails on any duplicate definition

The organization roles are owner(100) / admin(80) / member(40) / collaborator(20), with guest(10) for applications that model one (authz.DefaultRoleHierarchy), and authz.DefaultRolePermissions maps the first three to dotted org.*, member.* and resource.* permissions; a collaborator has none, since a collaborator's access is per resource (below). editor and viewer are not organization roles. An application's own roles are its vocabulary's: they appear in both Roles() and Hierarchy() and are separate from the organization roles and from the resource roles.

docs.title: The {app}_org facet
docs.text:
An application's SpiceDB fragment attaches to the shared organization through a facet definition that references it and adds the application's own relations; generic membership flows through arrows (org->view):

definition myapp_org {
    relation org: organization
    relation approver: principal

    permission read    = org->view
    permission write   = org->edit
    permission approve = org->manage + approver
}

definition myapp_document {
    relation app_org: myapp_org
    permission read  = app_org->read
    permission write = app_org->write
}

docs.title: Base schema (authz.BaseSpiceDBSchema)
docs.text:
Owned by the platform; applications never redefine these definitions.

Definition Relations Permissions principal guardian, educator (ADR-005 manager roles) manage_account = guardian; manage_credentials = guardian + educator; view_profile = guardian + educator; manage_managers = guardian organization owner, admin, member, collaborator manage = owner + admin; edit = manage; contribute = edit + member; view = contribute; list = view + collaborator; invite_member, remove_member, change_role, settings = manage; delete = owner platform admin super_admin = admin

The same grants exist as Go tables so the role-based provider evaluates them identically: authz.OrgRolePermissions / OrgRoleAllows (the PermOrg* constants in authz/org.go) and authz.ManagerRolePermissions / ManagerRoleAllows (authz/manager.go). authz/schema_parity_test.go parses the schema and fails if either table drifts from it.

docs.title: Providers
docs.text:
ADR-008 names the modes for what they evaluate. The packages were renamed ahead of the ADR; the old paths forward to the new ones as deprecated packages (// Deprecated: notices name the next major release as their removal). They forward only what existed under the old path.

Mode Package Formerly Evaluates Role-based (rbac) authz/rbac authz/simple (deprecated forwarder: simple.Provider = rbac.Provider, simple.New = rbac.New, options likewise) Roles, resource ownership, organization role, manager role Relationship-based (rebac) authz/rebac/spicedb authz/spicedb (deprecated forwarder) Permissions derived through relationships by a SpiceDB engine

Both implement authz.Authorizer (Can, CanAll, CanAny, Filter), authz.OrgAuthorizer (CanForOrg, GetRole, IsMember) and authz.PlatformAuthorizer (IsPlatformAdmin); rbac also implements authz.DecisionAuthorizer (Decide, returning a reason and policy ID). authz.FeatureAuthorizer is declared and has no implementation.

docs.title: Role-based provider (rbac.Provider)
docs.text:
Configured with options: WithRoleHierarchy, WithPermissions, WithRoleGetter (principal's role in an organization; wire organization.MembershipRoleGetter(svc)), WithPlatformAdminChecker and WithPlatformAdminBypass, WithManagerRoleGetter (wire managedprincipal.Service.ManagerRoles), WithOwnerFullAccess. Decide evaluates in this order:

  1. Platform admin bypass, when enabled and the checker says so.
  2. Resource owner, when WithOwnerFullAccess and Resource.OwnerID is the principal.
  3. Resource type principal with an ID: a manager role that grants the action (ManagerRoleAllows), through the manager role getter.
  4. A base organization permission (IsOrgPermission(action)) on an organization resource: the principal's organization role through the role getter, judged by OrgRoleAllows.
  5. No Resource.OrgID: owner only.
  6. Otherwise the organization role's permissions, keyed as {resource type}.{action} in RolePermissions.

Filter runs Can per resource.

docs.title: Relationship-based provider (spicedb.Provider)
docs.text:
A thin provider over spicedb.Client: Can is a Check with subject principal:<id>, resource <type>:<id> and the action as the permission; GetRole reads the organization's membership relations (owner, admin, member, collaborator), and IsMember checks list, which every membership grants, collaborators included; Filter checks per resource. The client wraps schema writes and reads, relationship writes and deletes (ReplaceRelationships applies deletes and writes in one request), LookupSubjects and LookupResources; a lookup stream that fails returns the error rather than a partial list. spicedb.Syncer implements authz.RelationshipSyncer by writing and deleting base-schema relationships, authz.AppRoleSyncer for application roles and authz.ResourceGrantSyncer for resource grants.

With spicedb.WithResourceGrants(store) the provider implements authz.ResourceGranter. The store is the same resourcegrant.Service the role-based provider uses, built with WithAuthzSyncer(spicedb.NewSyncer(c), mode): it keeps the rows the graph cannot (the collaborator membership behind the orgs claim, the last-grant test, access changes) and mirrors each change into the graph, so a deployment that switches modes rebuilds its relationships from the membership, role and grant tables. A grant is the relationship {type}:{id}#{role}@principal:{principal}; changing a role deletes the other two ladder relations in the same request; the collaborator membership is organization:{org}#collaborator@principal:{principal}. The application writes a resource's org relation when it creates the resource, which is what lets organization members reach it through org->view. ListResources is LookupResources for the permission; it follows every relationship the schema expresses, so its answer is IDs and OrganizationIDs is empty.

docs.title: Resource grants
docs.text:
ADR-008 gives a collaborator access to individual resources through a standard ladder of resource roles, reserved in the conventions:

Resource role Permissions on the resource authz viewer view ResourceRoleViewer contributor view, edit ResourceRoleContributor maintainer view, edit, manage ResourceRoleMaintainer

authz.ResourceRolePermissions holds the table, and authz.ResourceRoleFragment(type) generates the standard definition it mirrors; schema_parity_test.go keeps the two equal. The contract is authz.ResourceGranter:

GrantResourceRole(ctx, principalID, ref ResourceRef, role string, grantedBy uuid.UUID) error
RevokeResourceRole(ctx, principalID, ref ResourceRef) error
ListResourceGrants(ctx, ref ResourceRef) ([]Grant, error)
ListResources(ctx, principalID, resourceType string, permission Action) (ResourceSet, error)

ResourceRef{Type, ID, OrganizationID} names a resource by its definition name ({app}_{type}), the application's own string identifier and the organization that owns it. A first grant gives a non-member a collaborator membership; revoking their last grant removes it; a lower role or a revoke records a grant_reduced access change.

Role-based provider. rbac.WithResourceGrants(store) takes a store that is both a ResourceGranter and an authz.ResourceGrantReader; identity/resourcegrant.Service over the Ent client is the store (see Resource grants). The provider delegates GrantResourceRole, RevokeResourceRole and ListResourceGrants, and extends the evaluation order of Decide and Can with one step after the organization role:

  1. A resource with an ID whose action is view, edit or manage: the principal's grant on it, when its membership in the organization is active, judged by ResourceRoleAllows.

ListResources returns an authz.ResourceSet with two parts, which an application applies as organization_id IN (OrganizationIDs) OR id IN (IDs): IDs are the resources the principal holds a grant on whose role grants the permission; OrganizationIDs are the organizations in which the principal's organization role grants {resourceType}.{permission} in the provider's permission map, which makes the permission hold on every resource of the type there. Platform-admin bypass and resource ownership, which Can honors, are not enumerated. A provider built without a store answers as before and returns rbac.ErrNoResourceGrants from the grant operations.

docs.title: Conformance (authz/providertest)
docs.text: providertest.RunAll(t, Config{Provider: p}) runs the interface, behavior and integration tiers against any provider; RunOrgPermissionTests (with Config.GrantOrgRole) asserts the organization grants of the base schema, and RunManagerRelationTests (with Config.GrantManager) the manager grants. RunResourceGrantTests (with Config.ResourceGranter, GrantOrgRole and, for a database-backed provider, NewPrincipal and NewOrganization) covers the grant contract: the collaborator lifecycle, the ladder, reductions, revocation, what a collaborator may do on the organization, and ListResources for each permission. The role-based provider runs it in authz/rbac/resource_grants_test.go, on SQLite and on PostgreSQL; the relationship-based provider runs it in authz/rebac/spicedb/integration_grants_test.go (build tag integration) against an embedded in-memory SpiceDB, with the deployment schema composed from a registered vocabulary. The suites are what makes the modes interchangeable on the platform contract.

docs.title: Capability table
docs.text:
What each provider can answer:

Question rbac rebac Does the principal's organization or application role grant this action? yes yes Does the principal own this resource? yes (WithOwnerFullAccess, Resource.OwnerID supplied by the caller) yes Does the principal hold a direct grant on this specific resource? yes, from sf_resource_grants yes, as a relationship Which resources of a type may the principal view, edit or manage? yes: grants plus the organizations whose role grants it yes: LookupResources Does a permission reach the principal through relationships (team membership, a parent resource, a share with a group)? no yes, through the schema fragment

docs.title: Choosing a mode
docs.text:
Use rbac while Switch to rebac when Access is organization roles, application roles and direct grants on resources Permissions flow through relationships: nested groups or teams, folder-style hierarchies, "shared with me" graphs One level of inheritance (organization to resource) is enough Resources inherit from parents more than one level deep Listing a principal's resources is a SQL query Lookups span very large organizations or need SpiceDB's consistency tokens One deployment, one process Several services or regions share one authorization graph

An application written to the contract switches by configuration; the cost of rebac is operational (a service with its own datastore, schema management, relationship sync).

docs.title: Configuring the mode (authz key)
docs.text:
The mode is the authz key of the SystemAuth configuration file (systemauth.Config.Authz, an authz.ModeConfig), validated with the rest of the file:

authz:
  mode: rebac            # rbac (default) | rebac
  engine: spicedb        # rebac only; default spicedb
  spicedb:
    mode: remote         # embedded (default) | remote
    endpoint: spicedb.internal:50051
    token: ${SPICEDB_TOKEN}
    write_schema: false  # remote only: write the composed schema at startup
Key Meaning mode rbac evaluates roles and direct grants in process from the tables; rebac evaluates relationships with an engine. Default rbac engine The relationship engine, for rebac only; spicedb is the only one today and the default. Giving it with rbac is an error, so a leftover setting is not silently ignored spicedb.mode embedded runs an instance in the process (datastore_engine memory or postgres with datastore_uri); remote connects to endpoint with token, over TLS unless insecure spicedb.write_schema Embedded instances always get the composed schema (they start empty). A remote instance's schema is an operational decision, so it is written only when this is set

authz/mode.New(ctx, cfg, Deps{DB, Registry, ...}) builds the provider from it: it applies the defaults, validates, and for rebac starts or connects to the engine and writes the schema composed from the registered vocabularies. It returns a mode.Result carrying Provider (an authz.Provider: PlatformAuthorizer and ResourceGranter), the Syncer to pass to the identity services (the no-op syncer for rbac, which reads the tables at check time; the engine's for rebac), the grant store Grants (invite.WithResourceGrants) and Close(). The package is separate from authz because both providers import it, and so that loading a configuration file does not link the SpiceDB server: authz.SpiceDBConfig is the engine's configuration type (spicedb.Config is an alias).

The membership, role and grant tables are the record in both modes. Under rebac the identity services mirror each change into the graph as it is made (organization memberships, application roles, resource grants), so a deployment that switches from rbac starts with an empty graph: write the existing rows through the syncer before the first request is served. No bulk rebuild command ships yet.

docs.title: Keeping providers in step with identity
docs.text:
Identity changes reach the authorization backend through authz.RelationshipSyncer, called explicitly by the services after their database transaction commits; there are no Ent hooks.

Caller Syncer calls organization.Service RegisterOrganization (create), AddOrgMembership, UpdateOrgMembership (role change, both sides of an ownership transfer), RemoveOrgMembership, UnregisterOrganization (delete) approle.Service (with WithAuthzSyncer) AddAppRole (assign, and the new role of a change), RemoveAppRole (remove, the old role of a change, RemoveForMember) managedprincipal.Service RegisterPrincipal, AddPrincipalManager, RemovePrincipalManager marketplace (marketplace.AuthzSyncer, SpiceDBSyncer) Listing, license, license revocation, seat assignment and unassignment, subscription relationships

AddAppRole and RemoveAppRole belong to the optional interface authz.AppRoleSyncer, which noop, spicedb.Syncer and the test recorder implement. A syncer that implements only RelationshipSyncer keeps compiling and working: callers type-assert and skip application roles when it is not an AppRoleSyncer. spicedb.Syncer writes {application}_org:{org}#{role}@principal:{principal}, the facet an application's schema fragment attaches to the base organization; an application identifier that is not a valid app name is refused. An owner's implicit admin is not a stored role and is not written; an application's schema fragment must derive it from the owner relation. organization.Service.RemoveMember removes the member's application roles from the graph after its transaction commits; SCIM group member removal deletes the rows but, like its membership changes, makes no syncer call.

invite.Service.Accept writes the membership directly and makes no syncer call. authz.SyncMode decides what a sync failure does: strict returns it, eventual (the default) logs it. noop.NewSyncer() is the default syncer and what a role-based deployment uses, since rbac reads the membership and relationship tables through its getters at check time.

authz.Middleware (RequireAction, RequireAnyAction, RequireAllActions) adapts an Authorizer to HTTP, building the principal and organization from session/middleware claims. The organization, invite, marketplace and managed-principal APIs call the authorizer directly with the PermOrg* and manager permissions.

docs.title: Request authorization
docs.text: A request is authorized by the authenticator (requestprincipal.Middleware with relyingparty.RequestAuthenticator, or SystemAuth's own token middleware) establishing the principal and its scopes, and then by the handler's Authorizer.Can call. SystemAuth checks that a token's principal is still active on every token issue, refresh, introspection and userinfo call (PrincipalStatus). A token issued before a membership or role change is otherwise honored until it expires (10 minutes by default, 15 at most), unless the relying party consults a revocation cache: SystemAuth records each such change in sf_access_changes, and relyingparty.BearerMiddleware and the BFF refuse tokens issued before it (ADR-010; see the organizations page and Revocation cache in request authorization).

docs.title: Access-change reasons
docs.text:
Every row of sf_access_changes carries a reason. The reasons are an open, validated registry, not a database enum:

  • The column is a string, so adding a reason needs no migration.
  • The constants live in one package, identity/accesschange, and are listed in accesschange.Reasons(). accesschange.Record rejects a value that is not registered with an error naming it, and Reason.Valid() reports membership.
  • Every registered reason has a row in the table below. TestRegistry, TestReasonsAreDocumented and TestCallSitesUseRegisteredReasons fail when a constant is not registered, a reason has no row (or a row names no reason), or a call site builds an accesschange.Change with anything other than a registered constant.
  • Reasons are wire values. They are carried unchanged in the back-channel access_change event and in GET /access-changes, so a reason is never renamed or reused for a different meaning. Relying parties treat the reason as opaque and tolerate one they do not know, so adding a reason does not break an older relying party.

To add a reason: declare the constant and list it in Reasons(), add a row here, and use it at the call site that records the change. Record the reason that says what happened to the principal; do not reuse a near match, which is how an invitation that put a principal under management came to be recorded as a reduced grant.

Reason Meaning Recorded by membership_removed The principal was removed from, or deactivated in, an organization organization.RemoveMember; UpdateMember setting a membership inactive (scoped to the organization) org_role_changed The principal's organization role changed UpdateMember changing the role; TransferOwnership, for both principals (scoped) app_role_changed An application role was changed or removed approle.Change to a different role, Remove, RemoveForMember (scoped); assignment only adds access and records nothing deactivated The principal was deactivated principal.Deactivate; managedprincipal.Delete (every organization) sessions_revoked The principal's sessions or tokens were revoked token.RevokeAllForPrincipal, EntStorage.RevokeSubjectTokens for a principal subject, managedprincipal.RevokeSession and RevokeAll (every organization) management_granted The principal came under management and gave up the capabilities managed principals do not hold managedprincipal.AcceptManagerInvite (every organization) management_ended The principal's management ended and its own capabilities were restored managedprincipal.Release; RemoveManager removing the last manager of a principal with a verified email (every organization) grant_reduced A resource grant was reduced or removed resourcegrant.Service.GrantResourceRole giving a lower role, RevokeResourceRole (scoped to the resource's organization); granting or raising a role records nothing. Revoking a collaborator's last grant also records membership_removed

docs.title: Rules for application roles and revocation
docs.text: These rules are implemented as described; the ADR each names holds the reasoning.

docs.title: Resource-scoped collaborators (ADR-008)
docs.text:
• The base organization definition, authz.OrgRolePermissions, the parity test and the conventions carry the collaborator relation and the list permission. A collaborator is a principal with a membership of role collaborator, who has no view, edit or manage on the organization; personal organizations accept such memberships.
  • The standard resource-role ladder, the grant contract, both providers' implementations, the vocabulary validation of collaborator-able definitions and the shared suite across both modes are described in Resource grants.
  • sf_invites carries an optional resource type, resource ID and resource role; accepting such an invite creates the collaborator membership and the grant in one transaction (see Invites).
  • The authz configuration key and authz/mode.New are described in Configuring the mode.
  • The orgs claim (ADR-007) lists a collaborator's organizations with role collaborator; the resources are the application's to look up with ListResources. Agents and managed principals are principals like any other, so they are granted through the same operations, which confines them to the granted resources.

docs.title: Application roles (ADR-007)
docs.text:
• The sf_app_roles table records the application role per (principal, organization, application) (see Organizations). A seat-licensed application counts its rows against the license; the marketplace's seat assignments remain a separate record. Role changes reach the authorization graph through AppRoleSyncer.
  • Owners hold admin in every entitled application implicitly. Admins manage the organization but hold only the application roles assigned to them, like members; an admin may assign roles to themself, explicitly and audited. Members and admins have no application access by default.
  • The roles available in an application are the ones its vocabulary declares (standard ladder viewer, contributor, maintainer, admin); there are no custom roles, and organization-defined roles and teams do not exist.
  • Removal from the organization removes every application role and every resource grant.

docs.title: Revocation cache in request authorization (ADR-010)
docs.text:
• Request authorization has a step between token verification and the permission check: the relying party looks up its revocation cache by principal (and organization) and accepts the token only if its iat is at or after the recorded changed_at plus the clock-skew margin; otherwise it answers 401 with the standard expired-token error so the client refreshes.
  • The cache is filled from SystemAuth's sf_access_changes (shared memory in a modular monolith, polling across replicas, back-channel access_change events across deployments) and rebuilt after a restart from GET /access-changes?since=; the relyingparty package implements all three (see Token freshness and revocation). Applications that bypass relyingparty must implement the same check.
  • Changes to resource grants that reduce access (ADR-008) are access changes and invalidate the same way.
  • Agent tokens are out of scope: AAuth tokens carry their own cascading revocation keyed by jti.

docs.title: Managed Principals and Manager Relationships
docs.text:
This page describes managed principals as implemented in identity/managedprincipal, identity/credential and SystemAuth (identity/systemauth): what makes a principal managed, the invariants the service enforces, the built-in manager roles, the login_token credential and its exchange, the claims a managed session carries, what managers can see and revoke, how an email is attached, how management ends (release), how a self-managed human consents to be managed (manager invitations), and how a managed principal's slug is chosen. The user-facing guide is Managed Principals.

Decisions: ADR-005 (managed principals and manager relationships), ADR-009 (management is a relationship, not the absence of an email; amends ADR-005), ADR-006 (how a managed principal's slug is chosen), ADR-010 (access changes recorded when management starts or ends).

docs.title: Definition as implemented
docs.text:
A managed principal is a Principal(type=human) with at least one active row in sf_manager_relationships as the managed side (ADR-009). The email plays no part: a managed principal may have none, an unverified one, or a verified one. That is the test everywhere in the code:

Check Where Service.IsManaged(principalID) An active manager relationship exists (hasActiveManager) Manager authority checks (authorizeCredentials, authorizeAccount, checkIssuer) Require the target to be an active human with an active manager relationship before consulting the authorizer; otherwise ErrNotManaged Login-token exchange (verifyLoginToken) Requires the principal to be active and HumanPrincipal.Managed; an email does not matter managed claim Emitted when the session's principal has an active manager relationship (HumanPrincipal.Managed, loaded with the principal)

A managed principal is created with principal.ManagedHumanCapabilities() (CanAccessUI only: CanManageProfile and CanDelegate are false) and sf_principals.identifier = "human:<principal-id>", a lookup key rather than an address. signup.validateEmail requires a plain address, so a managed identifier can never be looked up as an email.

docs.title: Enabling
docs.text:
Managed principals exist only when both gates are open:

Gate Setting Deployment systemauth config managed_principals.enabled (ManagedPrincipalsConfig.Enabled), default off Client sf_oauth_apps.managed_principals_enabled or config clients[].managed_principals, default off

systemauth.Server.ManagedPrincipalsAllowed(ctx, clientID) evaluates both and is the managedprincipal.Gate the service consults; Server.LoginTokenPolicy(ctx, clientID) supplies lifetimes (below).

docs.title: sf_manager_relationships (identity/ent/schema/manager_relationship.go)
docs.text:
Column Notes managed_principal_id The principal being managed; immutable manager_principal_id The manager; immutable role guardian, educator, or a role registered with managedprincipal.WithRoles; immutable active Removal deactivates rather than deletes; re-adding reactivates created_by The actor that established the relationship

Unique on (managed_principal_id, manager_principal_id, role).

docs.title: sf_manager_claims (identity/ent/schema/manager_claim.go)
docs.text:
A single-use code with which a human with an email becomes guardian of a managed principal. Kept apart from sf_credentials so a claim code can never sign anyone in.

Column Notes managed_principal_id The principal the claim grants guardianship of code_prefix SFMC plus 8 characters, unique, used to look the claim up code_hash SHA-256 of the full code (SFMC + 160 random bits, base32) issued_by, expires_at Issuer and expiry (DefaultClaimTTL 7 days, WithClaimTTL) redeemed_at, redeemed_by Set once; a redeemed or expired claim is refused

docs.title: sf_manager_invites (identity/ent/schema/manager_invite.go)
docs.text:
A single-use invitation with which a human with a verified email offers to manage a self-managed human. Kept apart from organization invites (sf_invites), which grant membership rather than authority over a person.

Column Notes manager_principal_id The inviter, who becomes a manager on acceptance email Verified address of the invited human; only a principal whose verified email matches (case-insensitive) can accept role The manager role the inviter will hold token_prefix, token_hash SFMI plus 8 characters, unique, used to look it up; SHA-256 of the full token (SFMI + 160 random bits, base32) expires_at DefaultInviteTTL 7 days, WithInviteTTL accepted_at, accepted_by, revoked_at, declined_at, declined_by Set once; an accepted, revoked, declined or expired invitation is refused

docs.title: sf_credentials type login_token (identity/ent/schema/credential.go)
