docs.title: SystemForge OAuth 2.0 Server - Product Requirements Document
docs.text:
Status: Implemented in v0.1.0

This PRD defined the requirements for SystemForge OAuth 2.0 server. The features described below have been implemented in the following modules:

  • identity/oauth/ - OAuth 2.0 server with Fosite
  • identity/ent/schema/ - OAuth-related Ent schemas (oauth_app, oauth_token, service_account, etc.)

Implemented Grants: - Authorization Code + PKCE - Client Credentials - Refresh Token with rotation - JWT Bearer (RFC 7523)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: SystemForge OAuth Server provides a complete OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect implementation for multi-tenant SaaS applications. It enables first-party applications (SPAs, mobile apps) and third-party integrations to securely access APIs.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. Developer Self-Service: Developers can create OAuth apps and service accounts without admin intervention
  2. Security First: Implement modern OAuth 2.0 best practices (PKCE, token rotation, short-lived tokens)
  3. Multi-Tenant: OAuth apps can be scoped to organizations or platform-wide
  4. Batteries Included: Works out of the box with sensible defaults

docs.title: 1. Platform Developer (First-Party)
docs.text:
• Building the React SPA frontend
  • Needs secure authentication without exposing tokens to JavaScript
  • Uses BFF pattern or Authorization Code + PKCE

docs.title: 2. Integration Developer (Third-Party)
docs.text:
• Building integrations with the platform
  • Creates OAuth apps to get client credentials
  • Uses Authorization Code flow for user-context or Client Credentials for service-context

docs.title: 3. DevOps/Automation Engineer
docs.text:
• Running CI/CD pipelines, cron jobs, scripts
  • Creates service accounts with key pairs
  • Uses JWT Bearer grant for secure, keyless authentication

docs.title: 4. Platform Administrator
docs.text:
• Manages OAuth apps and service accounts across the platform
  • Reviews API access and usage
  • Revokes compromised credentials

docs.title: F1: OAuth App Management
docs.text:
F1.1: Create OAuth App - Developer provides: name, description, redirect URIs, app type - System generates: client_id, client_secret - App types: web (confidential), spa (public), native (public), service (confidential)

F1.2: App Settings - Allowed grant types (based on app type) - Allowed scopes - Token lifetimes (access, refresh) - Redirect URI validation (exact match or wildcard for subdomains)

F1.3: Secret Management - Rotate client secret (generates new, old valid for grace period) - View secret only at creation (hashed storage) - Multiple active secrets during rotation

F1.4: Organization Scoping - Apps can be organization-scoped (only org members can authorize) - Apps can be platform-wide (any user can authorize)

docs.title: F2: Service Accounts
docs.text:
F2.1: Create Service Account - Name, description, scopes - No human user - represents a service/automation - Tied to an organization or platform-wide

F2.2: Key Pair Management - Generate RSA or EC key pairs - Download private key (shown once) - Public key stored for JWT verification - Multiple keys for rotation (max 10) - Key expiration dates

F2.3: Impersonation (Optional) - Service account can impersonate users (with admin grant) - Useful for admin tools, migrations

docs.title: F3: OAuth 2.0 Grants
docs.text:
F3.1: Authorization Code + PKCE - Required for all public clients (SPAs, mobile, CLI) - Optional for confidential clients - S256 challenge method required

F3.2: Client Credentials - For confidential clients only - No user context - service-to-service - Scopes limited to what app is granted

F3.3: Refresh Token - Rotation on use (new refresh token each time) - Absolute expiration (max lifetime) - Revocation on reuse (theft detection)

F3.4: JWT Bearer (RFC 7523) - For service accounts - Client creates signed JWT assertion - Server verifies signature with stored public key - Short-lived assertions (max 1 hour)

docs.title: F4: Token Management
docs.text:
F4.1: Access Tokens - JWT format with standard claims - Short-lived (15 minutes default) - Contains: sub, aud, scope, org_id, client_id

F4.2: Refresh Tokens - Opaque tokens (database lookup) - Longer-lived (7 days default, 90 days max) - Tied to client and user

F4.3: Token Introspection (RFC 7662) - Check if token is active - Get token metadata - For resource servers

F4.4: Token Revocation (RFC 7009) - Revoke access or refresh token - Revoke all tokens for user/client

docs.title: F5: OpenID Connect
docs.text:
F5.1: Discovery - /.well-known/openid-configuration - Advertises supported features

F5.2: JWKS - /.well-known/jwks.json - Public keys for token verification

F5.3: UserInfo - /oauth/userinfo - Returns user profile based on scopes

F5.4: ID Tokens - JWT with user identity - Returned alongside access token - Standard OIDC claims

docs.title: F6: Scopes
docs.text:
F6.1: Standard Scopes 

openid        - Required for OIDC
profile       - User profile (name, picture)
email         - User email
offline_access - Request refresh token

F6.2: API Scopes 

read:users         - Read user data
write:users        - Modify user data
read:organizations - Read org data
write:organizations - Modify org data
admin:*            - Full admin access

F6.3: Scope Consent - First-party apps: auto-approve configured scopes - Third-party apps: user consent screen - Remember consent (don't ask again)

docs.title: F7: Security
docs.text:
F7.1: Rate Limiting - Token endpoint: 100 req/min per client - Authorization endpoint: 20 req/min per IP - Failed auth lockout: 5 failures = 15 min lockout

F7.2: Audit Logging - All token grants logged - Failed attempts logged - Token revocations logged

F7.3: Threat Detection - Refresh token reuse detection - Unusual grant patterns - Geographic anomalies (optional)

docs.title: Flow 1: Developer Creates OAuth App
docs.text:
1. Developer logs into Developer Portal
  2. Navigates to "OAuth Apps" → "Create App"
  3. Fills form: name, type (SPA), redirect URIs
  4. System generates client_id
  5. For confidential apps: shows client_secret once
  6. Developer copies credentials to their app config

docs.title: Flow 2: SPA User Login (Authorization Code + PKCE)
docs.text:
1. User clicks "Login" in React SPA
  2. SPA generates code_verifier and code_challenge
  3. SPA redirects to /oauth/authorize?...&code_challenge=xxx
  4. User sees login page, authenticates
  5. User sees consent screen (if third-party)
  6. SystemForge redirects to SPA with authorization code
  7. SPA exchanges code + code_verifier for tokens
  8. SPA stores access token, uses for API calls

docs.title: Flow 3: Service Account Access (JWT Bearer)
docs.text:
1. DevOps creates service account in portal
  2. Generates key pair, downloads private key
  3. CI/CD pipeline creates JWT signed with private key
  4. Pipeline calls /oauth/token with JWT assertion
  5. SystemForge verifies signature, issues access token
  6. Pipeline uses access token for API calls

docs.title: Flow 4: Third-Party Integration
docs.text:
1. Third-party developer creates OAuth app
  2. Their users click "Connect to [Platform]"
  3. User authorizes access on consent screen
  4. Third-party receives tokens
  5. Third-party stores refresh token, uses access token
  6. Third-party refreshes tokens as needed

docs.title: Success Metrics
docs.text:
1. Adoption: Number of OAuth apps created
  2. Security: Zero token leaks, low failed auth rate
  3. Reliability: Token endpoint 99.9% uptime
  4. Performance: Token issuance < 100ms p99
  5. Developer Experience: < 30 min to first successful API call

docs.title: Non-Goals (v1)
docs.text:
• SAML support
  • Social login providers (handled separately)
  • Fine-grained consent (scope-by-scope)
  • Dynamic client registration (RFC 7591)
  • Pushed Authorization Requests (RFC 9126)

docs.title: Timeline
docs.text: Phase Features Target Phase 1 OAuth App CRUD, Client Credentials, PKCE Week 1-2 Phase 2 Service Accounts, JWT Bearer Week 3 Phase 3 OpenID Connect, Discovery Week 4 Phase 4 Consent UI, Third-party flows Week 5 Phase 5 Audit logging, Rate limiting Week 6

docs.title: Open Questions
docs.text:
1. Should we support PAR (Pushed Authorization Requests) for enhanced security?
  2. Should service accounts support organization impersonation?
  3. What's the maximum number of OAuth apps per organization?
  4. Should we implement DPoP for access tokens (beyond BFF)?

Status: Implemented in v0.1.0

// oauth/ent/schema/oauth_app.go
package schema

type OAuthApp struct {
    ent.Schema
}

func (OAuthApp) Fields() []ent.Field {
    return []ent.Field{
        field.UUID("id", uuid.UUID{}).Default(uuid.New),

        // Identification
        field.String("client_id").Unique().Immutable().
            DefaultFunc(generateClientID), // cf_app_xxx
        field.String("name").NotEmpty().MaxLen(255),
        field.String("description").Optional().MaxLen(1000),
        field.String("logo_url").Optional(),

        // App type determines allowed grants
        field.Enum("app_type").
            Values("web", "spa", "native", "service").
            Default("web"),

        // Ownership
        field.UUID("owner_id", uuid.UUID{}),           // User who created
        field.UUID("organization_id", uuid.UUID{}).    // Org scope (optional)
            Optional().Nillable(),

        // Configuration
        field.JSON("redirect_uris", []string{}).Default([]string{}),
        field.JSON("allowed_scopes", []string{}).Default([]string{}),
        field.JSON("allowed_grants", []string{}).
            Default([]string{"authorization_code", "refresh_token"}),

        // Token settings
        field.Int("access_token_ttl").Default(900),      // 15 min
        field.Int("refresh_token_ttl").Default(604800),  // 7 days
        field.Bool("refresh_token_rotation").Default(true),

        // Flags
        field.Bool("first_party").Default(false),  // Skip consent
        field.Bool("active").Default(true),
        field.Time("revoked_at").Optional().Nillable(),

        // Timestamps
        field.Time("created_at").Default(time.Now),
        field.Time("updated_at").Default(time.Now).UpdateDefault(time.Now),
    }
}

func (OAuthApp) Edges() []ent.Edge {
    return []ent.Edge{
        edge.From("owner", User.Type).Ref("oauth_apps").Unique().Required(),
        edge.From("organization", Organization.Type).Ref("oauth_apps").Unique(),
        edge.To("secrets", AppSecret.Type),
        edge.To("tokens", OAuthToken.Type),
        edge.To("consents", Consent.Type),
    }
}

func (OAuthApp) Indexes() []ent.Index {
    return []ent.Index{
        index.Fields("client_id").Unique(),
        index.Fields("owner_id"),
        index.Fields("organization_id"),
    }
}

docs.title: Authorization Code + PKCE
docs.text:
// oauth/token/grants/authcode.go
type AuthCodeGrant struct {
    store      Store
    tokenSvc   *TokenService
    codeTTL    time.Duration
}

func (g *AuthCodeGrant) GrantType() string {
    return "authorization_code"
}

func (g *AuthCodeGrant) Validate(ctx context.Context, req *TokenRequest) error {
    // 1. Lookup authorization code
    code, err := g.store.GetAuthCode(ctx, hashCode(req.Code))
    if err != nil {
        return ErrInvalidGrant
    }

    // 2. Check expiration
    if time.Now().After(code.ExpiresAt) {
        return ErrInvalidGrant
    }

    // 3. Check if already used
    if code.Used {
        // Possible replay attack - revoke all tokens in family
        g.tokenSvc.RevokeFamily(ctx, code.FamilyID)
        return ErrInvalidGrant
    }

    // 4. Verify PKCE
    if code.CodeChallenge != "" {
        if req.CodeVerifier == "" {
            return ErrInvalidGrant
        }
        challenge := computeS256Challenge(req.CodeVerifier)
        if !secureCompare(challenge, code.CodeChallenge) {
            return ErrInvalidGrant
        }
    }

    // 5. Verify redirect_uri matches
    if req.RedirectURI != code.RedirectURI {
        return ErrInvalidGrant
    }

    // 6. Verify client
    if req.ClientID != code.AppID {
        return ErrInvalidGrant
    }

    return nil
}

func (g *AuthCodeGrant) Execute(ctx context.Context, req *TokenRequest) (*TokenResponse, error) {
    // Mark code as used
    code, _ := g.store.GetAuthCode(ctx, hashCode(req.Code))
    g.store.MarkCodeUsed(ctx, code.ID)

    // Generate tokens
    return g.tokenSvc.IssueTokens(ctx, TokenIssueRequest{
        AppID:   code.AppID,
        UserID:  code.UserID,
        Scopes:  code.Scopes,
        Nonce:   code.Nonce,
    })
}

docs.title: JWT Bearer Grant
docs.text:
// oauth/token/grants/jwtbearer.go
type JWTBearerGrant struct {
    store    Store
    tokenSvc *TokenService
    verifier *JWTVerifier
}

func (g *JWTBearerGrant) GrantType() string {
    return "urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer"
}

func (g *JWTBearerGrant) Validate(ctx context.Context, req *TokenRequest) error {
    // 1. Parse JWT without verification first
    unverified, err := jwt.ParseUnverified(req.Assertion)
    if err != nil {
        return ErrInvalidGrant
    }

    // 2. Extract issuer (service account ID)
    issuer := unverified.Claims.Issuer

    // 3. Lookup service account
    sa, err := g.store.GetServiceAccount(ctx, issuer)
    if err != nil || !sa.Active {
        return ErrInvalidClient
    }

    // 4. Get the key used to sign (from kid header)
    kid := unverified.Header["kid"].(string)
    keyPair, err := g.store.GetKeyPair(ctx, sa.ID, kid)
    if err != nil || keyPair.Revoked {
        return ErrInvalidGrant
    }

    // 5. Verify signature
    pubKey, err := parsePublicKey(keyPair.PublicKeyPEM)
    if err != nil {
        return ErrInvalidGrant
    }

    claims, err := g.verifier.Verify(req.Assertion, pubKey)
    if err != nil {
        return ErrInvalidGrant
    }

    // 6. Verify claims
    // - iss must equal sub (self-issued)
    // - aud must be token endpoint
    // - exp must be <= 1 hour from now
    // - iat must be in the past
    if err := g.verifyClaims(claims); err != nil {
        return err
    }

    return nil
}

func (g *JWTBearerGrant) Execute(ctx context.Context, req *TokenRequest) (*TokenResponse, error) {
    // Parse assertion to get service account
    claims, _ := jwt.Parse(req.Assertion)
    sa, _ := g.store.GetServiceAccount(ctx, claims.Issuer)

    // Issue access token (no refresh token for JWT bearer)
    return g.tokenSvc.IssueTokens(ctx, TokenIssueRequest{
        AppID:            sa.ClientID,
        ServiceAccountID: &sa.ID,
        Scopes:           sa.Scopes,
        NoRefreshToken:   true,
    })
}

docs.title: Token Endpoint
docs.text:
// oauth/handler/token.go
func (h *Handler) Token(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    if r.Method != http.MethodPost {
        h.errorResponse(w, ErrInvalidRequest, "method not allowed")
        return
    }

    // Parse form
    if err := r.ParseForm(); err != nil {
        h.errorResponse(w, ErrInvalidRequest, "invalid form")
        return
    }

    req := &TokenRequest{
        GrantType:    r.PostFormValue("grant_type"),
        ClientID:     r.PostFormValue("client_id"),
        ClientSecret: r.PostFormValue("client_secret"),
        Code:         r.PostFormValue("code"),
        RedirectURI:  r.PostFormValue("redirect_uri"),
        CodeVerifier: r.PostFormValue("code_verifier"),
        RefreshToken: r.PostFormValue("refresh_token"),
        Assertion:    r.PostFormValue("assertion"),
        Scope:        r.PostFormValue("scope"),
    }

    // Also check Basic auth for client credentials
    if req.ClientID == "" {
        if user, pass, ok := r.BasicAuth(); ok {
            req.ClientID = user
            req.ClientSecret = pass
        }
    }

    // Find grant handler
    handler, ok := h.grants[req.GrantType]
    if !ok {
        h.errorResponse(w, ErrUnsupportedGrantType, "")
        return
    }

    // Authenticate client (except for public clients with PKCE)
    if err := h.authenticateClient(r.Context(), req); err != nil {
        h.errorResponse(w, err, "")
        return
    }

    // Validate grant
    if err := handler.Validate(r.Context(), req); err != nil {
        h.errorResponse(w, err, "")
        return
    }

    // Execute grant
    resp, err := handler.Execute(r.Context(), req)
    if err != nil {
        h.errorResponse(w, err, "")
        return
    }

    // Success response
    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    w.Header().Set("Cache-Control", "no-store")
    w.Header().Set("Pragma", "no-cache")
    json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(resp)
}

docs.title: Authorization Endpoint
docs.text:
// oauth/handler/authorize.go
func (h *Handler) Authorize(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    // Parse request
    req := &AuthorizeRequest{
        ResponseType:        r.URL.Query().Get("response_type"),
        ClientID:            r.URL.Query().Get("client_id"),
        RedirectURI:         r.URL.Query().Get("redirect_uri"),
        Scope:               r.URL.Query().Get("scope"),
        State:               r.URL.Query().Get("state"),
        CodeChallenge:       r.URL.Query().Get("code_challenge"),
        CodeChallengeMethod: r.URL.Query().Get("code_challenge_method"),
        Nonce:               r.URL.Query().Get("nonce"),
    }

    // Validate client
    app, err := h.store.GetAppByClientID(r.Context(), req.ClientID)
    if err != nil {
        h.renderError(w, "invalid_client", "Unknown client")
        return
    }

    // Validate redirect_uri
    if !h.validateRedirectURI(app, req.RedirectURI) {
        h.renderError(w, "invalid_redirect_uri", "Invalid redirect URI")
        return
    }

    // Validate response_type
    if req.ResponseType != "code" {
        h.redirectError(w, req.RedirectURI, "unsupported_response_type", req.State)
        return
    }

    // Require PKCE for public clients
    if app.AppType == "spa" || app.AppType == "native" {
        if req.CodeChallenge == "" {
            h.redirectError(w, req.RedirectURI, "invalid_request", req.State)
            return
        }
        if req.CodeChallengeMethod != "S256" {
            h.redirectError(w, req.RedirectURI, "invalid_request", req.State)
            return
        }
    }

    // Get authenticated user
    user := auth.UserFromContext(r.Context())
    if user == nil {
        // Redirect to login, then back here
        h.redirectToLogin(w, r)
        return
    }

    // Check consent
    if !app.FirstParty {
        consent, err := h.store.GetConsent(r.Context(), user.ID, app.ID)
        if err != nil || !h.consentCoversScopes(consent, req.Scope) {
            // Show consent screen
            h.renderConsentScreen(w, r, app, req)
            return
        }
    }

    // Generate authorization code
    code, err := h.generateAuthCode(r.Context(), app, user, req)
    if err != nil {
        h.redirectError(w, req.RedirectURI, "server_error", req.State)
        return
    }

    // Redirect with code
    redirectURL := fmt.Sprintf("%s?code=%s&state=%s",
        req.RedirectURI, code, url.QueryEscape(req.State))
    http.Redirect(w, r, redirectURL, http.StatusFound)
}

docs.title: Token Security
docs.text:
1. Access tokens: Short-lived (15 min), JWT, can be validated without DB lookup
  2. Refresh tokens: Long-lived, opaque, stored hashed, rotation on use
  3. Authorization codes: Very short-lived (10 min), single-use, hashed storage

docs.title: PKCE Requirements
docs.text:
• Required for spa and native app types
  • Only S256 method supported (plain is insecure)
  • Code verifier: 43-128 characters, URL-safe

docs.title: Client Authentication
docs.text:
• Confidential clients: client_secret (Argon2id hashed)
  • Public clients: PKCE only, no secret
  • Service accounts: JWT Bearer with key pairs

docs.title: Refresh Token Rotation
docs.text:
Refresh #1 → Token A (active)
Refresh #2 → Token A revoked, Token B (active)
Refresh #3 → Token B revoked, Token C (active)

If Token A reused after rotation:
  → Entire family revoked (theft detected)
  → Alert generated

docs.title: Rate Limiting
docs.text: Endpoint Limit Window /oauth/token 100 1 min /oauth/authorize 20 1 min Failed auth 5 failures → 15 min lockout

Integrate omniobserve/observops into SystemForge to provide vendor-agnostic observability (metrics, traces, logs) with support for Datadog, New Relic, Dynatrace, and OTLP backends.

docs.title: PLAN — Unified Forge Platform — Authorization Contract, IAM Console, and Shell Composition
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-001 Status: Draft

docs.title: Entry Gate
docs.text:
1. Repos registered: systemforge, systemforge-web, actionforge, agentforge, dashforge (done).
  2. ActionForge's authz package accepted as the convention seed (it already implements namespaced types, {app}:{resource}:{verb} scopes, the two-gate Guard, and a prefixed SpiceDB schema).

docs.title: Phase 1 — Authorization Contract
docs.text:
The contract must land before the console (which introspects vocabularies) and before per-app migrations.

  1. RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-003 Convention doc + AppVocabulary interface and vocabulary registry (scope-format and duplicate-definition validation) in systemforge/authz.
  2. RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-004 Shared SpiceDB base schema (principal, organization, platform) + schema-composition helper.
  3. RMI-DASHFORGE-016 DashForge adoption: re-namespace schema to dashforge_* referencing the shared base; conform scopes/roles; conformance test.
  4. RMI-AGENTFORGE-001 AgentForge adoption: create org-role vocabulary (roles/permissions/scopes/schema) on the convention; conformance test.
  5. RMI-ACTIONFORGE-037 ActionForge alignment: switch to the shared base organization definition and register its AppVocabulary.

Exit criteria: composed schema of base + 3 apps validates with no collisions; all three apps pass conformance tests.

docs.title: Phase 2 — IAM Console
docs.text:
1. RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-005 Admin APIs: role-assignment CRUD per (org, principal, app); vocabulary introspection; token issuance bounded by AllowedScopes.
  2. RMI-SYSTEMFORGEWEB-001 IAM pages: Members + role assignment; Roles & Permissions matrix (vocabulary-driven); API Keys & Tokens with scope picker.

Exit criteria: PRD success criterion — assign a role and issue a scope-limited token entirely through the console.

docs.title: Phase 3 — Shell Composition
docs.text:
1. RMI-SYSTEMFORGEWEB-002 ForgeApp registration contract in @plexusone/shell (nav/route/scope gating), versioned, documented.
  2. RMI-SYSTEMFORGEWEB-003 Reference composed host: shell + auth + two Forge UI surfaces under one login/menu/session; role/scope-gated nav proven.

Exit criteria: PRD success criterion — the reference host runs with one session across both apps.

docs.title: Risks and Mitigations
docs.text: See TRD: DashForge schema migration timing (pre-production), vocabulary drift (conformance tests + startup validation), contract over-fit (minimal versioned ForgeApp).

docs.title: Follow-On
docs.text:
• ReBAC relationship browser in the IAM console.
  • Customer-embedded mode per app (iframe/web-component + scoped-token embed SDK) — the GoodData-style story.
  • Runtime micro-frontends (Module Federation) if independent deploy cadence emerges; ForgeApp is the remote-module contract when it does.
  • ActionForge UI as a React package for shell composition (its standalone single-file UI remains for actionforge serve).

docs.title: PRD — Unified Forge Platform — Authorization Contract, IAM Console, and Shell Composition
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-001 Status: Draft Home repo: github.com/plexusone/systemforge

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Three Forge products (ActionForge, AgentForge, DashForge) are converging on SystemForge for identity/tenancy/authorization, but each is inventing its own authorization surface:

  • DashForge defines a SpiceDB schema with unprefixed definitions (organization, platform, dashboard) that collide with any other Forge app's schema in a composed deployment.
  • ActionForge just defined app-namespaced types (actionforge.workflow), {app}:{resource}:{verb} OAuth scopes, and domain roles (approver, developer) — conventions that exist only in ActionForge's repo.
  • AgentForge has a runtime tool-policy layer but no org-role vocabulary at all.

There is also no administration UI: role assignments, permission introspection, and token/scope management have no console (the AWS IAM equivalent), and no formal contract exists for mounting Forge UIs into the @plexusone/shell (which already provides AppShell/nav/auth/session and is consumed by agentforge-web).

The intended product motion — start a SaaS app with SystemForge, then optionally add ActionForge/AgentForge/DashForge as embedded capabilities, composed under one menu, one login, one session — requires all three gaps closed in SystemForge itself, not per-app.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. One authorization contract, owned by SystemForge. A documented convention plus helpers every Forge app adopts: app-namespaced resource types ({app}.{resource}), OAuth scopes as {app}:{resource}:{verb} with {app}:admin implying all, a canonical role set (owner/admin/editor/ viewer) with rules for app domain roles (e.g. ActionForge's approver), the two-gate model (role permission ∩ token scope), and a shared SpiceDB base schema where SystemForge owns principal/organization/platform and apps contribute {app}_-prefixed resource definitions referencing them.
  2. An IAM console in systemforge-web. AWS-IAM-style administration: org members with role assignment, a role→permission matrix driven by each app's registered vocabulary, and API key/token management with a scope picker. ReBAC relationship browsing is a follow-on.
  3. A shell app-registration contract. Each Forge UI package exports a typed registration (id, nav sections gated by role/scope, routes, required scopes); @plexusone/shell mounts registered apps under one chrome. Composition is build-time by default; the contract is transport-agnostic so runtime micro-frontends can be adopted later without changing app code.

docs.title: Non-Goals (this initiative)
docs.text:
• Runtime micro-frontends (Module Federation/import maps) — deliberately deferred until independent deploy cadence demands it; the registration contract is designed not to preclude it.
  • The customer-embedded mode (GoodData-style iframe/web-component embedding of a single Forge capability into a third-party SaaS with scoped tokens) — specced as follow-on; it is a per-app embed SDK, not shell composition.
  • Migrating every existing Forge screen into the shell — the reference composition proves the contract with two apps; full migrations are each app's own roadmap.

docs.title: Users and Experience
docs.text:
• Product Builder starting a new SaaS: scaffold on SystemForge + systemforge-web, get login/org-switcher/settings out of the box; add a Forge capability by installing its UI package and registering it — it appears in the shared nav, gated by the user's role and the app's scopes.
  • Org admin: opens Administration → IAM: sees members and their roles per app, changes a member from editor to approver, issues a CI token scoped to actionforge:runs:write (and sees it cannot approve gates).
  • Forge app developer: implements the vocabulary interface once; their roles/permissions/scopes appear in the IAM console automatically.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
• The convention doc exists in SystemForge and all three Forge apps' authz vocabularies conform (DashForge schema re-namespaced; AgentForge vocabulary created; ActionForge aligned to the shared org definitions).
  • A composed SpiceDB deployment loads SystemForge base + ≥2 app schemas with no definition collisions.
  • The IAM console lists members, edits role assignments, and issues a token with a subset of an app's scopes — against real SystemForge APIs.
  • A reference host app composes @plexusone/shell + two Forge UI packages with one login/session and role/scope-gated nav.

docs.title: TRD — Unified Forge Platform — Authorization Contract, IAM Console, and Shell Composition
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-001 Status: Draft

docs.title: Current State
docs.text:
• systemforge (github.com/plexusone/systemforge): authz package with Principal/Action/Resource, Authorizer interface, simple role-hierarchy and SpiceDB providers, HTTP middleware; identity with a token service carrying Scopes []string and principals with AllowedScopes; multiapp schema-per-app hosting; marketplace.
  • systemforge-web (github.com/plexusone/systemforge-web): pnpm workspace with @plexusone/shell (AppShell, Navbar, Sidebar, OrgSwitcher, UserMenu, ShellContext; NavItem.roles already exists), @plexusone/auth (BFF), @plexusone/tenant, @plexusone/pages (Login, OrgMembers, OrgInvitations, OrgSettings, UserSettings), design-tokens, telemetry, api-client. agentforge-web consumes @plexusone/auth today.
  • Forge authz state: ActionForge has an authz package implementing the target conventions (this initiative hoists them); DashForge has a SpiceDB schema with unprefixed definitions (collision risk) and owner/admin/editor/ viewer + publisher-side creator/reviewer roles; AgentForge has runtime tool policy only, no org-role vocabulary.

docs.title: 1. Authorization contract (systemforge)
docs.text:
A convention doc (docs/authz-conventions.md) plus a small vocabulary interface in authz:

// AppVocabulary is what each Forge app registers with the platform.
type AppVocabulary interface {
    App() string                       // "actionforge"
    Roles() RolePermissions            // role -> dotted permissions
    Hierarchy() RoleHierarchy
    Scopes() []string                  // "{app}:{resource}:{verb}", "{app}:admin"
    SpiceDBSchema() string             // "{app}_"-prefixed definitions only
}

Conventions (normative):

  • Resource types: {app}.{resource} (e.g. actionforge.run).
  • Scopes: {app}:{resource}:{verb}; {app}:admin implies all app scopes; scopes gate credentials, roles gate principals; effective access is the intersection (two-gate model).
  • Roles: canonical owner(100)/admin(80)/editor(60)/viewer(20) shared across apps; app domain roles slot between (ActionForge approver(50), developer(40); DashForge creator, reviewer), and separation-of-duties pairs are documented per app.
  • SpiceDB: SystemForge owns base definitions principal, organization (generic membership relations), platform; app schemas contribute only {app}_-prefixed definitions that reference the base (e.g. actionforge_workflow { relation org: organization }). A registry helper concatenates base + registered app schemas and validates for duplicate definitions.

docs.title: 2. IAM console
docs.text:
Backend (systemforge): admin APIs over existing services — role-assignment CRUD per (org, principal, app), vocabulary introspection (GET /admin/apps → each registered AppVocabulary's roles/permissions/ scopes), and token/API-key issuance constrained to the principal's AllowedScopes (already modeled in identity).

Frontend (systemforge-web): new IAM pages in @plexusone/pages (or a dedicated @plexusone/iam): Members (role assignment per app), Roles & Permissions (matrix rendered from vocabulary introspection — apps appear automatically), API Keys & Tokens (scope picker grouped by app, consent-screen style). ReBAC relationship browser (SpiceDB read API) is follow-on.

docs.title: 3. Shell composition (micro-frontend decision)
docs.text:
Decision: build-time composition now; contract designed so runtime MFE can be added later without app changes. Rationale: all Forge UIs share one stack (React + @plexusone/*), one team, one release train — Module Federation's costs (version skew, shared-dep pinning, runtime failure modes) buy nothing today. The registration contract is the stable seam:

export interface ForgeApp {
  id: string;                    // "actionforge"
  title: string;
  navSections: NavSection[];     // items carry roles?/scopes? gating
  routes: ForgeRoute[];          // path -> lazy component
  requiredScopes?: string[];     // hidden entirely if session lacks these
}
registerForgeApp(app: ForgeApp)

@plexusone/shell renders the union of registered apps' nav (gated by the session's role/scopes), mounts routes under the shared chrome, and owns session/org context. Lazy route components keep per-app code split even in a single build. If independent deployment is later required, the same ForgeApp object is what a Module Federation remote would expose.

Customer-embedded mode (embedding one capability into a third-party SaaS) is explicitly a different mechanism — iframe/web-component + scoped token — and is specced per-app as follow-on, not via the shell.

Contract as specified. The registration contract is specified in INIT-SYSTEMFORGEWEB-001 as AppModule and Shell in @plexusone/host. ForgeApp's fields map onto it: id and title are id and name, navSections is navigation(context), and routes are the module's routes under /orgs/:org. Role gating is per application, from the session's membership roles, rather than by scopes. Instead of registering into one shell, a stack composes modules with its own Shell through createHost({ apps }) for one build, or createHost({ app }) per host, so the same application also runs on its own in a neutral DevShell.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• DashForge schema migration is breaking for any existing SpiceDB data (definition renames rewrite relationships). Mitigated: DashForge deployment is pre-production; migrate before real tenants.
  • Vocabulary drift between simple-provider grants and SpiceDB schemas (two expressions of the same rules). Mitigated by per-app consistency tests (ActionForge already has one) and by the registry validating apps at startup.
  • Shell contract over-fitting to today's three apps. Mitigated by keeping ForgeApp minimal (nav, routes, scopes) and versioning it from day one.

docs.title: Testing Strategy
docs.text:
• systemforge: unit tests for vocabulary registry (duplicate-definition detection, scope-format validation); admin API tests over the simple provider.
  • systemforge-web: component tests for IAM pages against a mocked api-client; the reference host app is the integration proof (one login, two apps, role/scope-gated nav).
  • Per-Forge adoption RMIs each carry their own conformance test (schema prefix check, scope naming check) so drift fails CI in the app repo.

This initiative retires them for SystemAuth / sf_ / sf_principal_id. Full rationale and per-item scope are in ADR-001; RMI titles below are summaries.

Because no consumer has shipped, this is a hard cutover — no dual-name compatibility window. Downstream consumers adopt the new names as a coordinated follow-on; those items are tracked in the initiative and intentionally not enumerated in this repo.

docs.text:
Initiative: INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-005 Repository: github.com/plexusone/systemforge

Builds the central "log in with GitHub/Google" capability that downstream relying-party applications have long referenced as RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-001 but which was never specced or built here (the roadmaps start at RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-003; the OAuth server PRD deferred social login as "handled separately"). Full rationale and the architecture decision — IdP-centralized in SystemAuth, not a per-app library — are in ADR-002; RMI titles below are summaries.

These RMIs are defined but not yet claimed or scheduled — they are the design of record for a later execution session. Commits implementing an item will carry the trailer Refs: RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-<NNN>; none exist yet. Phase status derives from member-RMI status.

The identity substrate is ready: sf_principal_id is defined once in the shared identity/ent/mixin.PrincipalMixin (ADR-001) and relying parties link upstream identities to it. What this initiative adds is the login surface and a single sanctioned place to build it.

docs.title: PLAN — SystemForge Learner Accounts — Optional Email, QR Login, Guardian and Educator Relationships
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-007

docs.title: Entry Gate
docs.text:
• ADR-005 accepted.
  • INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-008 complete: one human model, HumanPrincipal DTO, legacy tables gone. The two initiatives ship together in v0.14.0.
  • Null-uniqueness behavior of Human.email confirmed on the deployment database.

docs.title: Phase 1 — Model and Invariants
docs.text: Make Human.email optional and set the identifier rule; add the Application flag and deployment setting; add ManagerRelationship and the identity/managedprincipal service with its invariants and audit. Exit: a managed principal can be created and managed through the service, cannot be created without a manager or when either flag is off, and all existing suites pass with both flags off.

docs.title: Phase 2 — Sign-in and Control
docs.text: Add the login_token credential type with issue, verify, and revoke; the SystemAuth exchange endpoint with identical failure responses and rate limiting; managed claims and conditional email claims; manager listing and revocation of tokens and sessions; the base authorization relations. These land together because the mitigations for a reusable token are the other items in the phase. Exit: end-to-end sign-in of a managed principal with a token, visible to and revocable by its manager, authorized through authz.

docs.title: Phase 3 — Surfaces and Release
docs.text: Audit and adjust every email-assuming path; implement the educator → guardian claim flow and the attach-email flow; write the documentation; tag v0.14.0, the release INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-008 also ships in, after CI passes, and record the release. Exit: PRD success criteria hold.

docs.title: Risks and Mitigations
docs.text: Risk Mitigation Shipping tokens before mitigations Phase 2 is indivisible; no partial tag Missed email assumption Phase 3 audit item is checklist-driven from a repository-wide search; conformance suites carry no-email cases from Phase 1 Blocking on INIT-006 for attach-email Only the attach step depends on it; the claim flow and everything else do not

docs.title: Follow-On
docs.text:
• First consumer integration in the learning application (its own initiative), including consent recording and application facet permissions.
  • Optional device binding for login_token if a consumer requires stronger assurance than reusable tokens provide.

docs.title: PRD — SystemForge Learner Accounts — Optional Email, QR Login, Guardian and Educator Relationships
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-007 Status: Draft Home repo: github.com/plexusone/systemforge Design of record: ADR-005 Depends on: INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-008 (single Principal root; this initiative touches one human model, not two)

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
SystemForge requires every human to have a unique email and to hold their own credentials. Learning applications built on it need humans who cannot: children whose accounts are created by a parent or teacher, who sign in by scanning a code, and whose data a responsible adult must be able to see, revoke, and delete. Today the only options are a fake email (which corrupts mail, SCIM, audit, and recovery flows) or an application-local table (which gives the child no platform identity and splits authorization). Neither is acceptable for a product that must pass a privacy review before the first classroom uses it.

At the same time, no existing consumer wants email to become optional for its users, and recovery, compliance, and deliverability for ordinary accounts should not get harder.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. Email stays required by default. Nothing changes for an application that does not opt in.
  2. Managed principals. An opted-in application can create a human without an email, provided at least one manager with an email exists.
  3. Two built-in manager roles, guardian (full authority) and educator (operational authority), usable by learning and non-learning applications alike.
  4. Manager-issued sign-in via a login_token credential that applications render as a QR code, printed card, or link.
  5. Manager visibility and control over a managed principal's tokens and sessions.
  6. A path from managed to ordinary: attaching a verified email later.

docs.title: Non-Goals
docs.text:
• Parent, child, student, or teacher concepts in SystemForge. Applications map those onto managed principals and manager roles.
  • Recording consent, ages, or regulatory evidence. SystemForge supplies a manager with authority to consent; the application records that it did.
  • Application permissions over a managed principal's data (progress, certificates, limits). Those are application facets on the base schema.
  • Changing how ordinary humans sign in or recover accounts.

docs.title: Users and Stakeholders
docs.text: Who Needs Learning application (first consumer) Create child accounts from a teacher or parent, issue QR logins, let a parent claim a teacher-created child, revoke and delete Other SystemForge consumers No behavior change unless they opt in; Email becomes optional in Go types and claims SystemAuth operators A deployment-level switch, default off; audit of who issued and revoked each token Platform administrators Ability to see manager relationships and act on a managed principal when no manager can

docs.title: Functional
docs.text:
• F1. Human.email is optional. A human without an email is a managed principal with CanManageProfile = false and CanDelegate = false.
  • F2. Managed principals can be created only when the deployment setting and the requesting OAuth client's managed_principals_enabled flag are both on.
  • F3. Creating a managed principal requires at least one manager in the same transaction. Removing the last manager is refused; deactivation or deletion must be used instead.
  • F4. A manager must be an active human with an email. Managed principals cannot be managers.
  • F5. Built-in manager roles are guardian and educator, with the platform authority described in ADR-005. Applications may register additional roles through the authorization vocabulary.
  • F6. A login_token credential type: manager-issued, hashed at rest, expiring, revocable, reusable by default with a single-use option. Lifetime resolves as: explicit request value, else the Application's configured default, else the platform default (30 days); never above the platform ceiling. Single-use tokens default to 20 minutes.
  • F7. SystemAuth exchanges a login_token for a session whose claims identify the subject as managed; the exchange is rate-limited and returns the same response for unknown, expired, and revoked tokens.
  • F8. Managers can list a managed principal's login_token credentials and active sessions, and revoke any of them.
  • F9. An educator can issue a claim that lets a human with an email become guardian of the managed principal; a guardian can add or remove other managers directly.
  • F10. A managed principal can attach an email, verified through the INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-006 flow, after which it is an ordinary human and may hold its own credentials; existing manager relationships persist until removed.
  • F11. Principal.identifier is the email when present, otherwise human:<principal-id>; attaching an email updates it.
  • F12. The base SpiceDB schema gains guardian and educator relations on principal with manage_account, manage_credentials, and view_profile permissions.
  • F13. Every path that assumed an email handles its absence: social login linking, invitations, signup, SCIM, userinfo and ID-token claims, relying-party principal views, and marketplace purchasing (managed principals cannot purchase).

docs.title: Non-Functional
docs.text:
• N1. With both flags off, existing conformance suites pass unchanged apart from the Email type change.
  • N2. Every manager action on a managed principal (create, issue, revoke, add or remove manager, delete) is audited with the acting principal.
  • N3. golangci-lint reports no findings.
  • N4. Documentation describes managed principals as a platform primitive with a learning application as the worked example, not as a children's feature.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
• A learning application can: create a managed principal from an educator account, issue a login_token, sign the managed principal in with it, have a guardian claim it, and have the guardian revoke the token and delete the principal, with each step authorized and audited.
  • An application that has not opted in cannot create a human without an email, and its existing tests pass.
  • A managed principal who attaches a verified email can then set a password and sign in without any manager involvement.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text: Risk Mitigation A reusable token is password-equivalent Reduced capabilities on managed sessions, rate-limited exchange, expiry, manager visibility and revocation, single-use option An email-assuming path is missed F13 audit is its own roadmap item with a checklist derived from a repository-wide search; conformance suites gain no-email cases Database uniqueness with null email Verify that the target database permits multiple nulls under the unique index before changing the schema Scope creep into consent and age handling Explicit non-goal; the application owns these

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
• login_token lifetime. The platform default is 30 days, a conservative posture suited to a general SaaS identity platform. Applications that opt into managed principals may override it per Application (a learning application will typically choose a school year), bounded by a platform ceiling. Single-use tokens are short-lived by default (20 minutes), matching the "backup code" pattern common in classroom login systems. Comparable products sit between 90 days and one year for reusable codes and void them on an annual cycle.
  • educator may not delete a managed principal, including one that never received a guardian. Deletion is a guardian or platform administrator action. Start strict; revisit only if orphaned accounts accumulate in practice. The intent is to keep learners in the system, not to make removal easy.

docs.title: ROADMAP — SystemForge Learner Accounts — Optional Email, QR Login, Guardian and Educator Relationships
docs.text:
Initiative: INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-007 Repository: github.com/plexusone/systemforge

Design of record: ADR-005. Email stays required by default; managed principals are an opt-in state that always has a manager with an email. Builds on INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-008. Commits implementing an item carry Refs: RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-<NNN>.

docs.title: Phase 1 — Model and Invariants
docs.text:
Theme: A human without an email is a managed principal with a manager

  • [x] RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-102 Optional Human.email and identifier rule: nullable unique email, identifier = email or human:<id>, HumanPrincipal.Email optional, null-uniqueness verified on the target database
  • Depends on: RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-099
  • [x] RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-103 Enablement switches: the OAuth client's managed_principals_enabled and the managed_principals.enabled deployment setting, both default off
  • Depends on: RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-102

docs.text:
Theme: Manager-issued tokens with the mitigations that make them safe

  • [x] RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-105 login_token credential type: issue, constant-time verify, revoke, expiry, single-use option; lifetime resolved from request, then per-application login_token_ttl, then 30-day platform default, under a platform ceiling
  • Depends on: RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-104
  • [x] RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-106 SystemAuth token exchange: endpoint with identical failure responses and rate limiting, managed claim, conditional email claims in ID token and userinfo
  • Depends on: RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-105

  • Depends on: RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-104
  • [x] RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-108 Manager visibility: list and revoke a managed principal's login tokens and active sessions, authorized through manage_credentials
  • Depends on: RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-106
  • Depends on: RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-107

  • [x] RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-109 Email-assuming path audit: social login, invite, signup, SCIM, relying-party views, session/jwt, contract types, marketplace purchaser check
  • Depends on: RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-102

docs.title: TRD — SystemForge Learner Accounts — Optional Email, QR Login, Guardian and Educator Relationships
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-007 Design of record: ADR-005

docs.title: Current State
docs.text:
After INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-008, a human is Principal(type=human) + Human, with Human.email declared NotEmpty().Unique() and Principal.identifier set to the email. Credentials live in sf_credentials with the type enum password | api_key | keypair | webauthn | totp | client_secret. principal.Capabilities already carries CanManageProfile and CanDelegate. SystemAuth authenticates clients as OAuthApp rows (client_id, grants, TTLs, first_party, public) and static ClientConfig entries, with no feature flags. (The Application principal extension also has a client_id but is not what SystemAuth authenticates.) The base SpiceDB schema defines principal {} with no relations.

Paths that assume an email exists (non-test code): systemauth social login (FindByVerifiedEmail, account creation requires a verified email), GetHumanByEmail for password login, userinfo and ID-token email claims; invite (email is required on the invite request); signup; scim/mapper (userName and emails); relyingparty principal views; session/jwt claims; marketplace/stripe customer email.

docs.title: 1. Schema
docs.text:
Human

  • email: Optional().Nillable().Unique(). Confirm on the target database that the unique index admits multiple nulls (MySQL-compatible engines do; verify on the deployment target).
  • email_verified_at unchanged.

Principal

  • identifier: email when present, else human:<principal-id>, set by the service layer; documented as a lookup key.

OAuthApp (and ClientConfig.managed_principals for static clients)

  • managed_principals_enabled Bool, default false.
  • login_token_ttl Int (seconds), Optional().Nillable(); null means use the platform default. Ignored unless managed_principals_enabled.

Credential.type

  • Add login_token.

New ManagerRelationship (sf_manager_relationships)

Field Notes managed_principal_id → Principal, must be type=human manager_principal_id → Principal, must be type=human, active, with email role String, validated against the manager-role vocabulary; built-ins guardian, educator active Bool created_by → Principal (the acting manager or admin) timestamps via BaseMixin

Unique on (managed_principal_id, manager_principal_id, role).

docs.title: 2. identity/managedprincipal service
docs.text:
A new package owning the invariants:

  • Create(ctx, CreateInput{ClientID, DisplayName, Managers: []ManagerInput{PrincipalID, Role}, ActorID}) checks the deployment setting and the client's flag through Server.ManagedPrincipalsAllowed, validates every manager (human, active, has email), then creates Principal (identifier human:<id>, capabilities with CanManageProfile=false, CanDelegate=false), Human (no email), and the relationships in one transaction. Refused with a typed error if Managers is empty.
  • AddManager, RemoveManager: RemoveManager refuses to remove the last active relationship while Human.email is null (ErrLastManager). AddManager is idempotent and reactivates an inactive relationship; RemoveManager deactivates rather than deletes. Both update the managed principal's row first, so concurrent changes to one principal serialize on its row lock and cannot together remove the last manager.
  • IssueClaim(ctx, managedID, byManager) (claimCode, expiry) and RedeemClaim(ctx, code, claimantID): an educator or guardian issues a short-lived, single-use claim; a human with an email redeems it and becomes guardian. Stored hashed in sf_credentials as a login_token flagged metadata.purpose = "claim", or as its own small table if mixing purposes proves confusing; decide during implementation, documenting the choice.
  • AttachEmail(ctx, managedID, email): initiates INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-006 verification; on success sets Human.email, updates identifier, restores default human capabilities. Relationships are untouched.
  • IsManaged(ctx, principalID) bool for callers that need the distinction.

As implemented: claims live in their own table, sf_manager_claims (hashed SFMC codes of 160 bits, a lookup prefix, issuer, expiry, redemption), not in sf_credentials, so a claim code can never be verified as a login token. Issuing a claim requires manage_credentials; codes last seven days by default (WithClaimTTL) so a letter home can reach a parent; redemption spends the claim conditionally inside the transaction that adds the guardian, so it succeeds once. Because INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-006 is not yet implemented, the attach step is AttachVerifiedEmail(ctx, actorID, managedID, email, verifiedAt): it requires manage_account, and proving control of the address is the caller's job until SystemAuth's verification flow drives it.

Deployment setting: identity.managed_principals.enabled in the SystemAuth config, default false, surfaced through systemauthsvc.

docs.title: 3. login_token credential
docs.text:
In identity/credential:

  • IssueLoginToken(ctx, principalID, IssueInput{IssuedBy, ExpiresAt, SingleUse bool}) (plain, *Credential): 32 bytes of randomness, base32-encoded for QR friendliness, stored as a hash; identifier holds a short prefix for display; metadata records issued_by and single_use. The plain value is returned once.
  • VerifyLoginToken(ctx, plain) (*Credential, error): constant-time comparison against the hash; rejects expired, revoked, or inactive rows; updates last_used_at/last_used_ip; revokes the row when single_use.
  • Existing Revoke applies.

As implemented: tokens are SFLT followed by the base32 encoding of the random bytes without padding, so they use only uppercase letters and digits and a QR code can encode them in alphanumeric mode; verification also accepts lowercase and grouping spaces or hyphens for typed entry. The stored identifier is the first 12 characters and is the lookup key; the SHA-256 hash is then compared in constant time. Every unusable token yields the same ErrInvalidLoginToken. Recording a use re-checks active and revoked in the UPDATE, and a single-use token is revoked in that same statement, so it succeeds at most once under concurrent presentation. LoginTokenPolicy.ExpiresAt resolves the lifetime; systemauth.Server supplies the policy for a client through LoginTokenPolicy, and managedprincipal.IssueLoginToken requires the issuer to be an active manager until the authorization relations of RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-107 land.

Lifetime policy, resolved at issue time:

  1. An explicit ExpiresAt on the request, if present.
  2. Else the client's login_token_ttl (new nullable field on OAuthApp; a learning application sets a school year).
  3. Else the platform default identity.managed_principals.login_token_ttl, default 30 days.
  4. Never beyond the platform ceiling identity.managed_principals.login_token_max_ttl, default 400 days (one school year plus slack); a request above it is clamped and the clamp is logged.
  5. Single-use tokens ignore 2–3 and use identity.managed_principals.single_use_token_ttl, default 20 minutes.

The 30-day default reflects SystemForge's posture as a general SaaS identity platform; the override exists because classroom products conventionally issue codes that last a term or a school year.

docs.title: 4. SystemAuth exchange and claims
docs.text:
• New endpoint on SystemAuth: POST /login-token (name finalized in implementation) accepting the plain token and the requesting client. It verifies the token, confirms the principal is managed and active, confirms Server.ManagedPrincipalsAllowed for the client, and creates a SystemAuth session. Responses for unknown, expired, revoked, and disabled-application cases are identical, and the endpoint is rate-limited per client and per source address using the existing session/ratelimit.
  • Session and ID-token claims: email and email_verified are omitted when absent; a managed: true claim is added for managed principals. userinfo follows the same rule.
  • As implemented: POST /login-token with form fields token, client_id, and optional return_to, answering 303 to the target on success, one identical 401 for every rejection, and 429 with Retry-After when limited. Login sessions, cookies, and redirect policy are the existing browser-login ones; that component now also starts when managed principals are enabled without social providers, mounting only the session, consent, and login token routes. The default limits are 60 requests a minute per source address, enough for a classroom behind one address, and 600 per client; WithLoginTokenRateLimit sets shared storage and other limits. The source address follows the rate limiter's X-Forwarded-For handling, so the per-client limit is the bound that a spoofed header cannot evade. The managed claim is not scope-gated.
  • Capabilities already flow into PrincipalToken.capabilities; managed principals' tokens therefore carry can_manage_profile=false.

docs.title: 5. Manager visibility
docs.text:
In identity/managedprincipal with handlers mounted on SystemAuth:

  • ListLoginTokens(ctx, managedID) and ListSessions(ctx, managedID) (joining sf_credentials type login_token, sf_login_sessions, and active sf_principal_tokens).
  • RevokeLoginToken, RevokeSession, RevokeAll.
  • Every call authorizes the caller through authz with manage_credentials on the managed principal (§7).

As implemented: sessions are live browser login sessions, OAuth token families (subject is the principal), and principal token families; a family is listed once and revoked whole, so its refresh token cannot renew it. Listing returns live tokens and sessions only. The operations apply only to managed principals: once an email is attached, the principal manages its own credentials. managedprincipal.NewHandler serves them as JSON and identifies the manager through requestprincipal; mount it under /managed-principals on the SystemAuth router or an application's, behind requestprincipal.Middleware.

docs.title: 6. Email-assuming paths
docs.text:
Each becomes conditional on Human.email != nil:

Path Change Social login FindByVerifiedEmail already filters verified emails; nulls are excluded. No linking to managed principals. Password login GetHumanByEmail cannot match a null; managed principals have no password until an email is attached. invite Unchanged: invites target an email and never create managed principals; documented. signup Unchanged: requires an email. SCIM mapper and store userName = Principal.identifier; emails omitted when null; filters on emails exclude nulls. userinfo, ID token, session/jwt email/email_verified omitted when null; managed claim added. relyingparty principal view Email becomes optional; Managed bool added. marketplace Purchase and subscription creation reject managed purchasers with a typed error; Stripe customer email is the purchaser's. contract identity types Email optional.

As implemented, after a repository-wide audit (no path dereferenced a nil email; the defects were empty strings treated as values):

  • SCIM departs from the row above: managed principals are excluded from SCIM entirely (not listed, read, updated, deleted, or grouped). SCIM serves the humans an enterprise identity provider provisions; listing application-created learners would invite the provider to deprovision them, and a userName update would silently give one an email.
  • Relying party: VerifiedIdentity.Managed and Principal.Managed come from the managed claim; a managed identity is created on first sign-in without an email and never linked by email. Application PrincipalStore implementations must accept an identity without an email when Managed is set.
  • Marketplace: marketplace.PurchaserChecker (implemented by managedprincipal.Service) with stripe.WithPurchaserChecker refuses checkout with ErrManagedPurchaser (HTTP 403). Deployments that enable managed principals must configure it.
  • In-memory stores, password login, federation sync, signup: an empty email never matches or is adopted; signup requires a bare address, which also keeps human:<id> from matching its identifier lookup.
  • Left as is: invite acceptance has no email assumption, so a managed principal holding an invite token may accept it; SystemAuth Storage.UpdateHuman requires an email, which is correct because managed principals are changed through identity/managedprincipal, not SystemAuth storage or federation sync.

docs.title: 7. Authorization
docs.text:
Extend authz.BaseSpiceDBSchema:

definition principal {
    relation guardian: principal
    relation educator: principal

    permission manage_account     = guardian
    permission manage_credentials = guardian + educator
    permission view_profile       = guardian + educator
    permission manage_managers    = guardian
}

identity/managedprincipal writes and deletes these relationships through RelationshipSyncer.AddPrincipalManager and RemovePrincipalManager after a ManagerRelationship change commits, honoring the sync mode. The simple provider does not store relations; simple.WithManagerRoleGetter reads the active roles through managedprincipal.Service.ManagerRoles and applies authz.ManagerRolePermissions, which a test keeps equal to the schema, so both providers agree. Roles an application registers beyond the built-ins grant no platform permissions; they gain meaning only in the application's facets. Applications add domain permissions in their facets, for example learning_org granting view_progress = org->view + principal->view_profile.

docs.title: 8. Documentation
docs.text:
• New docs/identity/managed-principals.md: the primitive, invariants, roles, login_token, claim flow, attach-email flow, and the two configuration switches, with a learning application as the worked example.
  • Update docs/identity/users.md (email optionality, identifier rule), docs/identity/security.md (token handling), and the authorization conventions doc (new base relations).

docs.title: Sequencing Constraints
docs.text:
• §1 and §2 depend on INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-008 having removed the legacy model (RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-099), so there is one Human to change.
  • §3 and §4 depend on §1 (credential type enum) and §2 (managed check).
  • §5 depends on §3 and §7.
  • §6 can proceed in parallel with §3–§5 once §1 lands.
  • The claim flow in §2 depends on INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-006 only for the attach-email step; the claim itself does not.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• Null uniqueness. Verify on the deployment database before the schema change; if it does not admit multiple nulls, use a generated-column or partial-index approach and document it.
  • Token reuse. Reusable tokens are the product requirement; the mitigations in ADR-005 are structural and must all land before release, so the exchange endpoint, rate limiting, reduced capabilities, and manager revocation are in the same phase.
  • Vocabulary drift. Applications may be tempted to add parent/child roles; the manager-role vocabulary validator and docs steer them to the built-ins plus facet permissions.

docs.title: Testing Strategy
docs.text:
• storetest conformance suites gain managed-principal cases: create with and without managers, remove last manager, attach email, identifier updates.
  • credential tests for issue/verify/revoke of login_token, single-use behavior, expiry, and constant-time verification.
  • SystemAuth handler tests for the exchange endpoint: success, each failure class returning an identical response, rate limiting, claim shape.
  • authz/providertest cases for the new base relations in both providers.
  • A no-opt-in regression run: both flags off, full suite green.

docs.title: PLAN — Retire Legacy User — Principal as the Sole Identity Root
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-008

docs.title: Entry Gate
docs.text:
• ADR-004 accepted.
  • Confirmed that no consumer application reads sf_users or the legacy tables directly (downstream products link through relyingparty and sf_principal_id).
  • Current release is v0.13.0; the next tag is reserved as breaking v0.14.0.

docs.title: Phase 1 — SystemAuth on Principal
docs.text: Land the bootstrap and OAuth-app ownership change first so the client owner is valid before the storage layer stops looking at sf_users. Then move the storage methods, remove legacyUserID, and re-express federation sync as external identities. Exit: password login, social login, and federation sync all resolve to the same Principal + Human; the two legacy test files pass against the new storage.

docs.title: Phase 2 — SCIM and Service Accounts
docs.text: Expand SCIM tests to pin wire behavior, then rewrite the store on Principal/Human/PrincipalMembership. In parallel, settle the service-account question (TRD §5) so the removal list is fixed. Exit: SCIM suite green on the new store; service-account decision recorded in the removal RMI.

docs.title: Phase 3 — Removal and Release
docs.text: Delete the legacy schemas, regenerate Ent, add migration 0002, rewrite the identity docs and README bullets, fix rls/testing.go, extend the CI grep gate, update CHANGELOG.json, and tag v0.14.0 after CI passes. Record the release in visionstudio at the same moment. Exit: the success criteria in the PRD hold.

docs.title: Risks and Mitigations
docs.text: Risk Mitigation Removing schemas before every caller moved Phase 3 cannot start until Phases 1 and 2 are complete; Ent regeneration turns stragglers into compile errors SCIM regressions Tests first, rewrite second Service-account scope grows the initiative Time-box the decision in Phase 2; repoint the edge and defer table removal if needed

docs.title: Follow-On
docs.text:
• INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-007: optional Human.email under application configuration, QR login credential type, guardian/educator relationships.
  • The follow-ups found during execution (the identity/oauth provider panic, the sf_session cookie name, active-only membership listing, an opt-in for trusted SCIM email, the PostgreSQL case-insensitive email index, and the legacy-shaped mixins) are delivered by INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-009.
  • Implement the RFC 7523 JWT-bearer grant on ServicePrincipal plus keypair credentials. It was documented but never wired into Fosite; the service-account tables it described are removed by this initiative.

docs.title: PRD — Retire Legacy User — Principal as the Sole Identity Root
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-008 Status: Draft Home repo: github.com/plexusone/systemforge Design of record: ADR-004

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
SystemForge has two tables that each claim to be "the human user": sf_users (legacy User) and sf_principals + sf_humans (Principal with the Human extension). The platform was designed to converge on Principal as the single root for humans, applications, agents, and services, and most code has moved. The remainder is small but sits on the most important paths:

  • Password login and the SystemAuth user store read sf_users.
  • Social login writes sf_principals and never reads sf_users.
  • SCIM provisioning writes sf_users and sf_memberships.
  • The bootstrap creates a synthetic human in sf_users to own OAuth clients.

The result is that the same email address can exist as two unrelated identities depending on how the person first arrived, and features that look up "the human with this email" disagree with each other. This is a defect that will surface the first time a real organization mixes sign-in methods, which is the normal case for any school, team, or family.

No consumer application has shipped against these tables, and the first launches are near. This is the last point at which the fix is a schema deletion rather than a production data migration.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. One identity record per human. Every sign-in method (password, social, federation sync, SCIM) resolves to the same Principal + Human.
  2. Remove sf_users and the tables that exist only to support it, with no compatibility layer.
  3. Ship a breaking release (v0.14.0) before any consumer depends on the legacy tables.
  4. Leave INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-007 (learner accounts) a single model to extend.

docs.title: Non-Goals
docs.text:
• Making email optional, QR login, or guardian/educator relationships. Those are INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-007 and depend on this initiative.
  • Changing the identity/apikey interface that applications implement.
  • Changing the authorization vocabulary or SpiceDB schema (INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-001).
  • Any production data migration; none exists.

docs.title: Users and Stakeholders
docs.text: Who Impact Application developers on SystemForge One identity API; identity/ent/user and identity/ent/membership disappear and code importing them fails to compile; the identity/apikey interface stays but sf_api_keys is no longer a backing option SystemAuth operators Bootstrap owner becomes a service principal; dev databases run one drop migration Identity-provider admins using SCIM Provisioned users are principals, visible to every other sign-in method INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-007 Unblocked; single table to make email optional on

docs.title: Functional
docs.text:
• F1. Password login looks up the human by Human.email and verifies against a sf_credentials row of type password.
  • F2. The federation identity-sync API (create/update/delete by federation ID) operates on Principal + Human, recording the federation as an ExternalIdentity (provider + subject). Its request and response contract in contract/ is unchanged.
  • F3. SCIM user and group/membership operations run on Principal, Human, and PrincipalMembership with the same SCIM wire behavior as today, including filtering and pagination.
  • F4. Statically configured OAuth clients are owned by a Principal(type=service); OAuthApp.owner references Principal.
  • F5. OAuth tokens, authorization codes, and consents carry the subject as a principal ID and have no user edge.
  • F6. The User, Membership, OAuthAccount, RefreshToken, and APIKey Ent schemas and their tables are removed. ServiceAccount and ServiceAccountKeyPair are removed if the RFC 7523 path is confirmed to run on ServicePrincipal plus keypair credentials; otherwise their creator edge is repointed to Principal.
  • F7. A migration drops the retired tables.
  • F8. A CI gate fails on new references to sf_users, ent.User, identity/ent/user, identity/ent/membership, or cf_.
  • F9. systemauth exposes one human value type, HumanPrincipal, replacing both systemauth.User and systemauth.LoginPrincipal; storage method names follow (GetHumanByEmail, GetHumanByExternalIdentity).
  • F10. The identity/apikey interface is unchanged; its documented backing store is sf_credentials type api_key. Applications that intended to use sf_api_keys are told so in the release notes.

docs.title: Non-Functional
docs.text:
• N1. Hard cutover: no dual-write, no shim, no deprecation period.
  • N2. All existing tests pass or are rewritten against the new model; the two test files that touch legacy User are updated, not deleted.
  • N3. golangci-lint reports no findings.
  • N4. Documentation under docs/identity/ describes only the surviving model.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
• A human who signs in with Google and then sets a password, or who is SCIM-provisioned and then signs in with Google, has exactly one principal.
  • grep -r 'sf_users\|ent\.User\b' --include='*.go' . returns nothing outside the CI gate itself.
  • v0.14.0 is tagged with a BREAKING CHANGE note and CI green.
  • INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-007 can begin against one table.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text: Risk Mitigation A code path that reads sf_users is missed The CI gate plus Ent regeneration make any remaining import a compile error SCIM wire behavior drifts during the rewrite Keep the existing SCIM tests as the contract; add cases for filtering and memberships before rewriting RFC 7523 service accounts turn out to depend on sf_service_accounts Confirm the path first; if it does, repoint the creator edge and defer table removal to a follow-on rather than block the release Downstream code imports a removed Ent package Intended: it fails at compile time; downstream products link through relyingparty and were verified not to read the legacy tables

docs.title: Open Questions
docs.text:
• Does the service-account JWT-bearer flow already run on ServicePrincipal
  • keypair credentials, or on sf_service_accounts? Decides the scope of F6.
  • Should the bootstrap service principal's identifier be fixed (as the system user's UUID was) so repeated bootstraps are idempotent across instances? Default: yes, keep a fixed well-known ID.

docs.title: ROADMAP — Retire Legacy User — Principal as the Sole Identity Root
docs.text:
Initiative: INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-008 Repository: github.com/plexusone/systemforge

Design of record: ADR-004. Hard cutover, no compatibility window; tagged as breaking v0.14.0. Commits implementing an item carry Refs: RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-<NNN>.

docs.title: Phase 1 — SystemAuth on Principal
docs.text:
Theme: Every sign-in method resolves to one Principal + Human

  • [x] RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-093 Bootstrap owner as service principal: replace the synthetic system user with a fixed-ID Principal(type=service) and repoint OAuthApp.owner to Principal
  • [x] RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-094 Drop user edges on OAuthToken, OAuthAuthCode, and OAuthConsent; remove legacyUserID; subjects are principal IDs
  • Depends on: RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-093
  • Delivered: also moved the identity/oauth Fosite storage onto the subject column (it had dropped non-UUID subjects), and made CreateClient report only genuine duplicates as ErrClientExists.
  • [x] RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-095 SystemAuth storage on Principal/Human: merge User and LoginPrincipal into one HumanPrincipal DTO, rename storage methods to *Human*, reimplement over Principal + Human in Ent and memory storage, password login verified through sf_credentials
  • Depends on: RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-094
  • Delivered together with 096: removing the federation-ID lookup from storage left the federation handlers without a way to resolve identities, so both items landed in one change. Password login needs no new code: credential.Service.VerifyPassword matches the injectable verifier signature once identity IDs are principal IDs. Email uniqueness is enforced case-insensitively on writes, matching lookups.
  • [x] RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-096 Federation sync as external identities: create/update/delete resolve through ExternalIdentity(provider, subject); drop federation_id; wire contract unchanged
  • Depends on: RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-095
  • Delivered: create adopts an existing principal with the same email and links the federation identity, so later updates and deletes resolve to it; delete reports synced only for an identity that was never linked.

docs.title: Phase 2 — SCIM and Service Accounts
docs.text:
Theme: Provisioning and non-human identities on the same root

  • [x] RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-097 SCIM store on principals: pin wire behavior with filter, pagination, and membership tests, then rewrite the store over Principal, Human, and PrincipalMembership
  • Depends on: RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-095
  • Delivered: the store had no tests; pinning them exposed a panic on every ascending list sort, fixed before the rewrite. The pinning suite passed unchanged against the rewrite. Intentional changes: userName is not case-exact (RFC 7643), deleting a group member works, and memberships honor the active flag. SCIM-provisioned emails are not marked verified, so social login refuses to auto-link them rather than duplicating.
  • [x] RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-098 Service accounts: confirm the RFC 7523 path runs on ServicePrincipal + keypair credentials; retire sf_service_accounts if so, otherwise repoint creator to Principal
  • Depends on: RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-093

docs.text:
Theme: Delete the legacy model and lock it out

  • [x] RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-099 Remove User, Membership, OAuthAccount, RefreshToken, APIKey, ServiceAccount, and ServiceAccountKeyPair schemas with OAuthToken.service_account_id; regenerate Ent; add migration 0002 dropping the tables

Verified on PostgreSQL by seeding a database with the pre-initiative code: without 0002 the new version fails to start; with it, the new version migrates and starts.
  • [x] RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-100 Documentation: rewrite docs/identity/{users,memberships,api-keys}.md, docs/oauth/service-accounts.md, and README identity bullets around the principal model; fix the stale cf_memberships reference in rls/testing.go

Corrections to prior claims: the JWT-bearer grant is not implemented, and imported password hashes must be Argon2id (bcrypt was never accepted). The rls test helpers inserted into tables that no longer existed and are fixed and tested against PostgreSQL.
