    ListResources(ctx, principal uuid.UUID, resourceType, permission string) ([]string, error)
}

rbac stores rows and, in the same transaction, creates the collaborator membership when the principal has no membership in the resource's organization; RevokeResourceRole deletes the row and removes the membership when it was the principal's last grant and its role is collaborator. A grant to a lower role or a revoke records an access change with reason grant_reduced. Can consults the grant table after the organization role: view ⇐ any of the three, edit ⇐ contributor or maintainer, manage ⇐ maintainer, mapped through the vocabulary's resource permissions. ListResources in rbac is an indexed query over sf_resource_grants unioned with every resource of the organizations where the principal's organization role already grants the permission (returned as the organization IDs with a wildcard marker, so the application can apply it as org_id IN (...) OR id IN (...)).

docs.title: 4.3 Resource grants in rebac/spicedb (RMI-141)
docs.text: The same contract: grants are {resource}#<role>@principal:<id> relationships; ListResources is LookupResources for the permission; the collaborator membership is written as organization#collaborator. ValidateAppSchema additionally checks that any definition with viewer/contributor/maintainer relations declares all three, binds them to principal, and has an org: organization relation. providertest gains RunResourceGrantTests (grant, revoke, last-revoke removes membership, lower-role reduction, ListResources for each permission, collaborator sees list and nothing else on the organization) and runs it against both providers; the suite is written before the rebac implementation so it is the specification for both.

docs.title: 4.4 Resource-targeted invites (RMI-142)
docs.text: Invite gains nullable resource_type, resource_id, resource_role; Create validates them against the vocabulary and requires Role = collaborator when set. Accept creates the collaborator membership, the grant and the authz relationships in one transaction. Personal organizations accept only resource-targeted invites (§1.4).

docs.title: 4.5 authz.mode configuration (RMI-143)
docs.text: authz.Config{Mode: "rbac" | "rebac", Engine: "spicedb", SpiceDB: spicedb.Config} with authz.New(ctx, cfg, deps) returning the provider; systemauth.Config gains the authz key. authz/simple and authz/spicedb carry // Deprecated: notices naming the next major release as their removal; the stale package comments are fixed. The authorization architecture page gets the mode-choice tables from ADR-008.

docs.title: 5.1 Management derived from relationships (RMI-144)
docs.text: IsManaged becomes ManagerRelationship.Query().Where(managed == principalID, active).Exist. The managed claim in socialSessionProvider.GetUserClaims and the login-token exchange is built from the same query (through a ManagedChecker on the session provider), not from the email. ErrNotManaged reads "principal has no active manager"; ErrLastManager reads "the last manager of a principal without a verified email cannot be removed" and RemoveManager tests Email == nil || EmailVerifiedAt == nil. CreateInput gains Email *string; when set, the human is created with the email unverified and the existing verification flow verifies it, so it counts for release only afterward. ManagedHumanCapabilities apply while managed, whatever the email; AttachVerifiedEmail stops restoring default capabilities, which Release now does.

docs.title: 5.2 Release and manager invitations (RMI-145)
docs.text:
Release(ctx, actorID, managedID uuid.UUID) error

requires manage_managers, a verified email, and in one transaction deactivates every manager relationship, restores default capabilities, removes the authz manager relationships and audits the release. Invite gains kind (organization | manager, default organization) and manager_role; a manager invite names no organization, is created by the prospective manager (an active, verified, unmanaged human) for an existing self-managed principal's email, and is accepted only by the signed-in principal whose email matches, which creates the relationship, sets managed capabilities and audits the consent. IssueClaim/RedeemClaim remain the path from educator to guardian. Slug derivation for managed principals uses SlugForManaged only (§1.2).

docs.title: Migration Notes
docs.text:
• 0004_drop_organization_plan.sql drops the column; no data is carried over because the column was never consulted. Release notes state that API clients sending plan receive a validation error.
  • New tables are added by the Ent migration in the order the phases land: sf_slug_reservations, sf_app_roles, sf_access_changes, sf_resource_grants; new columns on sf_invites (app_roles, resource_*, kind, manager_role), sf_oauth_apps (backchannel_logout_uri), sf_listings (application) and sf_humans (none; email already optional).
  • Existing principals without a personal organization get one on their next login through the same SignupOrGetExisting path; a one-off sf-admin backfill personal-orgs command does it for principals that never return.
  • Existing sf_seat_assignments rows are converted to sf_app_roles rows with the listing's application and the ladder's lowest role, after which the seat-assignment API serves from sf_app_roles.
  • Relationship engines are rebuilt from the membership, app-role and grant tables by the existing sync on startup when switching modes.
  • Applications on LocalMemberships keep working until they choose a source; the default change is called out in the release notes.

docs.title: Sequencing Constraints
docs.text:
• §1.6 precedes §2.2: entitlements replace plan, so the summary exists before the derivation fills it.
  • §2.1 precedes §2.3 and §2.5; §2.2 precedes §2.3.
  • §3.1 precedes §3.2; §3.2 precedes §3.3 and §3.4. §3.1's grant-reduction site is wired when §4.2 lands.
  • §4.1 precedes §4.2 and §4.3; §4.2 and §4.3 precede §4.4 and §4.5. §4.1 needs only the collaborator role from §1.4.
  • §5.2's manager invite reuses the invite kinds introduced with §2.5.
  • Phase 6 follows everything.

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
• Slug squatting and handle theft. The reservation is bound to the releasing principal; reserved names are refused before any lookup; ResolveSlug never follows an expired reservation. Aliases are read-only redirects and never grant access to the previous organization.
  • Token freshness. The access token is the only thing a relying party trusts per request; the cache check runs after signature verification and before any application code; the margin floor prevents a misconfigured zero margin from accepting a token stamped by a slow clock after the change. The replay endpoint requires a client credential and returns no personal data beyond principal and organization IDs.
  • Back-channel tokens are signed by the issuer, verified against the JWKS, and carry iat/exp and a jti the receiver remembers for the token lifetime to reject replays.
  • Claims size. The 50-organization cap bounds the ID token and access token; the compact form omits names and slugs.
  • Collaborators never gain view, edit or manage on the organization; aggregates and cross-resource references are the application's to filter using ListResources, and the scope gate still applies to their credential.
  • Seats are enforced in the assignment transaction, so concurrent assignments cannot exceed the license.
  • Management consent. A self-managed human becomes managed only by accepting an invite while signed in; Release requires a verified email so a managed principal is never left unreachable.
  • Audit. Rename, conversion, role assignment, grant, revoke, release and every access change record the acting principal.

docs.title: Testing Strategy
docs.text:
• Ent-backed service tests (enttest SQLite in-memory) for signup on first login (first creates, second does not), slug derivation per provider, reserved slugs, rename with reclaim/stranger/expiry cases in every direction, ConvertToTeam, personal-organization refusals, plan absence, app roles with the owner overlay and seat limits, entitlement derivation, Release, manager invites.
  • SystemAuth handler tests for the orgs claim in ID token, userinfo and access token (shape, ordering, truncation), /oauth/userinfo/ memberships pagination, /access-changes, back-channel delivery with retry.
  • relyingparty tests for ClaimsMemberships, RemoteMemberships fallback on truncation, the provisioning hook's once-per-organization guarantee, and a table-driven RevocationCache test covering the margin boundary (iat == changed_at + margin − 1s refused, + margin accepted), per-organization scoping, expiry, floor enforcement, poller re-read of late rows, replay and suspect mode, back-channel receipt and replay rejection.
  • Access-change site tests: one test per recording site asserting a row in sf_access_changes and a sink call in the same transaction, and no refresh-token revocation on role change.
  • providertest resource-grant suite run against rbac and rebac/spicedb; schema_parity_test.go extended for collaborator and list; a test that marketplace.zed composes with the base schema.
  • Regression: the INIT-007 managed-principal suite runs unchanged for a child created without an email; existing conformance suites pass with personal-organization tests moved to team organizations.
  • Documentation: mkdocs strict build; golangci-lint clean.

docs.title: Discrepancies Found While Surveying
docs.text:
• ADR-007 decision 9 and ADR-010 decision 5 describe refresh-token revocation on membership change as current behavior; it never existed. RMI-135 adds the recording and leaves refresh tokens alone rather than removing a revocation.
  • ADR-007's context says authz.FeatureAuthorizer can answer feature questions; the interface has no implementation. Entitlements are derived by marketplace.Entitlements and the interface is left for a later initiative.
  • ADR-008's list example omits the base schema's editor relation. The owner decided to drop editor and viewer as organization roles rather than keep them (§4.1); list = view + collaborator covers what remains.
  • marketplace.zed defines its own organization, which the vocabulary rules forbid; §4.1 folds it into a facet.
  • invite.Accept does not sync memberships to the relationship engine; §2.5 fixes it as part of carrying application roles.
  • SignupOrGetExisting resolves by email only; §1.1 adds the provider identity lookup so it matches ADR-006's order.
  • The managed-principal switch is managed_principals.enabled, not identity.managed_principals.enabled as the INIT-007 TRD wrote; this initiative's new keys (authz, marketplace.default_entitlements, tokens.access_token_lifetime) follow the actual top-level layout.

docs.title: PLAN — Managed Principals for Relying-Party Applications
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-012

docs.title: Entry Gate
docs.text:
• INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-007 released: managed principals, login tokens, manager relationships, claims, and invitations.
  • Attaching a verified email stays in process until SystemAuth verifies email itself (INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-006).

docs.title: Phase 1 — SystemAuth Serves the Manager API
docs.text: Add bearer access that carries the token's client and adapt it to requestprincipal; give the handler a relying-party mode, the two missing routes, and a code rate limit; build and mount the service in systemauthsvc. Exit: a host that enables managed principals serves the API, and an end-to-end test creates a managed principal with a manager's token and signs it in through POST /login-token.

docs.title: Phase 2 — Client and Documentation
docs.text: Ship the typed client and document the API and its configuration. Exit: the client covers every route, and the managed-principals guide shows a relying party in another process using it.

docs.title: Risks and Mitigations
docs.text:
• Behavior change for in-process handler users: none. Relying-party mode is an option; existing NewHandler(svc) callers are unchanged.
  • Scope rollout: clients must be granted systemforge:managed_principals. The guide shows the client configuration.

docs.title: Follow-On
docs.text:
• An HTTP route to attach an email once SystemAuth verifies addresses itself.
  • Shared rate-limit storage for multi-instance SystemAuth deployments.

docs.title: PRD — Managed Principals for Relying-Party Applications
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-012 Status: Draft Home repo: github.com/plexusone/systemforge Design of record: ADR-005 Depends on: INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-007 (managed principals, login tokens, manager relationships)

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Managed principals exist only in process. managedprincipal.Service and managedprincipal.NewHandler need the SystemAuth database and a SystemAuth server as their gate, so only code running next to SystemAuth can create a managed principal or issue a login token.

Hosts compose SystemAuth and their products the other way round. SystemAuth is built once by systemauthsvc and owns the one principals table; each product is a relying party with its own database that refers to people by their SystemAuth principal ID, and may run in another process. Such a product cannot create a managed principal, add a manager, or print a login code without reaching into SystemAuth's database, which would split the principals table or bypass its invariants.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
1. SystemAuth serves the manager API. A host that enables managed principals in its SystemAuth configuration gets the manager-facing HTTP API on SystemAuth, with no code of its own.
  2. The manager is the caller. Every request carries the signed-in manager's SystemAuth access token. Authority comes from that manager's relationships and permissions (ADR-005), never from the application.
  3. The application is the token's client. The OAuth client that a create or login-token request is checked against is the one the access token was issued to, not one the request names.
  4. Complete for a relying party. Create a managed principal, list the caller's managed principals, add and remove managers, issue login tokens, list and revoke tokens and sessions, revoke everything, and issue and redeem claims.
  5. A typed Go client that relying parties import instead of writing HTTP calls.

docs.title: Non-Goals
docs.text:
• Attaching a verified email over HTTP. A relying party cannot prove that a principal controls an address, and a principal holding an address it does not control would be matched to that address's owner. Attaching an email waits for SystemAuth's own verification flow (INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-006); until then it stays an in-process operation.
  • New manager roles, consent records, or age rules. Those stay with the application.
  • A user interface. Applications render login codes and manager screens.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• R1. systemauthsvc builds the managed-principal service when the configuration enables managed principals and the deployment has a database, and mounts the API under /managed-principals. With managed principals off, the routes do not exist.
  • R2. Requests authenticate with a bearer access token issued by this SystemAuth, active, naming a principal, and granted the scope systemforge:managed_principals.
  • R3. Creating a managed principal over the API makes the caller its only initial manager, in a role the request names. Further managers join through the existing invitation and claim flows, which require their consent.
  • R4. Creating a managed principal and issuing a login token require the token's client to allow managed principals; lifetimes follow the existing policy (request, client default, deployment default, ceiling).
  • R5. Claim redemption and invitation acceptance are rate limited per caller, in addition to the codes' entropy.
  • R6. Every write is audited through the deployment's audit emitter when one is configured.
  • R7. SystemAuth built by systemauthsvc serves POST /login-token whenever managed principals are enabled.

docs.title: Success Criteria
docs.text:
• A relying party in another process creates a managed principal, issues a login token, and the token signs the principal in through POST /login-token, using only its SystemAuth client and the manager's access token.
  • A token without the scope, from another issuer, or for a non-manager is refused, and the refusal does not reveal whether the principal exists.

docs.title: Risks
docs.text: Risk Mitigation An application acts for a manager who did not ask The scope is granted per client and consented to like any other; the manager's own permissions bound every action An application names another client to get its policy The client is taken from the token; a different client_id in the body is refused Enumeration of managed principals Unknown, unmanaged, and forbidden principals answer alike (404 or 403 as today) Guessing claim or invitation codes 160-bit codes, single use, expiry, and a per-caller rate limit

docs.title: ROADMAP — Managed Principals for Relying-Party Applications
docs.text:
Initiative: INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-012 Repository: github.com/plexusone/systemforge

Design of record: ADR-005. SystemAuth serves the manager API that relying parties composed beside it call with the manager's access token. Builds on INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-007. Commits implementing an item carry Refs: RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-<NNN>.

docs.title: Phase 1 — SystemAuth Serves the Manager API
docs.text:
Theme: The manager is the caller and the application is the token's client

  • [x] RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-173 Bearer access with the client: systemauth.Server.BearerAccess and BearerAuthenticator, a requestprincipal adapter carrying the token's client, scopes, and token ID
  • [x] RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-174 Relying-party mode for the handler: client from the token, caller as sole initial manager, GET / listing the caller's managed principals, POST /{id}/login-tokens, and a per-caller rate limit on code redemption
  • Depends on: RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-173
  • [x] RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-175 systemauthsvc wiring: build the service when managed principals are enabled, mount /managed-principals behind the bearer authenticator, audit emitter and rate-limit options, Service.ManagedPrincipals(), and an end-to-end test through POST /login-token
  • Depends on: RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-174

docs.title: Phase 2 — Client and Documentation
docs.text:
Theme: Relying parties call the API through a typed client

  • [x] RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-176 identity/managedprincipal/mpclient: typed client over http.Client and a base URL, taking the manager's access token, with typed errors
  • Depends on: RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-175
  • [x] RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-177 Documentation: the HTTP API, scope, and systemauthsvc configuration in docs/identity/managed-principals.md; changelog
  • Depends on: RMI-SYSTEMFORGE-176

docs.title: TRD — Managed Principals for Relying-Party Applications
docs.text: Initiative: INIT-SYSTEMFORGE-012 Design of record: ADR-005

docs.title: Current State
docs.text:
• managedprincipal.Service holds the invariants, audit, and authorization of managed principals. managedprincipal.NewHandler serves create, managers, claims, invitations, release, delete, and login-token and session visibility behind requestprincipal.Middleware. It has no route to list a manager's principals or to issue a login token, and takes the OAuth client from the request body.
  • systemauth.Config already carries managed_principals and the per-client managed_principals and login_token_ttl settings, and systemauth.Server serves POST /login-token when managed principals are enabled and it has a credential service, which Ent storage provides.
  • systemauthsvc builds SystemAuth for hosts. It mounts the connections API with Server.BearerPrincipal, but builds no managed-principal service.

docs.title: 1. Bearer access with the client (identity/systemauth)
docs.text:
type BearerGrant struct {
    PrincipalID uuid.UUID
    ClientID    string
    Scopes      []string
    TokenID     string
    ExpiresAt   time.Time
}

func (s *Server) BearerAccess(r *http.Request, scope string) (*BearerGrant, error)
func (s *Server) BearerAuthenticator(scope string) requestprincipal.Authenticator

BearerAccess is BearerPrincipal plus the client the token was issued to. BearerAuthenticator adapts it to requestprincipal: no bearer token is ErrNoCredentials; an invalid token is a 401 and an insufficient scope a 403, each with the RFC 6750 challenge. The principal carries Protocol oidc, the scopes, Proof.Issuer (this server), Proof.TokenID, and the client ID in Claims["client_id"]. Tokens from other issuers never reach introspection as valid.

docs.title: 2. Remote callers (identity/managedprincipal)
docs.text:
NewHandler(svc, opts ...HandlerOption); existing callers are unchanged.

  • WithRequestClient(func(*http.Request) (string, bool)) puts the handler in relying-party mode. The OAuth client of create and login-token requests is the authenticated one; a body client_id that differs is a 400. Create accepts exactly one manager, the caller, so an application cannot place another person in management without their consent.
  • WithCodeRateLimit(ratelimit.Storage, ratelimit.Limit) limits /claims/redeem, /manager-invites/accept, and /manager-invites/decline per calling principal; over the limit is a 429 with Retry-After.
  • RequestClientFromPrincipal reads Claims["client_id"] from the request principal, the counterpart of BearerAuthenticator.

New routes:

Route Authorization GET / The caller's own active relationships; ?after=&limit= pages by principal ID, at most 200 a page POST /{principalID}/login-tokens The caller is an active manager (as Service.IssueLoginToken); the client allows managed principals

Service.ListManagedBy(ctx, managerID, after, limit) returns ManagedSummary{PrincipalID, DisplayName, Roles} for active managed principals the manager actively manages.

docs.title: 3. SystemAuth wiring (identity/systemauthsvc)
docs.text:
When managed_principals.enabled is set and the service has an Ent client:

  • build managedprincipal.NewService(client, server, WithAuditEmitter, WithLogger) with Options.AuditEmitter;
  • mount NewHandler at /managed-principals behind requestprincipal.Middleware(server.BearerAuthenticator(managedprincipal.Scope)) with WithRequestClient(managedprincipal.RequestClientFromPrincipal) and WithCodeRateLimit over in-memory storage (managedprincipal.DefaultCodeLimit, 10 a minute), or Options.ManagedPrincipalRates when several instances serve it;
  • expose Service.ManagedPrincipals() for a host in the same process.

managedprincipal.Scope is systemforge:managed_principals. Clients that call the API list it in their allowed scopes.

docs.title: 4. Client (identity/managedprincipal/mpclient)
docs.text:
func New(baseURL string, hc *http.Client) *Client
func (c *Client) Create(ctx, token string, in CreateInput) (uuid.UUID, error)
func (c *Client) List(ctx, token string, after uuid.UUID, limit int) ([]ManagedSummary, error)
func (c *Client) IssueLoginToken(ctx, token string, id uuid.UUID, in IssueLoginTokenInput) (*LoginToken, error)
// ListLoginTokens, RevokeLoginToken, ListSessions, RevokeSession, RevokeAll,
// ListManagers, RemoveManager, IssueClaim, RedeemClaim

token is the manager's access token. Errors: ErrUnauthorized, ErrForbidden, ErrNotFound, ErrInvalidCode, ErrConflict, ErrRateLimited, each wrapped in *APIError{Status, Message}.

docs.title: Testing Strategy
docs.text:
• systemauth: BearerAccess and BearerAuthenticator with a valid token, no token, an unknown token, and a missing scope.
  • managedprincipal: relying-party mode refuses a mismatched client and a second manager; list pages and excludes inactive relationships; login-token issue refuses non-managers and disallowed clients; the code rate limit answers 429.
  • systemauthsvc: with managed principals enabled, an access token with the scope creates a principal, issues a login token, and that token signs in through POST /login-token; without the scope the API answers 403; with managed principals off the routes are absent.
  • mpclient: against the handler, every method and error mapping.

docs.title: Deploying SystemAuth
docs.text: The cmd/systemauth binary is a self-contained SystemAuth server suitable for running under a process supervisor (systemd) behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy (Caddy, nginx). To run SystemAuth inside another Go binary instead, see Embedding.

docs.title: Production requirements
docs.text:
Unless started with --dev, the server refuses to start without:

  • a signing key (keys.private_key_file, keys.private_key_pem, --signing-key-file, or the SYSTEMAUTH_SIGNING_KEY environment variable),
  • a public https issuer (cookies are Secure/__Host-, and the issuer is what relying parties verify tokens against),
  • a persistent database (PostgreSQL or SQLite),

and it rejects social_login.insecure_cookies. --dev relaxes all of these (ephemeral key, in-memory storage, http://localhost issuer).

With a database configured, social login sessions, in-flight upstream logins and consent grants are stored in it (sf_login_sessions, sf_login_states, sf_consent_grants), so restarts keep users signed in and several instances can run behind a load balancer on one PostgreSQL database. Statically configured clients are updated from the configuration on each start. See Production Stores.

docs.title: Flags and environment
docs.text:
Running systemauth without a subcommand serves. Go-style single-dash flags (-addr) are accepted, and every flag can be set from an environment variable when it is not on the command line:

Flag Environment Default Notes --config, -c SYSTEMAUTH_CONFIG — YAML/JSON config; ${ENV} references are expanded --addr SYSTEMAUTH_ADDR :8080 e.g. 127.0.0.1:8081 behind a proxy (--listen is a deprecated alias) --issuer SYSTEMAUTH_ISSUER config Public URL, e.g. https://auth.example.com --signing-key-file SYSTEMAUTH_SIGNING_KEY_FILE config PEM RSA key (PKCS#1 or PKCS#8, ≥ 2048 bits) — SYSTEMAUTH_SIGNING_KEY — PEM key content (never a flag: command lines are visible to other users) --key-id SYSTEMAUTH_KEY_ID key thumbprint JWKS kid --db-driver, --db-dsn SYSTEMAUTH_DB_DRIVER, SYSTEMAUTH_DB_DSN config postgres (pgx) or sqlite --migrate SYSTEMAUTH_MIGRATE true Run schema migrations at startup --invite-only SYSTEMAUTH_INVITE_ONLY false Create accounts only for verified emails that hold a sign-up invite --signup-denied-url SYSTEMAUTH_SIGNUP_DENIED_URL — https page a refused sign-up is sent to, with error=invite_required; without it, SystemAuth's own waitlist page --dev SYSTEMAUTH_DEV false Development mode --log-level, --log-format SYSTEMAUTH_LOG_LEVEL, SYSTEMAUTH_LOG_FORMAT info, text Use json under a log collector

systemauth validate checks a configuration, including the production requirements; systemauth migrate runs migrations only.

docs.title: Invite-only sign-up
docs.text:
Start with --invite-only to let new accounts in only by invitation, for example while a deployment is being brought up. An invite is an email address, not a code: the person signs in with the upstream provider, and an account is created only when the provider's verified email holds a pending invite. People who already have an account sign in as before, and an unverified address never matches.

systemauth invite add ada@example.com grace@example.com --note "launch cohort" --expires-in 168h
systemauth invite list          # pending invites; --all includes redeemed ones
systemauth invite revoke ada@example.com
  • Redeeming: the first account created with an address consumes its invite. Revoking a redeemed invite does not touch the account; it only allows the address to be invited again.
  • No reason is given on refusal. A visitor cannot tell an address with no invite from one whose invite expired.
  • Waitlist. A refused sign-up lands on /signup/waitlist, served by SystemAuth while invite-only is on: a notify-me form that records the address with the consent text shown and its version. It answers the same whether or not the address was already listed, accepts posts only from SystemAuth's own or an allowed origin, and is rate-limited per client address and per submitted address. Nothing is emailed; operators export the list:
systemauth waitlist list          # oldest first; --csv to export
systemauth waitlist remove ada@example.com

A host binary sets the page's wording with Options.WaitlistPage and reads the list with Service.SignupWaitlist(). Behind a proxy, pass the client-address function (WithLoginTokenClientIP) so the per-address limit sees real clients. - Database: the commands read the configured database directly, so they work with the server running. The table is created by the schema migration. - In a host binary, set Options.InviteOnly and Options.SignupDeniedURL on systemauthsvc.New, and manage invites with Service.SignupInvites().

docs.title: App catalog
docs.text:
A deployment that hosts several applications can publish their catalog for the product switcher in each application's shell: name, launch URL, icon and order, keyed by the same identifier as the application's vocabulary. Pass Options.Apps (an appcatalog.Catalog) to systemauthsvc.New; SystemAuth serves it at /.well-known/sf-apps. It is public, since names and URLs are not secret.

A relying party lists it in its browser session ("apps" in the /bff/session response) by setting BFFConfig.Apps: appcatalog.Static when it runs in the same process, or appcatalog.Remote(issuer, ...), which fetches and caches the published catalog. A shell shows the entries the person holds a role in for the current organization (the membership's applications), so an application that is not registered or not entitled never appears.

docs.title: Connections to external services
docs.text:
Setting connections in the configuration lets organizations connect accounts at services such as a CDN or analytics product. It needs a database and the role-based authorization mode, and it adds a keys directory that must be backed up with the database:

connections:
  keys_dir: /var/lib/systemauth/keys
  vault: env://
  root_key: SYSTEMAUTH_KEYS_ROOT   # 32 bytes, base64 or hex; keep a copy offline

systemauth migrate creates the connectforge_* tables and, on PostgreSQL, enables row-level security on them. systemauth serve runs the key lifecycle jobs. See Connections and Key management.

docs.title: Signing key
docs.text:
Generate a key once and keep it in your secret store:

openssl genpkey -algorithm RSA -pkeyopt rsa_keygen_bits:3072 -out systemauth-signing.pem

Provide it as a file readable only by the service user, or as PEM content in SYSTEMAUTH_SIGNING_KEY. The JWKS kid defaults to the key's RFC 7638 thumbprint, so rotating the key changes the kid and relying parties fetch the new JWKS on the first token signed with it. Tokens signed with the old key stop verifying once it is replaced (overlapping keys are not supported yet).

docs.title: Example: systemd + Caddy
docs.text:
/etc/systemauth/env (mode 0600):

SYSTEMAUTH_ARGS=-addr 127.0.0.1:8081 -config /etc/systemauth/config.yaml -log-format json
SYSTEMAUTH_SIGNING_KEY_FILE=/etc/systemauth/signing.pem
DATABASE_URL=postgres://systemauth:secret@127.0.0.1:5432/systemauth?sslmode=disable
GITHUB_CLIENT_ID=...
GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET=...

/etc/systemd/system/systemauth.service:

[Unit]
Description=SystemAuth OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect server
After=network-online.target postgresql.service
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
EnvironmentFile=/etc/systemauth/env
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/systemauth $SYSTEMAUTH_ARGS
User=systemauth
Restart=on-failure
NoNewPrivileges=true
ProtectSystem=strict

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

systemd splits $SYSTEMAUTH_ARGS into words, so the flags can live in the environment file. /etc/systemauth/config.yaml:

issuer: https://auth.example.com
database:
  driver: postgres
  dsn: ${DATABASE_URL}
keys:
  private_key_file: ${SYSTEMAUTH_SIGNING_KEY_FILE}
features:
  require_pkce: true
  enable_jwt_access_tokens: true
social_login:
  github:
    client_id: ${GITHUB_CLIENT_ID}
    client_secret: ${GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET}
  allowed_redirect_origins:
    - https://app.example.com

Caddy terminates TLS and proxies to the loopback listener:

auth.example.com {
    reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8081
}

docs.title: Health checks
docs.text:
Endpoint Meaning GET /healthz Liveness: 200 {"status":"ok"} while the process serves HTTP GET /readyz Readiness: 200 when every check passes (the binary registers a database ping), otherwise 503 {"status":"unavailable","checks":{"database":"fail"}}; details are logged, not returned

Embedding applications add their own checks with systemauth.WithReadinessCheck(name, func(ctx) error).

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text: Startup migrations (--migrate, default on) add new columns automatically — for example the subject columns on sf_oauth_auth_codes / sf_oauth_tokens and the now-nullable sf_oauth_auth_codes.user_id. Run systemauth migrate first if the service user lacks DDL privileges.

docs.title: Embedding SystemAuth in a Host Binary
docs.text: The cmd/systemauth binary is a thin wrapper around the identity/systemauthsvc package. A host binary that serves several applications from one Go process (routing by Host header) can use the same package to run a production-grade SystemAuth next to them, with the same configuration file, production checks, database setup and stores as the standalone server.

docs.title: Security trade-off
docs.text:
Read this before choosing embedding over the standalone binary.

  • The signing key shares the process with application code. Anything that can read the host's memory, or any code path in any embedded application that leaks process state (a debug endpoint, a heap dump, a dependency with a vulnerability), can expose the key that signs every ID and access token. With the standalone binary only SystemAuth's own code runs next to the key.
  • A host restart is a login outage. Deploying, crashing or rolling back any application restarts SystemAuth too. Login sessions, in-flight logins, consent grants and tokens survive in the database, but requests during the restart fail, and a crash loop in one application takes login down for all.
  • Shared resource limits. A memory leak or CPU spike in one application affects token issuance for all relying parties.

Embedding is reasonable when the host runs a small set of first-party applications from one codebase and one deployment pipeline, and running a separate service is not worth the operational cost. Keep SystemAuth on its own host name (auth.example.com) so its __Host- cookies are not shared with the applications. Prefer the standalone binary when third-party code runs in the host or when the applications deploy independently.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
import (
    "github.com/plexusone/systemforge/identity/relyingparty"
    "github.com/plexusone/systemforge/identity/systemauthsvc"
)

cfg, err := systemauthsvc.LoadConfig("/etc/host/systemauth.yaml",
    systemauthsvc.WithDefaultSigningKeyPEM(os.Getenv("SYSTEMAUTH_SIGNING_KEY")),
)
if err != nil {
    return err
}
auth, err := systemauthsvc.New(ctx, cfg, systemauthsvc.Options{
    Logger:  logger,
    Migrate: true,
})
if err != nil {
    return err // e.g. ErrNotProductionReady: missing key, http issuer, no database
}
defer func() {
    if err := auth.Close(); err != nil {
        logger.Error("closing SystemAuth", "error", err)
    }
}()

// An application in the same process federates to SystemAuth without
// fetching the discovery document.
rp, err := relyingparty.NewClientWithMetadata(relyingparty.Config{
    Issuer:      auth.Issuer(),
    ClientID:    "app",
    RedirectURL: "https://app.example.com/bff/auth/callback",
}, auth.Metadata())
if err != nil {
    return err
}

mux := http.NewServeMux()
mux.Handle("auth.example.com/", auth.Handler())
mux.Handle("app.example.com/", appHandler)

Overrides are applied before defaults and validation, so an override can fill in a value the file leaves out (for example WithDefaultIssuer for a file without issuer). When the SystemAuth settings live inside the host's own configuration file, load them from memory with the same overrides:

// section is the raw YAML or JSON of the host's "systemauth" block.
cfg, err := systemauthsvc.LoadConfigBytes(section, "yaml",
    systemauthsvc.WithDefaultIssuer("http://localhost:8080"),
    systemauthsvc.WithDefaultSigningKeyPEM(os.Getenv("SYSTEMAUTH_SIGNING_KEY")),
)

Handler() serves every SystemAuth endpoint at the root of the issuer's host (discovery, JWKS, /oauth/*, /login/*, /logout, /consent, /healthz, /readyz); mount it on its own host name rather than under a path prefix, since endpoint URLs are derived from the issuer.

The relying party still calls the token, JWKS and UserInfo endpoints over HTTP at the issuer URL, so the host must be reachable at that URL from itself (normally through the same reverse proxy).

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Item Purpose LoadConfig(path, overrides...) Read YAML/JSON (with ${ENV} expansion), then apply overrides, defaults and validation, in that order. An empty path starts from an empty config. LoadConfigBytes(data, format, overrides...) The same for configuration already in memory. format is "yaml", "json" or "" (JSON when the data starts with {, otherwise YAML). systemauth.DecodeConfig, systemauth.DecodeConfigFile Lower level: decode and expand ${ENV} without defaults or validation; call ApplyDefaults and Validate after adjusting the result. WithIssuer, WithDefaultIssuer, WithDatabase, WithSigningKeyFile, WithDefaultSigningKeyPEM, WithKeyID Overrides, the same ones the command's flags use. Options.Dev Allow an ephemeral key, in-memory storage, an http issuer and insecure cookies. Never in production. Options.Logger *slog.Logger; NewLogger(w, level, format) builds one. Options.SigningKey An *rsa.PrivateKey from a secret manager, instead of a file or PEM. Options.DB + DBDialect, Options.EntClient Use an existing pool or Ent client (the caller keeps ownership; Close leaves it open). Options.Migrate Create or update the schema before the system user and static clients are written. Options.ServerOptions Extra systemauth.Options, e.g. WithObservability. Options.AuditEmitter Records managed-principal actions served by the /managed-principals API. Options.ManagedPrincipalRates, Options.ManagedPrincipalOptions Shared rate-limit storage for the API's code routes (the default is in memory, for one instance) and extra managedprincipal options. CheckProduction(cfg, opts) The checks New enforces, for a validate command. Migrate(ctx, cfg) Open, migrate and close (for a separate migration step). Service.Handler, Ready, Migrate, Close, Issuer, KeyID, Metadata, Discovery, Server, ManagedPrincipals The running service. ManagedPrincipals is the managed-principal service, nil unless managed principals are enabled; the API is then mounted at ManagedPrincipalsPath.

New enforces the production requirements whenever Options.Dev is false: a signing key, a public https issuer, a persistent database (configured or injected), and no social_login.insecure_cookies. It then connects, optionally migrates, creates the system user that owns statically configured clients, registers or updates those clients, and keeps tokens, login sessions, in-flight logins and consent grants in the database (see Production Stores).

Ready(ctx) runs the same checks as GET /readyz (the database ping); wire it into the host's own readiness endpoint.

docs.title: Database
docs.text: The package links the PostgreSQL (pgx) and SQLite (go-sqlite3, cgo) drivers. SystemAuth's tables can share a PostgreSQL database with the host's applications only if their schemas do not collide; a separate database (or Options.DB on a dedicated database) is simpler to operate and to back up.

docs.title: SystemAuth Overview
docs.text: SystemAuth provides authentication and OAuth 2.0 functionality through clean, swappable provider interfaces. This design allows you to start with embedded implementations and migrate to external services (like Ory Hydra/Kratos) when needed.

docs.title: Provider Interfaces
docs.text: Interface Purpose Maps to Ory IdentityProvider User CRUD operations Kratos Identity API AuthenticationProvider Session management Kratos Session API OAuthProvider OAuth 2.0/OIDC flows Hydra Public/Admin API OAuthClientStore OAuth client management Hydra Client API

docs.title: Option 1: Full OAuth Server
docs.text:
import "github.com/plexusone/systemforge/identity/systemauth"

// Create embedded OAuth server
server, err := systemauth.NewEmbedded(systemauth.Config{
    Issuer: "https://auth.example.com",
})

// Get all providers
providers := systemauth.NewProviders(server,
    systemauth.WithProviderSessionDuration(24 * time.Hour),
    systemauth.WithProviderPasswordVerifier(myPasswordVerifier),
)

// Use providers
identity, _ := providers.Identity.GetIdentity(ctx, userID)
session, _ := providers.Authentication.ValidateSession(ctx, token)
userInfo, _ := providers.OAuth.UserInfo(ctx, accessToken)

docs.title: Option 2: Identity/Auth Only (No OAuth)
docs.text:
// Create from storage directly
storage := systemauth.NewMemoryStorage() // or Ent storage
providers := systemauth.NewProvidersFromStorage(storage)

// Identity and Authentication available
// OAuth is nil (no server)

docs.title: HTTP Endpoints
docs.text:
A systemauth.Server (embedded or the standalone cmd/systemauth binary) serves:

Endpoint Method Description /.well-known/openid-configuration GET OIDC discovery /.well-known/jwks.json GET JSON Web Key Set /oauth/authorize GET/POST Authorization endpoint /oauth/token POST Token endpoint (refresh tokens rotate; see Social Login) /oauth/introspect POST Token introspection (RFC 7662) /oauth/revoke POST Token revocation (RFC 7009) /oauth/userinfo GET/POST OpenID Connect UserInfo /oauth/userinfo/memberships GET Paginated organization memberships of the token's principal (needs an OrgsSource)

With social_login configured, /login*, /logout and /consent are added (see Social Login).

docs.title: UserInfo
docs.text:
/oauth/userinfo implements OIDC Core §5.3. Send the access token as Authorization: Bearer <token> (or access_token in a form-encoded POST body; query parameters are not accepted). The token must have been granted the openid scope.

{
  "sub": "5f1c0a9e-...",
  "email": "octo@example.com",
  "email_verified": true,
  "name": "Octo Cat",
  "picture": "https://avatars.example.com/u/4242"
}

With systemauth.WithOrgsSource configured, userinfo and the ID token also carry orgs and orgs_truncated whatever the scopes, and JWT access tokens carry the compact form. GET /oauth/userinfo/memberships?limit=&cursor= returns every organization, paginated. See The orgs claim.

sub is the SystemAuth principal ID. Standard claims are released per granted scope — email → email, email_verified; profile → name, picture, … — and are read live from the principal (via the SessionProvider), so they reflect the current profile rather than the one at sign-in.

Condition Response No token 401, WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="systemauth" Unknown, expired or revoked token 401, WWW-Authenticate: Bearer ..., error="invalid_token" Token without openid scope 403, WWW-Authenticate: Bearer ..., error="insufficient_scope", scope="openid"

docs.title: Embedded vs Ory
docs.text: Aspect Embedded Ory Services Deployment Single binary Multiple services Database App's database Separate databases Scaling With app Independent Customization Full code control Config + webhooks Production Ready ✅ (Fosite-based) ✅ (Battle-tested)

docs.title: Migration Path
docs.text:
Start embedded, migrate to Ory when needed:

// Today: Embedded
providers := systemauth.NewProviders(server)

// Future: Ory adapters (same interface)
providers := &systemauth.Providers{
    Identity:       ory.NewKratosIdentityProvider(kratosClient),
    Authentication: ory.NewKratosAuthProvider(kratosClient),
    OAuth:          ory.NewHydraOAuthProvider(hydraClient),
    OAuthClients:   ory.NewHydraClientStore(hydraAdminClient),
}

// Application code using providers.* doesn't change!

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
• Identity Provider - User management
  • Authentication Provider - Sessions
  • OAuth Provider - OAuth 2.0 flows

docs.title: Production Stores
docs.text: SystemAuth and relying parties keep short-lived browser state server-side: login sessions, in-flight OAuth logins and consent decisions on SystemAuth, and application sessions (holding SystemAuth tokens) and in-flight logins on each relying party. The defaults are in-memory, which is fine for a single development process but means a restart signs everyone out and replicas do not share state. In production, use the durable stores described here.

docs.title: SystemAuth
docs.text:
When SystemAuth runs on EntStorage (any database configured for the systemauth binary), social login automatically uses database-backed stores. Nothing needs to be configured:

Store Implementation Table Login sessions (__Host-sf_login) EntLoginSessionStore sf_login_sessions Upstream login state EntLoginStateStore sf_login_states Consent grants EntConsentStore sf_consent_grants

The tables are part of SystemAuth's Ent schema and are created by systemauth migrate (or --migrate on serve). Without a database (--dev), the in-memory stores are used and a warning is logged.

Behavior:

  • Session tokens and OAuth state values are stored only as SHA-256 hashes. The upstream nonce and PKCE verifier are stored for the duration of the login (at most 10 minutes) and deleted when the callback consumes them.
  • Take on the login state is single-use across replicas: a row is returned only to the caller whose delete removed it.
  • Consent is one row per (principal, client, scope), so concurrent grants from several replicas never lose scopes.
  • Expired rows are removed opportunistically on writes, at most once every 5 minutes per instance. A scheduled job can also call DeleteExpired.

Library users embedding SystemAuth get the same defaults with WithStorage(NewEntStorage(client)), and can construct the stores directly:

sessions := systemauth.NewEntLoginSessionStore(entClient,
    systemauth.WithCleanupInterval(10*time.Minute)) // 0 disables
srv, err := systemauth.NewEmbedded(cfg,
    systemauth.WithStorage(systemauth.NewEntStorage(entClient)),
    systemauth.WithLoginSessionStore(sessions),
    systemauth.WithLoginStateStore(systemauth.NewEntLoginStateStore(entClient)),
    systemauth.WithConsentStore(systemauth.NewEntConsentStore(entClient)),
)

The Ent stores work on PostgreSQL (recommended for multiple replicas) and SQLite (single instance that survives restarts).

docs.title: Relying parties
docs.text:
Relying parties own their database and do not depend on SystemAuth's schema. The identity/relyingparty/pgstore package provides PostgreSQL implementations of relyingparty.SessionStore and relyingparty.LoginStateStore on database/sql with the pgx driver:

Store Constructor Table Browser sessions pgstore.NewSessionStore sf_rp_sessions In-flight logins pgstore.NewLoginStateStore sf_rp_login_states 
import (
    _ "github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/stdlib"

    "github.com/plexusone/systemforge/identity/relyingparty"
    "github.com/plexusone/systemforge/identity/relyingparty/pgstore"
)

db, err := sql.Open("pgx", os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL"))
if err != nil {
    return err
}
if err := pgstore.EnsureSchema(ctx, db); err != nil {
    return err
}

// Reads MYAPP_SESSION_KEY, MYAPP_SESSION_KEY_ID, and (during rotation)
// MYAPP_SESSION_KEY_PREVIOUS / MYAPP_SESSION_KEY_PREVIOUS_ID.
stores, err := pgstore.NewStores(db, pgstore.KeysFromEnv("MYAPP_"))
if err != nil {
    return err // pgstore.ErrNoSessionKey when no key is configured
}

bff, err := relyingparty.NewBFF(relyingparty.BFFConfig{
    Client:      client,
    Principals:  principals,
    Sessions:    stores.Sessions,
    LoginStates: stores.LoginStates,
})

NewStores validates the key configuration (pgstore.Keys) and builds both stores; Keys.Options() returns the equivalent options for callers that construct the stores individually with NewSessionStore / NewLoginStateStore. Run EnsureSchema from the application's setup or migration step — usually as a more privileged role than the serving connection.

docs.title: Schema
docs.text: EnsureSchema applies pgstore.SchemaSQL idempotently, under an advisory lock so replicas starting together do not race. Applications with their own migration tool can copy SchemaSQL into a migration instead. Indexes cover expires_at on both tables and subject and sid on sessions (used by DeleteBySubject / DeleteBySID for back-channel logout).

docs.title: Encryption at rest
docs.text:
Session rows hold SystemAuth access, refresh and ID tokens. They, the session's claims, and the login nonce and PKCE verifier are sealed with AES-256-GCM before they reach the database:

  • The key is supplied by the application (32 bytes; generate one with openssl rand -base64 32 and keep it in a secret manager). DecodeKey accepts hex or base64.
  • Each row records the ID of the key that sealed it. The ciphertext is bound to its table, row and key ID, so a value copied into another row or relabeled with another key fails to decrypt.
  • The constructors refuse to start without WithEncryptionKey. WithInsecurePlaintext() allows plaintext for local development only.
  • A row that fails decryption (tampered, or sealed with a key that is no longer configured) is logged and reported as an error wrapping both relyingparty.ErrSessionNotFound (the user is signed out) and pgstore.ErrDecrypt or pgstore.ErrUnknownKeyID.

Cookie tokens and OAuth state values are stored only as SHA-256 hashes.

docs.title: Key rotation
docs.text:
1. Deploy every instance with the new key as the encryption key and the old key as a decryption key — with KeysFromEnv, set the new key and ID in <PREFIX>SESSION_KEY / <PREFIX>SESSION_KEY_ID and move the old ones to <PREFIX>SESSION_KEY_PREVIOUS / <PREFIX>SESSION_KEY_PREVIOUS_ID (equivalently WithEncryptionKey("k2", newKey) plus WithDecryptionKey("k1", oldKey)).
  2. New sessions are sealed with k2; existing ones are re-sealed with k2 whenever they are updated (for example on token refresh).
  3. After the session lifetime (default 12 hours) has passed, every k1 row has expired or been re-sealed; remove the previous key.

Keep the key ID stable for a given key: it is stored in every row.

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text: Both stores delete expired rows opportunistically on writes, at most once every 5 minutes per instance (pgstore.WithCleanupInterval, 0 disables). DeleteExpired(ctx) can be called from a scheduled job instead.

docs.title: Testing custom stores
docs.text:
identity/systemauth/storetest and identity/relyingparty/storetest are conformance suites (round trip, expiry, single-use Take under concurrency, back-channel deletes). Run them against any custom store implementation. The PostgreSQL tests in this repository run when SF_TEST_PG_DSN points at a server where the test user may create databases:

SF_TEST_PG_DSN='postgres://user@127.0.0.1:5432/postgres?sslmode=disable' go test ./...

docs.title: Provider Interfaces
docs.text: SystemAuth defines four provider interfaces that abstract authentication and OAuth functionality. Each interface can be implemented by the embedded Fosite-based system or external services like Ory.

docs.title: Identity Provider
docs.text:
Manages user identities (CRUD operations).

type IdentityProvider interface {
    CreateIdentity(ctx context.Context, identity *Identity) error
    GetIdentity(ctx context.Context, id uuid.UUID) (*Identity, error)
    GetIdentityByEmail(ctx context.Context, email string) (*Identity, error)
    UpdateIdentity(ctx context.Context, identity *Identity) error
    DeleteIdentity(ctx context.Context, id uuid.UUID) error
    ListIdentities(ctx context.Context, filter *IdentityFilter) ([]*Identity, error)
}

docs.title: Identity Structure
docs.text:
type Identity struct {
    ID        uuid.UUID      `json:"id"`
    State     IdentityState  `json:"state"`      // active, inactive
    Traits    IdentityTraits `json:"traits"`     // email, name, etc.
    Metadata  map[string]any `json:"metadata"`
    CreatedAt time.Time      `json:"created_at"`
    UpdatedAt time.Time      `json:"updated_at"`
}

type IdentityTraits struct {
    Email         string `json:"email"`
    EmailVerified bool   `json:"email_verified"`
    Name          string `json:"name"`
    GivenName     string `json:"given_name"`
    FamilyName    string `json:"family_name"`
    Picture       string `json:"picture"`
    Locale        string `json:"locale"`
}

docs.title: Example Usage
docs.text:
// Create identity
identity := &systemauth.Identity{
    State: systemauth.IdentityStateActive,
    Traits: systemauth.IdentityTraits{
        Email:     "user@example.com",
        Name:      "John Doe",
        GivenName: "John",
    },
}
err := providers.Identity.CreateIdentity(ctx, identity)

// Get by email
identity, err := providers.Identity.GetIdentityByEmail(ctx, "user@example.com")

docs.title: Authentication Provider
docs.text:
Manages user sessions (login, validation, revocation).

type AuthenticationProvider interface {
    Authenticate(ctx context.Context, req *AuthenticateRequest) (*AuthSession, error)
    ValidateSession(ctx context.Context, sessionToken string) (*AuthSession, error)
    RefreshSession(ctx context.Context, sessionToken string) (*AuthSession, error)
    RevokeSession(ctx context.Context, sessionToken string) error
    RevokeSessions(ctx context.Context, identityID uuid.UUID) error
    ListSessions(ctx context.Context, identityID uuid.UUID) ([]*AuthSession, error)
}

docs.title: Authentication Methods
docs.text:
type AuthMethod string

const (
    AuthMethodPassword AuthMethod = "password"
    AuthMethodOIDC     AuthMethod = "oidc"
    AuthMethodWebAuthn AuthMethod = "webauthn"
    AuthMethodTOTP     AuthMethod = "totp"
)

docs.title: Example Usage
docs.text:
// Authenticate with password
session, err := providers.Authentication.Authenticate(ctx, &systemauth.AuthenticateRequest{
    Method:     systemauth.AuthMethodPassword,
    Identifier: "user@example.com",
    Password:   "secret",
    DeviceInfo: &systemauth.DeviceInfo{
        IPAddress: r.RemoteAddr,
        UserAgent: r.UserAgent(),
    },
})

// Validate session (in middleware)
session, err := providers.Authentication.ValidateSession(ctx, sessionToken)
if err != nil {
    // Invalid or expired session
}

// Revoke all sessions (on password change)
err := providers.Authentication.RevokeSessions(ctx, userID)

docs.title: OAuth Provider
docs.text:
Handles OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect operations.

type OAuthProvider interface {
    // Token operations
    Introspect(ctx context.Context, token string, tokenTypeHint string) (*OAuthIntrospection, error)
    Revoke(ctx context.Context, token string, tokenTypeHint string) error
    UserInfo(ctx context.Context, accessToken string) (*OAuthUserInfo, error)

    // Login/Consent flow (for custom UI)
    GetLoginRequest(ctx context.Context, challenge string) (*OAuthLoginRequest, error)
    AcceptLogin(ctx context.Context, challenge string, accept *OAuthLoginAccept) (*OAuthLoginResponse, error)
    GetConsentRequest(ctx context.Context, challenge string) (*OAuthConsentRequest, error)
    AcceptConsent(ctx context.Context, challenge string, accept *OAuthConsentAccept) (*OAuthConsentResponse, error)
}

docs.title: Example Usage
docs.text:
// Introspect token (validate and get info)
introspection, err := providers.OAuth.Introspect(ctx, accessToken, "access_token")
if !introspection.Active {
    // Token is invalid or expired
}

// Get user info (OIDC)
userInfo, err := providers.OAuth.UserInfo(ctx, accessToken)
fmt.Printf("User: %s <%s>\n", userInfo.Name, userInfo.Email)

docs.title: OAuth Client Store
docs.text:
Manages OAuth 2.0 client applications.

type OAuthClientStore interface {
    CreateClient(ctx context.Context, client *OAuthClient) error
    GetClient(ctx context.Context, clientID string) (*OAuthClient, error)
    UpdateClient(ctx context.Context, client *OAuthClient) error
    DeleteClient(ctx context.Context, clientID string) error
    ListClients(ctx context.Context) ([]*OAuthClient, error)
}

docs.title: Client Structure
docs.text:
type OAuthClient struct {
    ClientID      string   `json:"client_id"`
    ClientSecret  string   `json:"client_secret,omitempty"`
    ClientName    string   `json:"client_name"`
    RedirectURIs  []string `json:"redirect_uris"`
    GrantTypes    []string `json:"grant_types"`
    ResponseTypes []string `json:"response_types"`
    Scope         string   `json:"scope"`
    Public        bool     `json:"public"`  // No secret (SPA, mobile)
}

docs.title: Example Usage
docs.text:
// Register OAuth client
client := &systemauth.OAuthClient{
    ClientID:      "my-app",
    ClientSecret:  "super-secret",
    ClientName:    "My Application",
    RedirectURIs:  []string{"https://app.example.com/callback"},
    GrantTypes:    []string{"authorization_code", "refresh_token"},
    ResponseTypes: []string{"code"},
    Scope:         "openid profile email",
}
err := providers.OAuthClients.CreateClient(ctx, client)

// List all clients
clients, err := providers.OAuthClients.ListClients(ctx)

docs.title: Embedded Implementations
docs.text:
SystemAuth provides embedded implementations for all providers:

Interface Implementation Backend IdentityProvider EmbeddedIdentityProvider SystemAuth Storage AuthenticationProvider EmbeddedAuthProvider In-memory sessions OAuthProvider EmbeddedOAuthProvider Fosite OAuthClientStore EmbeddedOAuthClientStore SystemAuth Storage

docs.title: Creating Individual Providers
docs.text:
storage := systemauth.NewMemoryStorage()

identityProvider := systemauth.NewEmbeddedIdentityProvider(storage)
authProvider := systemauth.NewEmbeddedAuthProvider(identityProvider,
    systemauth.WithSessionDuration(24 * time.Hour),
    systemauth.WithPasswordVerifier(myVerifier),
)
clientStore := systemauth.NewEmbeddedOAuthClientStore(storage)

docs.title: Relying Parties (Federating to SystemAuth)
docs.text:
Applications do not implement GitHub/Google login themselves. They federate to SystemAuth as OpenID Connect clients with the identity/relyingparty package, which provides the whole browser and API surface:

Piece What it does Client Discovery, authorization URL (state + nonce + S256 PKCE), code exchange, ID-token verification against the SystemAuth JWKS, UserInfo, refresh, revocation ResolvePrincipal + PrincipalStore Find-or-create the app-local principal keyed by the OIDC sub → sf_principal_id, with a verified-email linking fallback BFF http.Handler for the /bff/* cookie-session surface the shared frontend auth package expects BearerMiddleware Authenticates programmatic clients (CLI, MCP, services) with SystemAuth JWT access tokens or API keys

See ADR-002 (docs/design/adrs/ADR-002-centralized-social-login-systemauth.md) for the design.

docs.title: SystemAuth setup
docs.text:
Register the application as a client and enable JWT access tokens if programmatic clients will call the application with SystemAuth tokens:

features:
  require_pkce: true
  enable_jwt_access_tokens: true   # needed by BearerMiddleware
clients:
  - id: my-app
    type: public                   # or confidential with a secret
    name: My App
    redirect_uris:
      - https://app.example.com/bff/auth/callback
    grant_types: [authorization_code, refresh_token]
    response_types: [code]
    scopes: [openid, profile, email, offline_access]
social_login:
  allowed_redirect_origins:
    - https://app.example.com

SystemAuth returns an RS256 id_token (with nonce, auth_time, and the scope-filtered email, email_verified, name, picture), rotating refresh tokens, and serves /oauth/userinfo. Every JWT carries the kid published in /.well-known/jwks.json.

docs.title: Application setup
docs.text:
import "github.com/plexusone/systemforge/identity/relyingparty"

client, err := relyingparty.NewClient(ctx, relyingparty.Config{
    Issuer:      "https://auth.example.com",
    ClientID:    "my-app",
    RedirectURL: "https://app.example.com/bff/auth/callback",
    // ClientSecret: os.Getenv("SYSTEMAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET"), // confidential clients
})
if err != nil {
    return err
}

principals := myapp.NewPrincipalStore(db) // implements relyingparty.PrincipalStore

bff, err := relyingparty.NewBFF(relyingparty.BFFConfig{
    Client:     client,
    Principals: principals,
    Sessions:   sessions, // e.g. pgstore.NewSessionStore; default: in-memory (single instance)
})
if err != nil {
    return err
}

r := chi.NewRouter()
r.Mount("/bff", bff)

// Browser-only routes: BFF session required.
r.With(bff.RequireSession).Get("/app/api/projects", listProjects)

// API used by browsers and programmatic clients alike.
r.Route("/api/v1", func(r chi.Router) {
    r.Use(relyingparty.BearerMiddleware(relyingparty.BearerConfig{
        Tokens:     client,         // SystemAuth JWT access tokens
        APIKeys:    apiKeyService,  // *apikey.Service
        Principals: principals,
        Sessions:   bff,            // also accept the BFF cookie
    }))
    r.Get("/projects", listProjects)
})

func listProjects(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    p, _ := relyingparty.PrincipalFromContext(r.Context())
    // p.ID, p.Type, p.Subject, p.Method, p.Scopes, p.Memberships
}

docs.title: /bff/* contract
docs.text:
The routes match the shared frontend auth package (BFFClient):

Route Response GET /bff/session 200 {"authenticated": false} or {"authenticated": true, "user_id", "expires_at", "user": User, "apps"} (apps only when BFFConfig.Apps is set) GET /bff/api/v1/users/me 200 User or 401 {"code": "UNAUTHENTICATED", "message"} GET /bff/auth/login?return_to= 302 to SystemAuth /oauth/authorize GET /bff/auth/{github,google}?return_to= Same, with idp_hint so SystemAuth skips its provider chooser GET /bff/auth/callback Verifies the login, creates the session, 302 to return_to POST /bff/auth/logout Deletes the session, revokes the SystemAuth refresh token, 204 POST /bff/auth/login 501 PASSWORD_LOGIN_UNSUPPORTED (password login is not offered)

User is {id, email, name, avatar_url?, memberships: [{id, organization_id, organization_name, organization_slug, role, joined_at}], created_at, updated_at?}. Errors are {code, message}.

Security properties:

  • The session cookie (__Host-sf_rp_session) is an opaque 256-bit token, Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, host-only; only its SHA-256 hash is stored. SystemAuth tokens never reach the browser. A new token is issued on every login and any presented session is deleted (no fixation).
  • Login state is single-use, server-side, and bound to the browser with a __Host-sf_rp_state cookie; PKCE and the OIDC nonce are always used.
  • The ID token is verified per OIDC Core §3.1.3.7 (RS256 signature against the JWKS, iss, aud/azp, exp, nonce), and the UserInfo sub must match it.
  • return_to must be a same-origin path or an absolute URL on the app origin or AllowedOrigins.
  • POST /bff/auth/logout and unsafe methods behind RequireSession require a JSON body and, when the browser sends one, an allowed Origin.

BFF.AccessToken(r) returns a SystemAuth access token for the session, refreshing it when it is about to expire and storing the rotated refresh token; a rejected refresh (revoked, reused, or past refresh_token_absolute_lifetime) ends the session.

Logging out of the app does not end the SystemAuth login session. To sign the user out everywhere, send the browser to SystemAuth GET /logout?return_to=... after POST /bff/auth/logout.

docs.title: Account linking
docs.text:
ResolvePrincipal applies the same rules as SystemAuth:

  1. The sub (SystemAuth principal ID), stored as sf_principal_id, is the primary key: a linked principal signs in even if its email changed.
  2. Otherwise a verified identity email links to an existing principal whose own email is verified and that is not linked to another SystemAuth principal.
  3. Otherwise a principal is created, which requires a verified email.

An unverified email never links to or creates a principal; an email held by an unverified (or differently linked) local principal is a conflict (409 ACCOUNT_CONFLICT).

docs.title: Memberships
docs.text:
Organization memberships (in /bff/session, /bff/api/v1/users/me and AuthenticatedPrincipal.Memberships) come from a MembershipSource, which receives the principal, its SystemAuth subject, and the verified SystemAuth claims of the request (the ID token + UserInfo claims stored with the BFF session, or the JWT access token's claims). SystemAuth is the source of truth for memberships, application roles and entitlements (ADR-007), so relying parties do not keep tables of their own. The sources:

Source Reads Use ClaimsMemberships (default) The orgs claim: organization id, role and apps (application identifier to role); the ID token and userinfo form also has slug, name and type. Needs no network call Production RemoteMemberships(client) GET /oauth/userinfo/memberships, all pages, with the request's access token Production, when the claims cannot answer ClaimsOrRemoteMemberships(remote, logger) Claims, then the endpoint when orgs_truncated is set or the claim is absent; if the endpoint fails it serves the claims Production, for users in more than 50 organizations LocalMemberships(lister) An app-local table (MemoryPrincipalStore implements MembershipLister) Development and tests only; it diverges from SystemAuth 
bff, err := relyingparty.NewBFF(relyingparty.BFFConfig{
    Client:      client,
    Principals:  principals,
    Memberships: relyingparty.ClaimsOrRemoteMemberships(relyingparty.RemoteMemberships(client), logger),
})

When Memberships is unset, ClaimsMemberships is used. A request without claims, such as one authenticated by an API key, then has no memberships; an application that accepts API keys supplies a source for them. Membership.Applications carries the principal's role in each application; an application absent from it is one the principal may not open.

An application provisions itself for an organization on first use, keyed by the SystemAuth organization ID, with ProvisioningMemberships(source, application, hook): the hook runs once per organization per process for a principal who holds a role in application and must be idempotent.

docs.title: Access changes
docs.text:
Claims in a JWT access token are fixed when it is issued, so removing a person from an organization does not reach a token already issued until it expires. SystemAuth records each access change (ADR-010) and a RevocationCache remembers the recent ones:

cache := relyingparty.NewRevocationCache() // margin 30 s (floor 15 s), covers 15 min tokens

// In a modular monolith, hand the same cache to SystemAuth's services:
orgs := organization.NewService(db, organization.WithAccessChangeSink(accesschange.ToSink(cache)))

mw := relyingparty.BearerMiddleware(relyingparty.BearerConfig{
    Tokens: client, Principals: principals,
    Revocation:   cache,
    Organization: func(r *http.Request) string { return r.PathValue("org") }, // optional
})
bff, _ := relyingparty.NewBFF(relyingparty.BFFConfig{Client: client, Principals: principals, Revocation: cache})

A JWT is accepted only if its iat is at or after the change plus the clock-skew margin (WithSkewMargin, default 30 s, never below 15 s); a token stamped inside the margin counts as issued before the change. Otherwise the middleware answers 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token", error_description="token expired", which makes an OIDC client refresh and obtain claims that reflect the change. When the request names an organization, a change scoped to another organization does not refuse it; without one, any change to the principal does. A token with no iat is accepted only for a principal with no recorded change. Entries are dropped once the change plus the maximum token lifetime (WithMaxTokenLifetime, default 15 minutes) plus the margin has passed, so the cache holds only the changes of the last token lifetime.

A BFF session does not end on a change. The BFF refreshes the session's tokens, re-reads the claims from the userinfo endpoint, and keeps the person signed in with reduced claims; a refresh SystemAuth refuses (deactivation, revoked sessions) ends the session. The session is then stamped valid from the latest change plus the margin, so one change causes one refresh. Session stores persist this stamp (Session.ClaimsIssuedAt); pgstore keeps it in the sealed secrets document.

docs.title: Replicas and restarts
docs.text:
Replicas of a monolith share the database, not memory. Each one polls sf_access_changes once every second or two, independent of request volume, and a restarted relying party replays the last token lifetime before it trusts its cache:

// Replicas sharing SystemAuth's database (PostgreSQL):
cache := relyingparty.NewRevocationCache(relyingparty.WithSuspectStart())
poller := relyingparty.NewAccessChangePoller(pgstore.NewAccessChangeSource(db), cache)
go poller.Run(ctx) // the first successful poll also ends suspect mode

// A relying party in another process, replaying through SystemAuth:
src := client.AccessChangesSource(client.ClientCredentialsToken(id, secret))
go relyingparty.ReplayWithRetry(ctx, src, cache, logger)

WithSuspectStart (or MarkSuspect) puts the cache in suspect mode: changes made while it was not listening are unknown, so only tokens issued at least one margin after it started are accepted, and the rest are answered "token expired" so clients refresh. A successful Replay, or the first successful poll, rebuilds the cache and ends suspect mode; a failure leaves it suspect, so a restart never widens the window in which a revoked token is honored. Replay retries with backoff and the server may start serving at once.

The poller re-reads from one margin behind its newest change, so a row that committed late with an earlier timestamp is still seen. Its interval is limited to 1 to 2 seconds. accesschange.NewSource(entClient) reads the same table through Ent.

SystemAuth serves GET /access-changes?since=<RFC 3339>[&limit=] when built with systemauth.WithAccessChanges(accesschange.NewSource(db)). The caller needs a token with the access_changes:read scope, for example from the client-credentials grant for a client registered with that scope. The response is {"changes": [{"principal_id", "organization_id", "changed_at", "reason"}], "next_since": ...}; next_since appears when more follow, and the source follows it.

docs.title: Back-channel events
docs.text:
A relying party in another process can be told at once instead of polling. Register an endpoint as the client's backchannel_logout_uri (an https URL, or http for a loopback host; ClientConfig.BackchannelLogoutURI, stored on sf_oauth_apps) and run SystemAuth's sender, passing it to the services that record changes:

bc := auth.NewBackchannel()
orgs := organization.NewService(db, organization.WithAccessChangeSink(bc))
go bc.Run(ctx)

For each change SystemAuth POSTs logout_token=<jwt> to every registered client: an OpenID Connect Back-Channel Logout token (typ logout+jwt, signed with the issuer key) with sub, aud (the client ID), jti, iat, exp and an events claim. The urn:systemforge:event:access_change event carries organization_id (absent for every organization), changed_at and reason; for deactivation and session revocation the standard http://schemas.openid.net/event/backchannel-logout event is added too. Delivery is queued, retried with exponential backoff until one maximum access-token lifetime after the change, and each failure is logged against the client ID; a 4xx other than 408 and 429 is not retried, and redirects are never followed. Every registered client receives every change; the token holds only opaque identifiers.

The receiver is relyingparty.BackchannelHandler(cache, client, relyingparty.WithBackchannelSessions(store)): it verifies the token against the issuer's keys (Client.VerifyLogoutToken: signature, issuer, audience, typ, jti, expiry, no nonce, a known event), records the access change into the cache, and on a logout event deletes the sessions of the sid, or of the sub when there is none. A repeated jti is refused, and a failure to end sessions answers 500 so SystemAuth retries. The BFF already serves it at <BasePath>/auth/backchannel-logout (BFF.BackchannelLogoutHandler() mounts it elsewhere), ending its own sessions and feeding BFFConfig.Revocation.

docs.title: Sessions and back-channel logout
docs.text: Each session records the SystemAuth sub and, when the ID token carries one, the SystemAuth session ID (sid). SessionStore.DeleteBySubject and DeleteBySID remove all matching sessions, which is what a back-channel logout receiver needs.

docs.title: Implementing PrincipalStore
docs.text:
The package is storage-agnostic. An application with its own Ent schema implements PrincipalStore over it; a principal entity using identity/ent/mixin.PrincipalMixin already has the unique, indexed sf_principal_id field:

type entPrincipals struct{ db *ent.Client }

func (s entPrincipals) FindBySubject(ctx context.Context, sub string) (*relyingparty.Principal, error) {
    id, err := uuid.Parse(sub)
    if err != nil {
        return nil, relyingparty.ErrPrincipalNotFound
    }
    p, err := s.db.Principal.Query().Where(principal.SfPrincipalIDEQ(id)).Only(ctx)
    if ent.IsNotFound(err) {
        return nil, relyingparty.ErrPrincipalNotFound
    }
    if err != nil {
        return nil, err
    }
    return toRP(p), nil
}

// LinkSubject: UPDATE ... SET sf_principal_id = ? WHERE id = ?; map the unique
// violation to relyingparty.ErrSubjectLinked. CreatePrincipal: insert with
// sf_principal_id and a verified email; map unique violations to
// ErrSubjectLinked / ErrEmailConflict.

MemoryPrincipalStore is provided for development and tests.

docs.title: Programmatic clients
docs.text:
BearerMiddleware accepts, in order:

  • Authorization: Bearer <JWT> — a SystemAuth JWT access token, verified against the JWKS (iss, exp, and Config.AccessTokenAudience when set). Its sub must already be linked to a local principal (the user signed in to the app once). Client-credentials tokens (sub = client_id) are accepted as a client principal only with AllowClientTokens.
  • Authorization: Bearer <api key> or X-API-Key — validated by an APIKeyValidator (*apikey.Service); the key's owner is the principal and an organization-scoped key only carries that organization's membership.
  • The BFF session cookie, when Sessions is set.

Failures return 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="api" (plus error="invalid_token" for bad credentials).

docs.title: Managed principals
docs.text:
A relying party can create and manage managed principals, people without an email whose accounts are controlled by managers, without holding SystemAuth's database. SystemAuth serves the manager API at /managed-principals when managed principals are enabled, and the application calls it with the signed-in manager's access token through managedprincipal/mpclient:

import "github.com/plexusone/systemforge/identity/managedprincipal/mpclient"

mp := mpclient.New(issuer+"/managed-principals", httpClient)
learnerID, err := mp.Create(ctx, managerToken, mpclient.CreateInput{
    DisplayName: "Robin",
    Role:        "educator",
})

The client must have managed_principals: true and the systemforge:managed_principals scope, and the manager's token must be granted it. The client is taken from the token, the caller is the only initial manager, and further managers join by invitation or claim. See Managed Principals for the routes, their permissions, and configuration.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• JWT access tokens are verified statelessly: a revoked token stays usable until it expires (default 10 minutes, at most 15) unless the application configures a RevocationCache (see Access changes). Opaque SystemAuth access tokens are not accepted by BearerMiddleware (no introspection client yet).
  • The default session and login-state stores are in-memory; use relyingparty/pgstore (encrypted at rest) or another shared implementation in production. See Production Stores.
  • Back-channel notifications are sent only to clients that register a backchannel_logout_uri; there is no front-channel logout.

docs.title: Social Login (GitHub / Google)
docs.text:
SystemAuth can act as the single identity provider for "log in with GitHub / Google". Upstream OAuth credentials live only in the SystemAuth deployment. Relying-party applications do not implement social login themselves: they send users to SystemAuth's /oauth/authorize as OIDC clients, and SystemAuth signs the user in upstream when needed.

See ADR-002 (docs/design/adrs/ADR-002-centralized-social-login-systemauth.md) for the design rationale.

docs.title: Routes
docs.text:
When social_login is configured, these routes are mounted next to the OAuth endpoints:

Route Purpose GET /login?return_to=... Provider chooser. Redirects straight to the provider when only one is configured. GET /login/{provider}?return_to=... Starts the upstream authorization-code flow (github or google). GET /login/{provider}/callback Upstream callback. Resolves the principal, sets the __Host-sf_login session, and redirects to return_to. GET /logout?return_to=... Renders a sign-out confirmation form (never signs out by itself). POST /logout Deletes the login session, clears the cookie, revokes all of the principal's access and refresh tokens, and redirects (303) to the validated return_to (default default_redirect). GET /consent?return_to=<authorize URL> Consent page naming the client and the requested scopes (only when skip_consent is off). POST /consent Records the decision. allow saves the grant and resumes /oauth/authorize; deny returns error=access_denied to the client's redirect URI.

/oauth/authorize sends unauthenticated users to /login?return_to=<authorize URL>, so after login the authorization request resumes and the relying party receives an authorization code. No token ever appears in a redirect URL. An idp_hint=github|google authorization parameter skips the chooser.

Applications consume this through the identity/relyingparty package; see Relying Parties.

docs.title: Logout
docs.text: Relying parties sign the user out of SystemAuth by sending the browser to GET /logout?return_to=https://app.example.com/ (a confirmation page) or by submitting a form POST /logout from their own origin. The POST must carry an Origin (or Referer) of the issuer or one of allowed_redirect_origins; anything else is rejected with 403. Logout revokes every token issued to the principal, for every client, through the storage's SubjectTokenRevoker support (implemented by MemoryStorage and EntStorage).

docs.title: Consent
docs.text: With skip_consent: false, /oauth/authorize sends a signed-in user to /consent the first time a client asks for a set of scopes. The page is deliberately minimal (client name, scope descriptions, Allow/Deny). Decisions are kept in a ConsentStore; with EntStorage the default is the database (sf_consent_grants), otherwise in-memory (users are asked again after a restart). See Production Stores. The consent form is protected by a CSRF token derived from the login session, a same-origin check, and frame-ancestors 'none'. Deployments whose clients are all first-party should set skip_consent: true instead.

docs.title: Refresh tokens
docs.text:
SystemAuth issues refresh tokens to clients granted offline_access (and the refresh_token grant). They are rotated on every use:

  • Each refresh returns a new refresh token and retires the previous refresh and access tokens.
